Chapter 1 — Introduction: how is it examined?
column4:
7 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in all 41 papers  \(\cdot\) 6 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 337 marks, 9.9 % of every mark ever set  \(\cdot\) no numerical component.
Read this first:
  • Every paper opens here. Q1 is nearly always a two- or three-part Introduction question for 7 or 8 marks, and it is the cheapest 8 marks in the subject.
  • Four questions carry the whole chapter:
    • Turing test TOP 10 \(-\) what it is, when it is passed, what a machine needs to pass it.
    • Applications of AI TOP 8 \(-\) almost always the tail of the Turing-test question, never a question on its own.
    • Intelligent agents HOT 7 \(-\) define, then the types, with diagrams.
    • PEAS HOT 7 \(-\) write the four rows for a named system.
  • The one idea everything hangs off is the four-approaches grid (§1.1). Thinking Vs acting, humanly Vs rationally. Every define AI answer is that grid; the Turing test is the acting humanly box; the rational agent is the acting rationally box. Learn the grid and three separate questions collapse into one.
  • Pairs the examiner reliably asks together: Turing test \(+\) applications (7 papers), intelligent agent \(+\) PEAS (6 papers), knowledge \(+\) learning (5 papers).
  • PEAS is worth memorising cold. It is asked in 9 papers for a named system (taxi, medical diagnosis, self-driving car, robot in a manufacturing plant, medicine-delivery drone) and no lecture deck works a full example. Four rows, four columns, §1.4.
  • Do not write history as prose. The examiner wants year \(\rightarrow\) event lines, and one of those questions asks specifically which period was the “AI research failure” and why.

column1: Define Artificial Intelligence. Describe AI and its subfields
column4:
Definitions worth quoting
  • Elaine Rich: the study of how to make computers do things at which, at the moment, people are better.
    • Best one to write: it explains why the field keeps moving. Once machines win at a task, it stops counting as AI.
  • Kurzweil: the art of creating machines that perform functions requiring intelligence when performed by people.
  • Minsky: the science of making computers do things that require intelligence when done by humans.
  • Working definition: a branch of computer science that builds machines which solve complex problems in a human-like fashion.
Intelligence, unpacked
  • Ability to understand, to reason, to learn, to create.
  • No machine has all four. That gap is the whole subject.
Intelligent behaviour: three task classes
  • Everyday tasks: recognise a friend, recognise a caller's voice, translate a language, interpret a photograph, talk, cook a meal.
    • Easiest for people, hardest for machines. Worth saying: this is Moravec's paradox.
  • Formal tasks: prove a theorem, do calculus, play chess, checkers, Go.
  • Expert tasks: engineering design, medical diagnosis, financial analysis.
    • Hardest for people, easiest for machines, because the knowledge is explicit and narrow.
Subfields of AI
  • Search and problem solving \(\cdot\) knowledge representation and reasoning \(\cdot\) planning \(\cdot\) machine learning \(\cdot\) neural networks \(\cdot\) expert systems \(\cdot\) natural language processing \(\cdot\) machine vision and image processing \(\cdot\) robotics \(\cdot\) fuzzy logic and evolutionary computing.

column1: The four approaches to AI (the grid everything sits on)
column4:
Humanly (measured against people)Rationally (measured against an ideal)
ThinkingThinking humanly \(-\) the cognitive modelling approach. Build a precise theory of how the human mind works, then write it as a program. Needs psychology and introspection. Eg General Problem Solver, Newell and Simon, 1961.
Criticism: we have no scientific theory of the brain's internal activity, so the model cannot be verified.		Thinking rationally \(-\) the laws of thought approach. Encode correct reasoning as formal logic, then let an inference engine derive conclusions. Eg “Socrates is a man; all men are mortal; therefore Socrates is mortal.”
Criticism: informal, uncertain knowledge is very hard to state in logical notation, and solving a problem in principle is not solving it in practice.
ActingActing humanly \(-\) the Turing test approach. Model what people do, not how they think. Judged purely on external behaviour. Eg ELIZA.
This is the box §1.2 lives in.		Acting rationally \(-\) the rational agent approach. Do whatever is expected to achieve the best outcome. Covers reflex action, which needs no reasoning at all.
The approach modern AI actually uses, because it is general and it can be measured. This is the box §1.3 lives in.
How to answer “justify that X is part of AI”
  • Name the box, give its yardstick, give an example system, give its criticism.
  • Thinking rationally is part of AI because logic-based inference (FOPL, resolution, Ch 4) derives new true facts from known ones without any human in the loop.
  • Acting rationally is part of AI because an agent that maximises its performance measure in an uncertain environment is doing what intelligence is for, whether or not it reasons the way people do.
  • Say which is preferred and why: acting rationally, because rationality is mathematically well defined and generalises, while “humanly” needs a theory of mind we do not have.
Types of AI by capability
  • Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI, weak AI): one task or one narrow domain. Everything that exists today. Eg spam filter, chess engine, a speech recogniser.
  • Artificial General Intelligence (AGI, strong AI): any intellectual task a human can do, transferring skill between domains. Does not exist.
  • Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI): exceeds human ability in every field including creativity and social skill. Hypothetical.
Weak Vs strong AI, the philosophical sense
  • Weak: the machine simulates thinking.
  • Strong: the machine genuinely has a mind.
  • Searle's Chinese Room argues strong AI is impossible: symbol manipulation is not understanding. verified/added

column1: What is the Turing test? When is a machine said to have passed it?
column4:
The setup
  • Proposed by Alan Turing, 1950, in Computing Machinery and Intelligence, to replace the unanswerable “can machines think?” with a testable question, “can machines behave intelligently?”
  • Three rooms, no sight or sound between them:
    • a human interrogator,
    • a human respondent,
    • the machine.
  • The interrogator questions both over a text-only channel (a teletype, so voice and handwriting give nothing away) and must say which is which.
When it is passed
  • The machine passes when the interrogator cannot do better than chance, i.e. is wrong about half the time.
  • Turing's own operational figure: an average interrogator has under a 70 % chance of identifying correctly after 5 minutes of questioning, so the machine fools them 30 % of the time.
  • Write both: the half-the-time principle, then the 5-minute / 30 % figure as the concrete criterion.
The four capabilities a machine needs to pass
  • Natural Language Processing \(\rightarrow\) to communicate in English at all.
  • Knowledge Representation \(\rightarrow\) to store what it knows and what it is told during the interview.
  • Automated Reasoning \(\rightarrow\) to answer questions and draw new conclusions from what is stored.
  • Machine Learning \(\rightarrow\) to adapt to new circumstances and detect patterns it was not given.
Total Turing test adds two more
  • The plain test deliberately avoids physical contact, so it never tests perception or manipulation. The total Turing test puts a video link and a hatch for passing objects into the setup, adding:
    • Computer vision \(\rightarrow\) to perceive objects,
    • Robotics \(\rightarrow\) to manipulate them and move about.
  • 6 capabilities in total. (77 Ch and 76 Bh ask for the total test by name)
ELIZA, the standard example
  • Written at MIT, 1964–66, by Joseph Weizenbaum. First script DOCTOR, imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist.
  • Mechanism: a table of syntactic patterns, each with a canned reply that echoes part of the input back after simple substitutions (my \(\rightarrow\) your). No understanding, no knowledge base, no memory.
  • Weizenbaum was disturbed by the reaction: psychiatrists thought it clinically useful and users confided in it.
  • The exam point: ELIZA shows a machine can be taken for a human without any intelligence behind it, which is the standing objection to the test itself.
Importance of the Turing test
  • Turns a philosophical question into an operational, repeatable one.
  • Sets a behavioural yardstick: judge output, not internal mechanism, so it does not need a theory of mind.
  • Defines the research agenda: its four required capabilities are four whole subfields of AI, and this syllabus is mostly those four.
  • Still the benchmark by which conversational systems are reported.
Limitations
  • Rewards deception, not competence. Passing needs human-like error and delay, so a machine that answers arithmetic instantly and correctly fails.
  • Not reproducible and not mathematically definable; the result depends on the interrogator.
  • Tests only what people happen to do, so it caps machine intelligence at human behaviour rather than measuring intelligence itself.

column1: If the Turing test is passed, does that show computers exhibit intelligence?
column4:
Case for “yes”
  • Intelligence has no agreed internal definition, so behaviour is the only thing that can be measured at all.
  • We attribute intelligence to other people on exactly this evidence, and nothing else. Refusing the machine the same inference is inconsistent.
  • Passing is not a trick: it requires NLP, knowledge, reasoning and learning working together, which is a real and general capability.
Case for “no” (the stronger answer)
  • Imitation is not cognition. ELIZA fooled people with pattern substitution and knew nothing.
  • Searle's Chinese Room: a person following symbol-manipulation rules can answer Chinese questions perfectly while understanding no Chinese. Syntax does not give semantics. verified/added
  • Tests only one narrow channel, text conversation. Says nothing about perception, physical skill, creativity or goals.
  • Recommended stance: passing shows intelligent behaviour, not intelligence. It is a sufficient test of appearing intelligent and a necessary-but-not-sufficient test of being so.
Reverse Turing test 34
verified/added 81 Bh 3, 80 Ch 4  \(\cdot\)  2 papers, both under 6 marks, so no tier chip  \(\cdot\)  not in any lecture deck in this folder, researched and added, and it has been asked twice in the last three years
What it is
  • The roles are swapped: a machine interrogates, and a human must prove it is human.
  • The test succeeds when the machine can tell human from machine, which is the opposite goal to Turing's.
  • CAPTCHA is the everyday instance: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. A distorted-text or image-grid challenge that people pass easily and programs do not.
Turing Vs reverse Turing, side by side
  • Who judges: human, Vs machine.
  • Who is on trial: machine, Vs human.
  • Passed when: the judge cannot tell them apart, Vs the judge can.
  • Purpose: measure machine intelligence, Vs block bots from a web service.
  • Note the irony worth a mark: every CAPTCHA solved by a program is a small Turing test passed, which is why CAPTCHAs keep getting harder.

column1: What is an intelligent agent? Explain the different types with examples
column4:
Definitions to write first
  • Agent: anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators.
    • Human agent: eyes and ears as sensors; hands, legs and mouth as actuators.
    • Robotic agent: cameras and infrared range finders as sensors; motors as actuators.
    • Software agent: keystrokes and file contents as sensors; screen writes and network packets as actuators.
  • Percept: what the agent perceives at one instant. Percept sequence: everything it has ever perceived.
  • Agent function maps percept sequence to action, \(f: P^{*} \rightarrow A\).
  • Agent program is the concrete implementation that runs on the hardware.
  • Agent \(=\) architecture \(+\) program. One line, and it is often a mark on its own.
The agent, its sensors and actuators, and the environment loop. Draw this first in any agent answer; every later diagram is this one with a box added inside the agent.
Rational agent
  • For each possible percept sequence, a rational agent selects the action expected to maximise its performance measure, given the evidence in the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge it has.
  • Performance measure: the objective criterion for success, fixed by the designer, not the agent. Eg for a vacuum cleaner: dirt collected, time taken, electricity used, noise made.
  • Rationality is not omniscience. An omniscient agent knows the actual outcome of its actions; that is impossible. Rationality maximises expected performance given what is knowable.
  • Autonomy: an agent is autonomous when its behaviour is determined by its own percepts and experience rather than only by built-in knowledge. Autonomy requires learning.
  • Information gathering and exploration are rational acts: it can be rational to act now purely to get a better percept later.
Environment properties (worth 2 marks when asked)
  • Fully Vs partially observable: can the sensors see the whole relevant state?
  • Deterministic Vs stochastic: does the next state follow from the current state and action alone?
  • Episodic Vs sequential: does the current action affect later ones?
  • Static Vs dynamic: does the world change while the agent deliberates?
  • Discrete Vs continuous: countable states and actions, or not?
  • Single agent Vs multi-agent: is anything else optimising against it?
  • Eg a taxi driver's world is partially observable, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous and multi-agent. The hardest kind on every axis.
The five agent types, in increasing generality
1. Table-driven agent
  • Holds a lookup table indexed by the entire percept history, and reads the next action out of it.
  • Impractical: the table grows exponentially with the length of the history. A taxi with a camera would need more entries than there are atoms in the universe.
  • Included only to show why the later types exist.
2. Simple reflex agent
  • Acts on the current percept only, through condition-action (if-then) rules. Implemented as a production system (Ch 2).
  • Stateless: no memory of past world states.
  • Eg if car-in-front-is-braking then initiate-braking; the vacuum-cleaner agent that sucks whenever the current square is dirty.
  • Fails when the environment is partially observable, and can loop forever in that case.
3. Model-based reflex agent
  • Keeps internal state \(=\) the part of the world it cannot currently see.
  • Needs two pieces of knowledge, together called the model of the world:
    • how the world evolves on its own,
    • what my actions do to it.
  • Fixes partial observability. Eg a taxi remembering which cars are in the lanes it cannot see right now.
4. Goal-based agent
  • Adds goal information describing desirable situations, and asks “what will it be like if I do action A?”
  • Considers the future, so it can plan and search (Ch 3), not just react.
  • Far more flexible: change the goal and the behaviour changes, with no rules rewritten. A reflex agent needs every rule rewritten.
  • Eg a taxi told to go to a different destination.
5. Utility-based agent
  • A goal is binary: reached or not. A utility function maps a state to a number saying how happy the agent is there.
  • Needed for two cases a goal cannot settle:
    • conflicting goals \(-\) fast Vs safe Vs cheap: utility trades them off;
    • uncertain goals \(-\) pick the action with the highest expected utility.
  • Eg a taxi choosing between a quick risky route and a slow safe one.
Learning agent (asked by name, 75 Bh 8)
  • Any of the four above, wrapped in machinery that improves it with experience. Four parts:
    • Performance element \(-\) the old agent: takes percepts, chooses actions.
    • Critic \(-\) judges the outcome against a fixed performance standard and reports feedback. The standard must be external, or the agent could just lower its own bar.
    • Learning element \(-\) uses that feedback to change the performance element.
    • Problem generator \(-\) deliberately suggests exploratory actions that look suboptimal now, so the agent discovers better behaviour later.
  • The exam point: learning is what makes an agent truly autonomous, which is the link straight to §1.9 and to Ch 6.

column1: Define PEAS. Give the PEAS information for a named system
column4:
What and why
  • Before designing an agent, its task environment must be specified. PEAS is that specification:
    • P \(-\) Performance measure: what counts as success. Must be about the environment, not the agent's internal state.
    • E \(-\) Environment: what the agent operates in and on.
    • A \(-\) Actuators: how it acts.
    • S \(-\) Sensors: how it perceives.
  • Why it must come first: the performance measure decides what “rational” means, and the sensors and actuators decide what the agent can even represent. Design before PEAS is design without a specification.
Three mistakes that cost marks
  • Writing the performance measure as “work well”. Give measurable terms: safe, fast, legal, comfortable, maximise profit.
  • Putting an actuator in the sensor row. A horn is an actuator; a microphone is a sensor.
  • Forgetting that a display is an actuator when the agent uses it to tell a person something.
Ready-made answers for the systems actually asked
  • Taxi driver (81 Ash)
    • P: safe, fast, legal, comfortable trip, maximise profits.
    • E: roads, other traffic, pedestrians, customers, weather.
    • A: steering, accelerator, brake, indicator, horn, display.
    • S: cameras, sonar, speedometer, GPS, odometer, accelerometer, engine sensors, keyboard.
  • Medical diagnosis system (80 Ba)
    • P: healthy patient, minimise costs and lawsuits.
    • E: patient, hospital, staff.
    • A: screen display of questions, tests, diagnoses, treatments, referrals.
    • S: keyboard entry of symptoms, findings and the patient's answers.
  • Part-picking robot in a plant (81 Ash, 82 Ka)
    • P: percentage of parts placed in the correct bin.
    • E: conveyor belt with parts, the bins.
    • A: jointed arm, gripper.
    • S: camera, joint angle sensors.
Self-driving car (82 Ba 6)
  • P: reach the destination safely, obey traffic law, minimise journey time and fuel, ride comfort, zero collisions.
  • E: roads and lane markings, other vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists, traffic signals, road signs, weather, the passenger.
  • A: steering, throttle, brakes, gear selection, indicators, horn, headlights, passenger display and speaker.
  • S: cameras, LIDAR, radar, ultrasonic parking sensors, GPS, IMU and accelerometer, wheel-speed sensors, microphone.
Medicine-delivery drone (82 Bh 5) verified/added
  • No source note covers this one; state your assumptions, as the paper explicitly allows, then give four clean rows.
  • P: medicine delivered intact, to the right address, within the time window, maximum payload per charge, no collision, no airspace violation.
  • E: air corridor, buildings, terrain and hills, trees and power lines, weather and wind, other drones and aircraft, the recipient, the dispatch centre.
  • A: rotors and motors, payload release hatch, landing gear, status lights, radio downlink to the dispatch centre.
  • S: GPS, camera, LIDAR or ultrasonic altimeter, IMU and gyroscope, barometer, wind and temperature sensors, battery gauge, radio uplink.

column1: Differentiate natural and artificial intelligence. Can AI replace humans?
column4:
Human intelligenceArtificial intelligence
OriginBiological, inherited and grownEngineered, programmed and trained
Learns fromA few examples, plus intuition and contextVery large data sets, no context of its own
SpeedSlow, tires, needs restConstant, no fatigue, runs continuously
AccuracyErrs when tired or emotionalExact and repeatable within its domain
BreadthGeneral: transfers skill to a new taskNarrow: fails outside the trained task
CreativityOriginal ideas, imaginationRecombines what it was trained on
EmotionEmpathy, judgement, ethicsNone; only what is coded as a measure
AdaptingHandles the wholly unfamiliarNeeds retraining or reprogramming
CostSalary, training timeHigh to build, near-zero to copy
Can AI replace humans? Answer: in tasks, yes; in roles, no
  • Where it replaces: repetitive, rule-bound, data-heavy work. Data entry, first-line support, defect inspection, routine diagnosis, translation drafts.
  • Where it cannot, and why:
    • No common sense outside the training distribution.
    • No moral or legal responsibility; someone must be accountable.
    • No genuine creativity or empathy, both needed in teaching, care, negotiation, design.
    • Depends on data that people must collect, label and correct.
  • Conclusion to write: AI is a tool that shifts human work up the skill ladder, not a replacement for the worker. The realistic risk is displacement of specific tasks, not obsolescence of people.
Importance and advantages of AI
  • Automates repetitive work \(\rightarrow\) people move to judgement work.
  • Better decisions: finds patterns in data volumes no person can read.
  • Available always: no fatigue, no shift limits, consistent output.
  • Works where people cannot: deep sea, space, reactor cores, disaster zones, mine clearance.
  • Fewer human errors in exact, repetitive tasks.
  • Reaches scarce expertise: an expert system puts specialist knowledge in a village clinic.
  • Speeds research: drug discovery, protein folding, materials.
Growth areas (71 Bh)
  • Machine learning and deep learning \(\cdot\) NLP and speech \(\cdot\) computer vision \(\cdot\) robotics and autonomous vehicles \(\cdot\) expert and decision-support systems \(\cdot\) recommender systems \(\cdot\) medical imaging and diagnosis.
Disadvantages and limitations (78 Ba 2)
  • Cost: high to build, and needs specialists to maintain.
  • No common sense: fails absurdly on inputs slightly outside its training.
  • No creativity: recombines, does not originate.
  • Job displacement in routine occupations.
  • Opaque: a neural network cannot explain its decision, which is unacceptable in medicine and law.
  • Inherits bias from its training data, then applies it at scale.
  • No ethics or accountability, so misuse is easy: surveillance, autonomous weapons, deepfakes.
  • Data-hungry and energy-hungry.
Two named ethical positions worth a line
  • Weizenbaum (1976): a real AI would be autonomous and would not share our motives or ethics, so the research is unethical.
  • Asimov's three laws of robotics: do not harm a human or by inaction allow harm; obey humans; protect itself. Precedence runs lower number first.

column1: Describe AI and its subfields; which fields contributed to AI?
column4:
What each field gave AI
  • Philosophy: logic, the idea of the mind as a physical system, foundations of learning, language and rationality.
  • Mathematics: formal representation and proof, algorithms, computation, decidability and intractability, probability, statistics, linear algebra.
  • Psychology: perception, motor control, adaptation, and the experimental methods behind cognitive modelling.
  • Economics: formal theory of rational decision, utility, game theory.
    • This is where the utility in a utility-based agent comes from.
  • Linguistics: grammar, syntax and knowledge representation. NLP sits directly on it.
  • Neuroscience: the physical substrate of mental activity. Neural networks are a deliberate, loose imitation of it.
  • Control theory: stability, feedback, optimal agent design. The agent-environment loop is a control loop.
  • Computer engineering: the machines fast enough to run any of it.
Fields AI overlaps with, and how it differs
  • Machine learning is a subfield of AI, not a synonym: AI also covers search, logic and planning, which do not learn at all.
  • Data mining (Ch 6 and the Data Mining elective) shares algorithms but aims at discovering patterns in stored data; AI aims at acting well.
  • Robotics supplies the body; AI supplies the decision making.
  • Cognitive science is the joint enterprise of AI and psychology: AI wants machines that work, cognitive science wants a theory of the mind.
  • Operations research shares optimisation and search but assumes a fully specified model.
Programming languages of AI
  • LISP: McCarthy, late 1950s. Functional, symbolic, interactive.
  • PROLOG: France 1970, developed at Edinburgh 1975–79. Logic programming: a program is facts \(+\) rules, and running it is inference. The syllabus lab is in one of these two.

column1: Discuss the brief history of AI with chronological development
column4:
The founding era, 1943–1979
YearEvent
1943McCulloch and Pitts: Boolean circuit model of the neuron. The first neural network.
1950Turing, Computing Machinery and Intelligence. The Turing test.
1956Dartmouth meeting: the term “Artificial Intelligence” is adopted. The birth of the field.
1950sSamuel's checkers program, which learned and beat its author; Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist; Gelernter's Geometry Theorem Prover (1959).
1957Rosenblatt's Perceptron.
1958McCarthy defines LISP and describes the Advice Taker.
1963McCarthy starts the Stanford AI lab. Slagle's SAINT solves first-year calculus.
1965Robinson's resolution: a complete theorem-proving algorithm for first-order logic. Ch 4 is built on it.
1966ELIZA, Weizenbaum.
1969–79Knowledge-based and expert systems: DENDRAL, MYCIN, SHRDLU. Minsky's frames (1975).
Industry, science and the modern era, 1980–
YearEvent
1980AI becomes an industry. XCON saves DEC an estimated $40 million a year.
1986Neural networks return, on back-propagation.
1987AI becomes a science: results measured against benchmarks, and statistics and probability adopted.
1995The intelligent agent becomes the unifying idea of the field.
1997Deep Blue beats Kasparov at chess.
2011IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!
2016AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go.
2020–Large language models, GPT-3 onward.
  • Write it as a table, not as prose. Year, then event, then one clause on why it mattered. Dates with no significance score badly.
The “AI research failure” period
  • Two collapses in funding and confidence, both called AI winters. The question almost always means the first.
  • First AI winter, 1966–73, the “dose of reality”. In 1957 Simon predicted a computer chess champion and a major theorem proved within 10 years; both took roughly 40. Three reasons it failed:
    • No subject knowledge. Early programs succeeded by syntactic manipulation alone. Machine translation is the standard example: word-by-word substitution with no meaning behind it.
    • Intractability. Programs solved toy problems by trying combinations of steps. Scaling the problem exploded the search, and the 1965 discovery of NP-completeness explained why faster hardware could not fix it.
    • Structural limits. Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons (1969) proved a single-layer perceptron cannot represent XOR, and neural network research nearly stopped for fifteen years. This is the same XOR result you prove in Ch 7.
The second winter, and what ended both
  • Second AI winter, late 1980s to early 1990s: the expert-system market collapsed. The systems were brittle outside their narrow domain, could not learn, and cost more to maintain than they saved.
  • What ended each:
    • the first ended with knowledge-based systems \(-\) stop searching blindly and put the domain knowledge in;
    • the second ended with statistical machine learning, then cheap parallel hardware and large data sets.
  • The pattern behind both, and the sentence that earns the last mark: each winter followed a period of over-promising on a technique that did not scale, and each ended when the field adopted a different technique rather than more of the same.

column1: Discuss fields of daily life where AI has been applied
column4:
How to answer for full marks
  • The question says explain two fields, not list ten. A list scores badly.
  • For each field give: the task, the AI technique behind it, and a named example. Three sentences each is the whole answer.
  • 81 Ch asks for applications as a problem-solving tool, so frame each one as “the problem, and how AI solves it”.
Two safe choices, worked
  • Healthcare. Problem: expert diagnosis is scarce and slow. Technique: neural networks over medical images (Ch 7), plus rule-based expert systems for diagnosis. Examples: tumour detection on CT and MRI, IBM Watson for Oncology, diabetic-retinopathy screening from retinal photographs.
  • Transport. Problem: driving needs continuous perception and decision under uncertainty. Technique: computer vision and sensor fusion feeding a utility-based agent, plus A* and its variants for route search (Ch 3). Examples: self-driving cars, Google Maps ETA prediction, Pathao and inDrive dispatch and pricing.
The wider list, grouped
  • Everyday software: search-engine ranking and autocomplete, social-media feeds, Netflix and YouTube recommendation, spam filters, photo tagging.
  • Language: machine translation, speech recognition, chatbots and virtual assistants, Nepali NLP tools (Ch 7).
  • Finance: fraud and money-laundering detection, credit scoring, algorithmic trading.
  • Industry and agriculture: robotic assembly and part picking, predictive maintenance, visual quality inspection, crop-disease detection from leaf images, yield prediction.
  • Games: Deep Blue, AlphaGo, and the bots in Dota 2 and PUBG.
  • Science and space: astronomical object classification, protein folding, space-mission monitoring, drug discovery.
  • Public services: weather and flood forecasting, traffic signal control, disaster response, biometric identification.
Nepal-specific examples, if the question invites them
  • Pathao and inDrive dispatch \(\cdot\) eSewa and Khalti fraud detection \(\cdot\) Nepali speech and OCR \(\cdot\) landslide and flood early warning \(\cdot\) crop-disease apps.

column1: What is knowledge and learning? Why are they important?
column4:
DataInformationKnowledge
WhatRaw facts, unorganisedData processed into a meaningful, usable formInformation organised and understood, ready to act on
FormNumbers, symbols, a databaseTables, reports, summariesRules, procedures, models
Answersnothing on its ownwho, what, where, whenhow and why
Example\(V=12\), \(I=6\), \(R=2\)\(V = I \times R\) holds for these readingsUse \(V=IR\) to design a circuit
  • Intelligence sits one step above knowledge: the ability to use knowledge to solve new problems and adapt to new situations.
  • Write the chain: data \(\rightarrow\) information \(\rightarrow\) knowledge \(\rightarrow\) intelligence. Each step adds structure and context.
Knowledge, and why AI needs it
  • Knowledge: the condition of knowing something with familiarity gained through experience or association; what lets us explore and decide.
  • Stored by people in natural language, by machines as symbols, strings and structures.
  • Forms it takes: simple facts, relations between concepts, associations, inheritance hierarchies, procedures.
  • Importance: enough knowledge is what produces intelligence. A search algorithm with no domain knowledge is blind (Ch 3); the same algorithm with a heuristic is informed and vastly faster. Knowledge is what turns search into intelligence.
  • The three designer problems (they run through Ch 4 and Ch 5):
    • Knowledge acquisition \(-\) getting it out of the domain and its experts.
    • Knowledge representation \(-\) encoding it: logic, semantic nets, frames, rules.
    • Knowledge manipulation \(-\) inferring new conclusions from it.
Learning
  • Herbert Simon (1983): “Learning is the phenomenon of knowledge acquisition in the absence of explicit programming.”
  • Fuller form: learning denotes changes in the system that are adaptive, in the sense that they let it do the same task, or a task drawn from the same population, more efficiently and more effectively next time.
  • Three factors in any learning system:
    • Changes \(-\) what in the system is altered, and how it is represented.
    • Generalisation \(-\) performance must improve on similar tasks, not only the one seen. Without this it is memorisation.
    • Improvement \(-\) the change must not degrade performance; the system must detect and prevent that.
  • Knowledge Vs learning in one line: knowledge is the content an agent holds; learning is the process that changes that content.
“Learning is an essential characteristic for intelligent agents”
  • Agree, and justify in four steps:
    • The designer cannot foresee every situation. A fixed rule table is only as good as its author's imagination, and the table-driven agent shows how quickly enumeration becomes impossible.
    • Environments change. Roads are rebuilt, spam changes its wording, prices move. A non-learning agent's performance decays with no fault of its own.
    • Autonomy requires it. An agent whose behaviour comes only from built-in knowledge is running the designer's intelligence, not its own. Learning is exactly what makes it autonomous.
    • The Turing test demands it. Machine learning is one of the four capabilities needed to pass, so an agent that cannot learn cannot be judged intelligent on the field's own benchmark.
  • Example to close with: a spam filter shipped with fixed rules is beaten within weeks; one that learns from each user's marking of messages keeps working. Same architecture, and learning is the only difference.

column1: Belief, hypothesis and knowledge
column4:
TermMeansConfidence
BeliefAny statement an agent holds to be true. It need not be verified and may turn out false.Subjective, unverified.
HypothesisA belief put forward for testing, backed by some evidence and held provisionally until confirmed or refuted.Justified belief, not yet confirmed.
KnowledgeA belief that is true and justified. Verified, and safe to reason from.Confirmed.

  • Why AI cares: an agent must act on beliefs, because it rarely has knowledge. That is precisely why Ch 4 needs probability and belief networks rather than plain logic.

Write the variables, the domains, the constraints and the carries, then reason. An answer with no working scores badly even when the arithmetic is right.

column1: Discuss the steps of problem solving. What is state space, successor function, goal test, path cost?
column4:
The four steps of problem solving
  • 1. Goal formulation \(-\) decide which world states count as success. Without it the agent has no way to prefer one action over another.
  • 2. Problem formulation \(-\) decide what states and actions to consider: the initial state, the successor function, the goal test and the path cost.
  • 3. Searching \(-\) find a sequence of actions leading from the initial state to a goal state, and choose the best such sequence. This is Ch 3.
  • 4. Execution \(-\) carry out the returned solution.
  • Order matters and is often the mark: goal before formulation, and the whole search happens before any action is executed.
State space representation
  • A state space is a set of nodes, one per state of the problem, joined by arcs representing the legal moves from one state to another, with a designated initial state and goal state.
  • When a problem is defined with all its states, it is a complete state space.
  • A state space is drawn as a directed graph, or a tree when no state repeats. Nodes are search states, arcs are the operators.
The five terms, with the 8-puzzle as the example
TermMeans, and for the 8-puzzle
StateA configuration of the world the agent may be in. The positions of the eight tiles and the blank.
Initial stateWhere the agent starts. The given starting board.
Successor functionGiven a state, returns the set of \(\langle\)action, resulting state\(\rangle\) pairs reachable in one step. Move the blank left, right, up or down.
Goal testDecides whether a state is a goal. Does the board match the given goal board?
Path costThe sum of the step costs along a path. 1 per move, so the cost is the number of moves.
  • A solution is a sequence of actions from the initial state to a goal state. An optimal solution is one of lowest path cost.
Why enumerating rules by hand does not work
  • The chess example (Insights §2.1.1). A knight at \((4,4)\) can move to \((2,3)\), \((2,5)\), \((3,2)\), \((3,6)\), \((5,2)\), \((5,6)\), \((6,3)\) and \((6,5)\).
  • Writing that out as a rule for every square gives an enormous rule set, and a chess position has around \(10^{120}\) complete game paths.
  • The fix, and the point of the example: describe the move as a pattern rather than a list, i.e. current position \(\pm\) (2 vertical \(+\) 1 horizontal) or (1 vertical \(+\) 2 horizontal). One rule replaces sixty-four.
  • This is exactly why the next section exists: a production system is a set of patterns, not a table of cases.
Problem space, and how to answer “define a problem”
  • Problem space \(=\) every state reachable, plus every action that can be taken, for a given goal. Eg the highways and cities of Nepal, when the problem is “get from Kathmandu to Dharan”.
  • The four-line answer that scores full marks for “what are the criteria for defining a problem” (82 Ka 2):
    • define the state space the problem lives in,
    • specify the initial state,
    • specify the goal state or a goal test,
    • specify the operators, with their preconditions and effects.
  • Add path cost if the question mentions optimality or “best”.

column1: What makes a problem well defined? List the characteristics
column4:
Definition
  • A problem is well defined when the agent knows, before it starts, exactly what the problem consists of. Formally, it is composed of:
    • an initial state,
    • the actions, given by a successor function,
    • a goal test, and
    • a path cost function.
  • Equivalently: the starting position, the allowable operations and the goal state are all clearly specified.
Characteristics (81 Ash asks for these by name, 8)
  • Unambiguous: one reading of what is being asked.
  • Complete: everything needed to solve it is stated; nothing has to be assumed.
  • Verifiable: the goal test can decide, mechanically, whether a state is a solution.
  • Finite and discrete state space, so the states can be enumerated.
  • Deterministic operators with known preconditions and effects.
  • Solvable in principle: at least one action sequence reaches the goal.
Well defined Vs ill defined, with examples
Well definedIll defined
GoalStated exactlyVague or subjective
StatesEnumerableOpen-ended
OperatorsFixed and knownNot fully known
TestMechanicalNeeds judgement
ExampleWater jug, 8-puzzle, chess, crypt-arithmetic“Write a good poem”, “design a beautiful building”, medical diagnosis from an unclear history
  • The 5-litre / 2-litre trap (81 Ash): the paper asks “is this a well-defined problem? Justify.” The answer is yes \(-\) the jugs, the pump, the operators and the target are all given, so every clause above is satisfied. Say that, then solve it. The companion works the solution.

column1: Problem types and how a problem is classified
column4:
By whether a move can be undone (Insights §2.2.1)
  • Ignorable \(-\) intermediate steps can simply be ignored; a wrong move costs nothing. Eg theorem proving, the water jug.
    • Solvable with a simple control strategy, no backtracking needed.
  • Recoverable \(-\) steps can be undone to get back to an earlier state. Eg the 8-puzzle.
    • Needs backtracking, so the control strategy must keep a history.
  • Irrecoverable \(-\) steps cannot be undone. Eg tic-tac-toe, chess.
    • Needs planning: consider the consequences before moving, because there is no second chance. This is why games need adversarial search (Ch 3).
  • Decomposable \(-\) the problem breaks into independent sub-problems whose answers combine. Eg symbolic integration, word puzzles.
By what the agent can see and predict
  • Single-state problem \(-\) deterministic and fully accessible. The agent always knows exactly which state it is in. Eg chess with the board in view.
  • Multiple-state problem \(-\) deterministic but inaccessible. The agent knows the rules but not its exact state, so it reasons over a set of possible states. Eg walking across a dark room. It may have no sensors at all.
  • Contingency problem \(-\) non-deterministic and inaccessible. The environment is partially observable or the actions are uncertain, so the agent must sense during execution and cannot plan the whole path in advance.
  • Exploration problem \(-\) the state space itself is unknown. The agent discovers states and operators as it acts. Eg a robot in an unmapped maze. The hardest of the four, and the one that needs learning.

column1: Define a production system. What are its essential terms? Explain its role with an example
column4:
Definition and the four components
  • A production system is a set of rules, each of the form \(C_i \rightarrow A_i\):
    • LHS \(C_i\), the pattern or condition, which decides whether the rule applies;
    • RHS \(A_i\), the action to perform if it is applied.
  • The right-hand side is read as an action recommendation, not as a logical conclusion. That is what separates a production rule from an implication.
  • The four components, and the answer to “essential terms”:
    • Rule base (production rules / rule memory) \(-\) the rules themselves.
    • Working memory (database) \(-\) the current state of the world, updated as rules fire.
    • Control strategy (inference engine) \(-\) decides which applicable rule to fire when several match, and when to stop.
    • Rule applier \(-\) carries out the chosen action.
  • The recognise-act cycle: match the rules against working memory \(\rightarrow\) conflict resolution picks one from the matching set \(\rightarrow\) act, i.e. fire it and update working memory \(\rightarrow\) repeat until the goal test passes or nothing matches.
Two requirements of a good control strategy
  • It must cause motion. A strategy that can pick the same rule forever never leaves the initial state.
  • It must be systematic. Choosing at random causes motion but wanders, and may revisit states endlessly.
  • Both are one-line answers and both are asked.
Example: the vacuum world
Pattern (LHS)Action (RHS)
\([A,\ \text{clean}]\)move Right
\([A,\ \text{dirty}]\)Suck
\([B,\ \text{clean}]\)move Left
\([B,\ \text{dirty}]\)Suck
  • The example that earns the marks is the water jug, whose eight production rules are in the companion. A question asking for a production system with an example almost always means that one.
  • Practical uses: expert systems (Ch 7), autonomous robots, and cognitive architectures modelling human reasoning such as ACT and SOAR.

column1: Problems solvable by production rules
column4:
Which problems suit a production system
  • The state can be written down compactly \(-\) the water jug's whole state is the pair \((x,y)\).
  • The legal moves are few, uniform and pattern-like, so a handful of rules covers every case.
  • Progress is made by repeatedly rewriting the state, not by evaluating a formula.
  • The goal is a recognisable pattern, so the goal test is a match.
The standard examples, and what each shows
  • Water jug \(-\) 8 rules, state \((x,y)\). The canonical answer.
  • 8-puzzle \(-\) 4 rules (move the blank up, down, left, right), state \(=\) the board. Shows a recoverable problem needing backtracking.
  • Missionaries and cannibals, farmer/wolf/goat/cabbage \(-\) rules with a safety precondition, which is what makes them interesting.
  • Tower of Hanoi \(-\) shows a decomposable problem.
  • Tic-tac-toe \(-\) shows an irrecoverable one, where rules alone are not enough and search over an opponent is needed.

column1: What is a Constraint Satisfaction Problem? Discuss it and list its constraints
column4:
Definition
  • A constraint satisfaction problem is a search procedure that operates in a space of constraints rather than a space of states.
  • States are defined by the values assigned to variables, and the goal test is a set of constraints those values must obey.
  • Formally, a CSP is the triple:
    • Variables \(X = \{X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\}\), the unknowns to be assigned.
    • Domains \(D = \{D_1, D_2, \dots, D_n\}\), the set of values each variable may take.
    • Constraints \(C = \{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_m\}\), the restrictions on which combinations of values are allowed.
  • Solution: an assignment of one domain value to every variable that violates no constraint. Write these three lines first in any crypt-arithmetic answer \(-\) they are worth marks on their own.
How it is solved: constraint propagation
  • Constraints are discovered and propagated as far as possible through the system. Where propagation stalls, a guess is made and added as a new constraint, and propagation resumes.
  • If the guess leads to a contradiction, backtrack and guess otherwise.
The two termination conditions
  • A contradiction is detected \(-\) no solution is consistent with the constraints now known.
  • Propagation has run out of steam \(-\) no further change can be made from current knowledge. Either a solution has been found, or a guess must be made.
  • Both are asked as a pair. Two lines, two marks.
Types of constraint
  • Unary \(-\) restricts one variable. Eg a leading letter is not 0.
  • Binary \(-\) relates two. Eg two regions differ in colour.
  • Higher-order \(-\) relates three or more. Eg a crypt-arithmetic column, \(D + E = 10C_1 + Y\).
  • Global / AllDiff \(-\) all variables take different values. Every crypt-arithmetic puzzle carries this one.
Other standard CSP examples
  • Map colouring \(-\) no two adjacent regions share a colour.
  • \(n\)-queens \(-\) no queen attacks another.
  • Class scheduling, VLSI layout, Sudoku.

column1: The crypt-arithmetic rules, and how to set the answer out
column4:
The rules, as every paper states them
  • Different letters denote different digits, and identical letters denote the same digit. This is the AllDiff constraint.
  • No leading letter may be 0.
  • Digits come from \(D = \{0,1,2,\dots,9\}\), so a puzzle with more than 10 distinct letters has no solution at all.
  • Any extra restriction the question prints overrides these.
The five-step method
(Insights §2.3)
  • 1. Write the sum in columns with a carry variable \(C_1, C_2, \dots\) above each column boundary.
  • 2. List \(X\), the set of variables.
  • 3. List \(D\), the domain.
  • 4. List \(C\): the leading-letter constraints, the AllDiff constraint, and one equation per column, \(\text{(column sum)} + C_{\text{in}} = 10\,C_{\text{out}} + \text{(result digit)}\).
  • 5. Reason column by column, redrawing the sum with the digits filled in after each deduction, until every letter is fixed. Close with the arithmetic check.
The three deductions that crack most puzzles
  • A carry out of the leftmost column can only be 1. If the answer is one digit longer than the addends, that leading digit is 1. This is what gives \(M = 1\) in SEND \(+\) MORE \(=\) MONEY immediately.
  • A letter added to itself. \(2N\) ends in the same letter only when that letter is 0 or 5, which is how TEN \(+\) TEN \(+\) FORTY \(=\) SIXTY is cracked.
  • A column where a letter repeats. If \(E + O + C_2 = N\) and also \(N + R + C_1 = E + 10\), substitute one into the other; the unknowns cancel.
Two things that lose marks
  • Giving only the digits. Most of these puzzles have many solutions, so an unjustified assignment cannot be marked. Show the columns.
  • Forgetting the AllDiff check at the end. It is the single commonest way a nearly-right answer fails, and it is what rules out \(B = 9\) in the \(AB + CD = AAA\) question (76 Bh).

column1: Formulate a game as a search problem
column4:
A game, defined as a search problem
  • Initial state \(-\) the board as set up, plus whose turn it is.
  • Operators \(-\) the legal moves.
  • Terminal test \(-\) says when the game is over.
  • Utility / payoff function \(-\) a number on each terminal state saying who won and by how much. Eg \(+1\) win, \(0\) draw, \(-1\) loss.
  • What makes it different from ordinary search: there is an opponent, choosing to make things as bad as possible for you. So a plan cannot be a fixed sequence of moves; it must be a strategy, an answer for every reply.
  • Two-player, perfect information, zero-sum games are solved by minimax (§3.4), made efficient by alpha-beta pruning.
Why games were chosen as an AI testbed
  • Rules are simple and unambiguous, so no knowledge acquisition problem gets in the way.
  • The state is fully observable, so no perception problem either.
  • Yet the search space is enormous, so brute force fails and real technique is needed. That combination is rare and useful.
  • Performance is measurable against human players.
Production systems Vs game playing
  • A production system fires rules against its own working memory.
  • A game must additionally model another agent choosing against it, which no rule set alone can express. That is precisely why Ch 3 needs a separate family of algorithms.

column1: Chapter 2 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
Every worked problem here opens with the exam question exactly as the paper prints it, typos and all, so it can be attempted from this document alone. Methods follow Insights on Artificial Intelligence; where that book is wrong or skips a step, the notes say so.  \(\cdot\) Every answer in this file is machine-checked by verify.py.
The five things everything here is built on:
  • 1. A crypt-arithmetic column is an equation. \((\text{column sum}) + C_{\text{in}} = 10\,C_{\text{out}} + (\text{result digit})\). Every deduction in §2.N.1 comes from one of these.
  • 2. A carry is 0 or 1. Adding two digits plus a carry gives at most \(9+9+1=19\). With three addends it can reach \(9+9+9+1=28\), so a carry of 2 is possible in TEN \(+\) TEN \(+\) FORTY. Nothing else in these papers has three addends.
  • 3. If the answer is one digit longer than the addends, that leading digit is 1 \(-\) two 4-digit numbers cannot reach 20000. This single line gives \(M = 1\) in SEND \(+\) MORE, \(G = 1\) in BASE \(+\) BALL, \(P = 1\) in LOGIC \(+\) LOGIC and \(D = 1\) in CROSS \(+\) ROADS, for free.
  • 4. \(2X\) ends in \(X\) only when \(X = 0\). (\(X=5\) gives 10, whose last digit is 0, not 5.) This cracks TEN \(+\) TEN \(+\) FORTY and LOVE \(+\) LOVE.
  • 5. A jug state is the ordered pair of contents. Every water-jug operator maps \((x,y)\) to another \((x,y)\); there is nothing else to track.
Read this before the crypt-arithmetic problems
  • Seven of the thirteen puzzles set in these papers have more than one valid answer. ONE \(+\) ONE \(+\) TWO \(=\) FOUR has 107. RIGHT \(+\) RIGHT \(=\) WRONG, WRONG \(+\) WRONG \(=\) RIGHT and ONE \(+\) ONE \(=\) TWO pin no letter at all.
  • So the marks are in the column reasoning, not the digits. Write \(X\), \(D\), \(C\) and the carries, then argue. Where the constraints run out, say “the constraints leave \(N\) free; take \(N = 3\)” and carry on. That sentence is worth more than the answer.
  • Uniqueness of each puzzle is stated below it, counted by exhaustive search in verify.py over every letter-to-digit assignment.

column1: 2.N.1 Crypt-arithmetic: the six puzzles with a unique answer — SEND \(+\) MORE \(=\) MONEY
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 72 Ash · Q2 · 1+6
Solve the following crypto-arithmetic problem through constraint satisfaction, showing all steps. Different letters denote different integers and identical letters denote the same integer.
SEND
\(+\)MORE
MONEY
column4:
Formulation

The chain
  • Two four-digit numbers give a five-digit answer, so the leading digit is only a carry: \(\mathbf{R = 1}\).
  • Column 2 is \(I + A + c_1 = 10c_2 + A\), and the \(A\) cancels: \[ \boxed{\;I + c_1 = 10c_2\;} \]

  • So \(c_2 = 0\) and \(\mathbf{I = 0}\), \(c_1 = 0\).
  • Column 1 with \(c_1 = 0\): \(M + 1 = X\), so \(X = M + 1\). The two move together.
  • Column 3: \(W + E + c_2 = 10c_3 + L\).  Column 4: \(S + W + c_3 = 10 + E\).
  • \(A\) meets no constraint but AllDiff \(-\) worth saying out loud.

  • Column 3: \(4 + 3 + 0 = 7\), so \(\mathbf{L = 7}\) and \(c_3 = 0\) ✓.
  • \(A = 2\), free. \(M = 5\), so \(X = 6\) by \(X = M + 1\).

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 76 Bh · 4
In a correctly worked out crypt-arithmetic problem AB \(+\) CD \(=\) AAA, what could be the possible values of B? Justify your answer.
column4:
Reasoning
  • \(A = 1\). Two 2-digit numbers sum to at most \(99 + 99 = 198\). The only 3-digit repdigit AAA in range is 111, so \(A = 1\).
  • So \(\text{AB} = 10 + B\) and \(\text{CD} = 111 - (10 + B) = \mathbf{101 - B}\).
  • \(B \geq 3\). CD must be a 2-digit number, so \(101 - B \leq 99\), giving \(B \geq 2\). And \(B = 2\) makes \(\text{CD} = 99\), i.e. \(C = D = 9\), which the AllDiff rule forbids. So \(B \geq 3\).
  • \(B \leq 8\). For \(B\) from 3 to 9, \(\text{CD} = 101 - B\) runs \(98, 97, \dots, 92\), so \(C = 9\) throughout. \(B = 9\) would make \(B = C = 9\). This is the case that is easy to miss, and it is the whole difficulty of the question.
  • \(B = 1\) is out because \(A = 1\), and \(B = 0\) would need \(\text{CD} = 101\).
Answer: \(B \in \{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}\), six values

41497\(14 + 97 = 111\) ✓
51596\(15 + 96 = 111\) ✓
61695\(16 + 95 = 111\) ✓
71794\(17 + 94 = 111\) ✓

21299× \(C = D = 9\)
91992× \(B = C = 9\)
  • In every case \(A = 1\) and \(C = 9\); only \(B\) and \(D\) move, and they move together since \(D = 8 - (B - 3)\).

column1: 2.N.3 The water jug problem
column4:
The eight production rules, state \((x, y)\)
\(x\) is the contents of the larger jug, \(y\) of the smaller. Written here for the 4-gallon and 3-gallon pair; swap the capacities for any other version. This is the rule set Insights and the lecture decks both use, and it is what “write down the production rules” means.
#ConditionResultMeaning
1\((x,y)\) and \(x < 4\)\((4, y)\)Fill the 4-gallon jug
2\((x,y)\) and \(y < 3\)\((x, 3)\)Fill the 3-gallon jug
3\((x,y)\) and \(x > 0\)\((0, y)\)Empty the 4-gallon jug on the ground
4\((x,y)\) and \(y > 0\)\((x, 0)\)Empty the 3-gallon jug on the ground
5\((x,y)\) and \(x + y \geq 4\) and \(y > 0\)\((4,\ y - (4 - x))\)Pour from the 3 into the 4 until the 4 is full
6\((x,y)\) and \(x + y \geq 3\) and \(x > 0\)\((x - (3 - y),\ 3)\)Pour from the 4 into the 3 until the 3 is full
7\((x,y)\) and \(x + y \leq 4\) and \(y > 0\)\((x + y,\ 0)\)Pour all of the 3 into the 4
8\((x,y)\) and \(x + y \leq 3\) and \(x > 0\)\((0,\ x + y)\)Pour all of the 4 into the 3
Formulating it as a state space
  • State: the ordered pair \((x, y)\), \(0 \leq x \leq 4\), \(0 \leq y \leq 3\). 20 states in all.
  • Initial state: \((0, 0)\), both jugs empty.
  • Goal state: \((2, y)\) for any \(y\) \(-\) the question asks only for 2 gallons in the 4-gallon jug, so \(y\) is unconstrained.
  • Operators: the eight rules alongside.
  • Path cost: 1 per rule application.
  • Why the state is just a pair: the jugs have no markings, so nothing about how the water got there can matter. This is the whole point of the exercise and it is worth one sentence in the answer.
  • Problem type: ignorable (§2.3) \(-\) a wrong move can simply be emptied out, so no backtracking machinery is needed.

Assume you are given two jugs, a 4-gallon one and a 3-gallon one, and a pump which has unlimited water. How can you get exactly 2 gallons of water in the 4-gallon jug? Formalize the problem, write down Production Rules and draw the Search Tree for the water jug problem.

column1: 2.N.3 The water jug problem — 7 gallons in the 9-gallon jug, from a 3, a 5 and a 9
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 79 Bh · 2+1+2+3
What are the steps of Problem solving? You are given three empty jugs: a 3-gallon, a 5-gallon and a 9-gallon, and a pump can fill water only in the 3-gallon jug. How do you get exactly 7 gallons in the 9-gallon jug? Formalize the problem, write production rules and draw the search tree.
column4:
What makes this one different
  • Only the 3-gallon jug may be filled from the pump. So rule 1 applies to jug A alone; there is no “fill the 5” and no “fill the 9”.
  • Every gallon that reaches the 9-gallon jug arrives in multiples of 3, unless the 5-gallon jug is used to strand a remainder. \(9 = 3 \times 3\), so a direct route gives only 3, 6 or 9 gallons: the 5-gallon jug is not optional, it is the whole trick.
  • State: the triple \((a, b, c)\) for the 3, 5 and 9-gallon jugs. Initial \((0,0,0)\), goal \((a, b, 7)\).
  • Operators: fill A from the pump; empty any jug; pour \(i\) into \(j\) until \(i\) is empty or \(j\) is full.
Solution, 9 moves (shortest)
#\((a,b,c)\)Action
\((0,0,0)\)start
1\((3,0,0)\)fill A from the pump
2\((0,3,0)\)pour A into B
3\((3,3,0)\)fill A
4\((1,5,0)\)pour A into B; B takes 2 and is full, leaving 1 in A
5\((0,5,1)\)pour A into C
6\((3,5,1)\)fill A
7\((0,5,4)\)pour A into C
8\((3,5,4)\)fill A
9\((0,5,\mathbf{7})\)pour A into C
  • The whole idea is step 4: fill B to strand exactly 1 gallon in A, tip that 1 into C, then add \(3 + 3\) on top. \(1 + 3 + 3 = 7\).
  • B is never emptied after step 4; it has done its job.

column1: 2.N.3 The water jug problem — 1 litre, from a 5-litre and a 2-litre jug
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 81 Ash · 8
You are given two jugs, a 5-litre one and a 2-litre one. Neither has any measuring markers on it. There is a pump that can be used to fill the jugs with water. You are required to measure exactly 1 litre of water. Is this a well-defined problem? Justify your argument and list all the attributes to design an intelligent agent. Solve this problem by specifying states and the operations used.
column4:
Part 1: is it well defined? Yes
  • Initial state given: both jugs empty, \((0,0)\).
  • Operators given: fill from the pump, empty on the ground, pour one into the other.
  • Goal test given and mechanical: does either jug hold exactly 1 litre?
  • Path cost: 1 per operation.
  • Every clause of §2.2 is satisfied, so it is well defined. It is also solvable, since \(\gcd(5,2) = 1\) divides 1.
Part 2: attributes for designing an intelligent agent
  • This is asking for PEAS plus the environment properties (Ch 1):
    • P: measure exactly 1 litre, in the fewest operations, spilling least.
    • E: the two jugs, the pump, the ground.
    • A: fill, empty, pour.
    • S: whether a jug is full, empty, or neither.
  • Environment: fully observable, deterministic, sequential, static, discrete, single agent. A goal-based agent is the right type, because the answer needs a sequence planned ahead, not a reflex.
Part 3: solution, 4 moves (shortest)
#\((x,y)\)RuleAction
\((0,0)\)\(-\)start
1\((5,0)\)1fill the 5-litre jug
2\((3,2)\)6pour into the 2-litre jug until full
3\((3,0)\)4empty the 2-litre jug
4\(\mathbf{(1,2)}\)6pour again; the 2 takes 2 more, leaving 1 in the 5
  • The 1 litre ends up in the 5-litre jug, which is what the question asks for: it says “measure exactly 1 litre”, not “in the 2-litre jug”.
  • State space: \(6 \times 3 = 18\) states.
  • The general rule worth one extra mark: with jugs of capacity \(m\) and \(n\), exactly the multiples of \(\gcd(m,n)\) up to \(\max(m,n)\) are measurable. Here \(\gcd(5,2) = 1\), so every whole number of litres from 0 to 5 can be measured.

column1: 2.N.4 Farmer, wolf, goat and cabbage — Formulate the river crossing as search and solve it
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 73 Ma · 8
A farmer has a goat, a wolf and a cabbage on the west side of a river and wants to move everything to the east side. The boat holds the farmer and one other thing. The wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage if left alone. Formulate this puzzle as search and solve it (any method); draw the search tree and final solution.
column4:
Formulation
  • State: the 4-tuple \((F, W, G, C)\) giving which bank the Farmer, Wolf, Goat and Cabbage are on. Write \(0\) for west, \(1\) for east.
  • Initial state \((0,0,0,0)\); goal state \((1,1,1,1)\).
  • Operators: the farmer crosses, taking nothing or exactly one item that is currently on his own bank. Four operators.
  • Safety constraint (this is what makes it a puzzle): a state is illegal if
    • the goat and the wolf are together without the farmer, or
    • the goat and the cabbage are together without the farmer.
  • Path cost: 1 per crossing.
  • State space: \(2^4 = 16\) states in total, of which only 10 are safe and reachable. Six are pruned by the constraint, and that pruning is the answer to “how does a constraint reduce the search”.
Solution: 7 crossings
#\((F,W,G,C)\)Crossing
W W W Wstart, everything on the west
1E W E Wtake the goat across
2W W E Wreturn alone
3E E E Wtake the wolf across
4W E W Wbring the goat back
5E E W Etake the cabbage across
6W E W Ereturn alone
7E E E Etake the goat across
  • Step 4 is the step everyone misses. Nothing else works: after the wolf is delivered, the goat cannot stay with it, so it must come back and wait while the cabbage goes over.
  • The goat is the only item that is dangerous in both directions, which is why it moves first, and why it is the one that gets brought back.
  • 7 is the minimum. There is a mirror-image solution that takes the cabbage third instead of the wolf; it is also 7 crossings and equally correct.

column1: 2.N.5 Tic-tac-toe as a state space — Describe tic-tac-toe in terms of state space, data structure and goal
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 72 Ma · 7
Consider a Tic-Tac-Toe game playing as a problem. Prepare a brief description of your problem in terms of complete state-space, efficient data structures and goal, which are to be used for a machine to play that game.
column4:
1. Complete state space
  • A state is an assignment of blank, X or O to each of the 9 squares, plus whose turn it is.
  • Naive count: \(3^9 = \mathbf{19{,}683}\) boards. Most are not reachable \(-\) they have five O's and no X's, or two completed lines.
  • Reachable, legal count: \(\mathbf{5{,}478}\) states, counting every board that can arise in a real game with X moving first and play stopping at a win.
  • Branching factor 9 at the root, falling by one each ply; at most \(9! = 362{,}880\) complete play sequences, which is small enough to search exhaustively. That is the point worth making: tic-tac-toe is one of the few games where minimax can see to the end of the game.
  • Initial state: the empty board. Operators: place your mark on any blank square. Problem type: irrecoverable (§2.3) \(-\) a placed mark cannot be lifted, so the machine must plan before moving.
2. Efficient data structure
  • A 9-element vector indexed 1–9, holding 0 for blank, 1 for X, 2 for O. Simple, and a move is one array write.
  • The efficient version: two 9-bit masks, one for X and one for O. Then
    • a legal-move test is a bitwise AND against the union,
    • a win test is mask & line == line over the 8 winning lines (3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals), which is 8 AND operations and no loops,
    • the whole board fits in one integer, so states can be hashed and cached.
  • A move-indexed lookup table of best replies is the fastest of all, but it is the table-driven agent of Ch 1: correct, and impractical to build by hand.
3. Goal
  • Goal test: any of the 8 lines is filled with one player's mark, or all 9 squares are taken (a draw).
  • Utility: \(+1\) win, \(0\) draw, \(-1\) loss, which is what minimax (§3.4) needs.
  • The honest closing line: with both players optimal, tic-tac-toe is a forced draw. The machine's real goal is therefore never to lose, and to win only when the opponent errs.

column1: Why is searching necessary in AI? On what basis are search algorithms evaluated?
column4:
Why searching is necessary
  • Most AI problems have no formula that computes the answer. There is only a start state, a set of legal moves and a test for the goal, so the answer has to be found rather than calculated.
  • Once a problem is written as a state space (Ch 2), solving it is searching that space for a path from initial state to goal.
  • The space is far too large to enumerate: chess has around \(10^{120}\) game paths, the 24-puzzle around \(10^{25}\) states. Brute force is not an option, so the search must be directed.
  • Search is the mechanism behind almost every other topic on this syllabus: game playing (§3.4), resolution refutation (Ch 4), rule chaining, planning, and the learning algorithms of Ch 6.
  • The one-line answer: searching is how an agent converts knowledge of the rules into a sequence of actions, when it has no direct way to compute one.
The four evaluation criteria
  • Completeness \(-\) is the algorithm guaranteed to find a solution when one exists?
  • Optimality \(-\) when it finds one, is it guaranteed to be the least-cost solution?
  • Time complexity \(-\) how many nodes are generated?
  • Space complexity \(-\) how many nodes must be held in memory at once?
  • Say what the symbols mean or the complexities score nothing:
    • \(b\) \(=\) branching factor, the maximum successors of any node;
    • \(d\) \(=\) depth of the shallowest goal;
    • \(m\) \(=\) maximum depth of the search tree, possibly infinite;
    • \(\ell\) \(=\) the depth limit, for depth-limited search.
  • Some papers add admissibility (does it find the optimal path when one exists) and dominance (does one heuristic expand fewer nodes than another). Mention both in a 4-mark answer.

column1: Explain BFS and DFS and compare their performance criteria
column4:
What “uninformed” means
  • The algorithm is given nothing beyond the problem definition: it can generate successors and test for the goal, and that is all.
  • It has no estimate of how close a state is to the goal, so it cannot prefer one frontier node over another on merit. Hence blind search. That is the answer to “why are BFS and DFS called blind even though they search systematically”: systematic is not the same as informed.
Breadth first search
  • Expand all nodes at depth \(k\) before any at depth \(k+1\). FIFO queue.
  • ✓Complete, and ✓optimal when every step costs the same.
  • ×Memory is the killer: it must hold the whole frontier, \(O(b^d)\) nodes.
Depth first search
  • Expand the deepest unexpanded node; go back only when stuck. LIFO stack, or plain recursion.
  • ✓Memory is linear, \(O(bm)\): only the current path and its siblings.
  • ×Not complete (it can run down an infinite branch or loop), and ×not optimal (it returns the first goal found, however deep).
The comparison table. Learn this.

Optimal✓yes

Time\(O(b^d)\)\(O(b^m)\)\(m \geq d\), so DFS can be far worse

  • The sentence that earns the last mark: BFS trades memory for a guarantee; DFS trades the guarantee for memory.
  • With \(b = 10\) and \(d = 12\), BFS needs about \(10^{12}\) nodes in memory and DFS about 120. That is the whole argument in one number.
Iterative deepening (IDS) verified/added
  • Run DLS with \(\ell = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) until a goal is found.
  • Gets BFS's guarantees at DFS's memory cost: complete, optimal for unit steps, \(O(b^d)\) time, \(O(bd)\) space.
  • The repeated work is negligible: re-expanding the top of the tree costs a constant factor, because the bottom level has more nodes than all the levels above it combined.
  • The preferred blind search when the depth is unknown. Worth one line whenever a paper asks for a comparison of blind strategies.

column1: Depth limited search (DLS)
column4:
• DFS with a hard cut-off at depth \(\ell\): treat any node at depth \(\ell\) as having no successors.
  • The advantage, which is what the paper asks: it fixes DFS's infinite-branch failure while keeping DFS's \(O(b\ell)\) memory.
  • ×Still not optimal, and ×incomplete in a new way: if \(\ell < d\) it reports failure even though a solution exists. If \(\ell > d\) it is not optimal either.
  • Choosing \(\ell\) needs knowledge of the problem. Eg for a route between 20 cities, no path needs more than 19 steps, so \(\ell = 19\).

column1: Explain A* search. How does it overcome the drawback of greedy best-first search?
column4:
The three evaluation functions
  • \(g(n)\) \(=\) the cost already paid to reach \(n\) from the start.
  • \(h(n)\) \(=\) the estimated cost from \(n\) to the goal, the heuristic.
  • Best first search is the family: keep an OPEN list of generated but unexpanded nodes and a CLOSED list of expanded ones, and always expand the OPEN node with the best evaluation.
    • Greedy best first: \(f(n) = h(n)\). Ignores what has already been spent.
    • Uniform cost: \(f(n) = g(n)\). Ignores the goal. This is blind search.
    • A*: \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\). Uses both.
The A* algorithm, as it should be written
  • 1. Put the start node on OPEN with \(g = 0\), \(f = h(\text{start})\).
  • 2. If OPEN is empty, fail.
  • 3. Remove the node of lowest \(f\) from OPEN, call it \(n\), and put it on CLOSED.
  • 4. If \(n\) is the goal, stop; trace the parent pointers back for the path.
  • 5. Expand \(n\). For each successor \(m\): compute \(g(m) = g(n) + \text{cost}(n,m)\) and \(f(m) = g(m) + h(m)\); record \(n\) as its parent; and if \(m\) is already on OPEN or CLOSED with a larger \(g\), replace the old entry and reopen it.
  • 6. Re-order OPEN by \(f\) and go to 2.
Greedy's drawback, and A*'s fix
  • Greedy asks only “which node looks nearest to the goal?”. It therefore walks into whatever the heuristic flatters, and a long detour that starts with a promising-looking step will be taken in full.
  • ×Greedy is not optimal and not complete: it can loop between two nodes that each look good from the other.
  • A* adds \(g(n)\), so a node is judged on the whole journey, not the remainder. A cheap-looking node that cost a fortune to reach is ranked accordingly.
  • The worked case in the companion: on the 80 Ch graph, greedy takes \(S \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow F \rightarrow G\) at cost 25, which is the worst of the four routes, because \(h(C) = 5\) looks closest. A* takes \(S \rightarrow B \rightarrow E \rightarrow F \rightarrow G\) at cost 18, the optimum.
Comparison in one line each
  • Greedy: fast, small memory, no guarantees.
  • A*: optimal and complete with an admissible \(h\), but stores every generated node, so memory is its limit.

column1: Admissibility and optimality of A*
column4:
The two properties of a heuristic
  • Admissible: \(h(n) \leq h^{*}(n)\) for every \(n\), where \(h^{*}\) is the true cost to the goal. The heuristic never overestimates; it is optimistic.
    • Guarantees A* is optimal in tree search.
  • Consistent (monotone): \(h(n) \leq \text{cost}(n,m) + h(m)\) for every edge, and \(h(\text{goal}) = 0\). A triangle inequality on the heuristic.
    • Guarantees A* is optimal in graph search, i.e. with a CLOSED list that is never revisited. Consistency implies admissibility; the converse is false.
  • Conditions for A* to be admissible and optimal: \(h\) admissible, every step cost \(> 0\), and the branching factor finite. Add consistent if a closed list is used.
Why this is not a pedantic point
  • Both graphs printed in these papers carry heuristics that are admissible but not consistent. In 81 Ch, \(h(B) = 13\) while \(\text{cost}(B,E) + h(E) = 6 + 4 = 10\).
  • The consequence is visible in the trace: A* first reaches \(E\) at \(g = 12\) through \(A\), and later finds \(E\) at \(g = 11\) through \(B\). An implementation that refuses to reopen a closed node returns 19 instead of the optimal 18.
  • So step 5 of the algorithm above, the replace and reopen clause, is not decoration. Write it, and the trace comes out right.
  • Dominance: if \(h_2(n) \geq h_1(n)\) for all \(n\) and both are admissible, \(h_2\) dominates \(h_1\) and A* with \(h_2\) expands no more nodes. A better heuristic is one that is larger while staying under \(h^{*}\).

column1: Discuss hill climbing, the problems associated with it, and their solutions
column4:
The algorithm
  • A local search: keep only the current state, and move to a neighbour that improves the objective function. No frontier, no backtracking, no memory of where it has been.
  • 1. Evaluate the initial state; if it is the goal, stop. 2. Generate a neighbour. 3. If the neighbour is better, make it the current state. 4. Repeat until no neighbour is better.
  • Variants: simple hill climbing takes the first better neighbour; steepest ascent evaluates all neighbours and takes the best; stochastic picks randomly among the better ones.
  • ✓Almost no memory, and very fast. ×Not complete and not optimal: it finds a local optimum and stops.
The whole answer in one picture: climbing from the current state reaches the local maximum, not the global one.
The three problems, and their cures
ProblemWhat happensCure
Local maximumA peak higher than all its neighbours but lower than the global maximum. Every move looks worse, so the search stops on a suboptimal answer.Backtrack to an earlier node and try a different direction. Or restart from a new random state (random-restart hill climbing).
PlateauA flat region where all neighbours score the same, so the search has no gradient to follow and wanders at random.Make a big jump in some direction, to reach a new region of the space. A single step is not enough to get off it.
RidgeA sequence of local maxima along a slope where the ascent runs across the ridge rather than along it, so every single-step move goes down.Apply two or more rules at once before testing, i.e. move in several directions at a time. Bidirectional search also helps.
  • Name all three and pair each with its own cure. A generic “use random restarts” for all three loses half the marks.

column1: Simulated annealing
column4:
The idea
  • Named after annealing in metallurgy: heat a metal, then cool it slowly so its atoms settle into a low-energy crystal instead of freezing into a flawed one.
  • Hill climbing accepts only improving moves, which is exactly why it gets stuck. Simulated annealing sometimes accepts a worse move, and does so less and less as the search proceeds.
  • A move is picked at random:
    • if it improves the state, accept it always;
    • if it worsens the state by \(\Delta E\), accept it with probability \(P = e^{-\Delta E / T}\).
  • \(T\) is the temperature, lowered on a fixed annealing schedule.
Why that fixes hill climbing
  • An accepted downhill move is exactly what escapes a local maximum: the search can go down one side of the small peak and up the big one.
  • It also crosses a plateau, since a sideways or slightly worse move costs almost nothing in probability.
  • The role of \(T\), which is where the marks are:
    • High \(T\) \(\rightarrow\) \(P\) near 1, most bad moves accepted, the search explores wildly. Nearly a random walk.
    • Low \(T\) \(\rightarrow\) \(P\) near 0, bad moves refused, the search becomes ordinary hill climbing.
    • Starting hot and cooling slowly explores first and refines later.
  • Note the shape of \(e^{-\Delta E/T}\): a slightly worse move is much likelier to be accepted than a much worse one, at any temperature.
  • The theoretical guarantee worth quoting: if \(T\) is lowered slowly enough, simulated annealing finds the global optimum with probability approaching 1.

column1: Explain the min-max algorithm. What are its drawbacks, and how does alpha-beta pruning solve them?
column4:
Minimax
  • For a two-player, zero-sum, perfect-information game. One player (MAX) maximises the score, the other (MIN) minimises it.
  • Build the game tree to the terminal states, score each with the utility function, then propagate values upward:
    • at a MAX node, take the largest child value;
    • at a MIN node, take the smallest.
  • The root's value is the best MAX can force against an opponent playing perfectly, and the move to play is the child that achieves it.
  • Implemented as a depth-first traversal, so space is \(O(bm)\); time is \(O(b^m)\).
The drawbacks (the part the papers ask for)
  • Exponential time, \(O(b^m)\). Chess has \(b \approx 35\) and \(m \approx 100\), so the complete tree can never be built. This is the drawback; everything else is a consequence.
  • It examines every leaf, including branches whose outcome cannot possibly change the root value.
  • It assumes a perfect opponent, so it can play too cautiously against a weak one.
  • In practice the tree must be cut off at a fixed depth and the cut-off nodes scored by an evaluation function, which makes the answer approximate.
Alpha-beta pruning
  • Same answer, fewer leaves. It returns exactly the minimax value; it only skips work that cannot affect it.
  • Carry two bounds down the tree:
    • \(\alpha\) \(=\) the best value MAX can already guarantee. It only rises.
    • \(\beta\) \(=\) the best value MIN can already guarantee. It only falls.
  • The two cut rules:
    • at a MIN node, if its value \(\leq \alpha\), stop \(-\) MAX will never choose this branch (alpha cut-off);
    • at a MAX node, if its value \(\geq \beta\), stop \(-\) MIN will never allow it (beta cut-off).
What pruning buys, and what it does not
  • Effect: with a perfect move ordering the time complexity falls from \(O(b^m)\) to \(O(b^{m/2})\), i.e. the same time searches twice as deep, or an effective branching factor of \(\sqrt{b}\). With random ordering it is about \(O(b^{3m/4})\).
  • ×It does not change the value returned.
  • ×It does not help in the worst case: with the best move examined last everywhere, nothing is pruned and the cost is exactly minimax's.
  • So it depends entirely on move ordering, which is why real game programs invest in ordering heuristics before they invest in searching deeper.
How to run alpha-beta in an exam, without losing the thread
  • Go strictly left to right, depth first. The examiner's expected answer depends on that order.
  • Write \((\alpha, \beta)\) beside every internal node as you enter it, starting \((-\infty, +\infty)\) at the root.
  • A child inherits its parent's current \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
  • After each child returns, update the node's own value, then update \(\alpha\) (at a MAX node) or \(\beta\) (at a MIN node).
  • Test the cut rule immediately after each child, not at the end. Cross out the skipped leaves so the pruning is visible.
  • State how many leaves were pruned at the end. It is usually worth a mark and it proves the trace was actually run.
Worked in the companion
  • 79 Ch: a 12-leaf, 5-level tree. Minimax value 3; alpha-beta prunes 2 of the 12 leaves.
  • 76 Ba: a 9-leaf, 2-level tree. Minimax value 3; alpha-beta prunes 4 of the 9, because the first branch returns 3 and sets a high \(\alpha\) straight away.
  • The contrast between the two is the lesson: the second tree prunes twice as large a fraction, purely because its best branch happened to come first.
Other adversarial ideas worth a line
  • Horizon effect: a fixed-depth cut-off can hide a disaster just beyond the last ply, so the agent plays a move that merely postpones it.
  • Quiescence search: keep searching past the cut-off while the position is still volatile.
  • Expectiminimax: for games with chance, add a chance node whose value is the expected value over its children.
