column1: Chapter 3 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
Every problem opens with the exam question and the figure exactly as the paper prints them. The OPEN / CLOSED table format is the one Insights §3.4.2 uses.  \(\cdot\) Every path, cost and minimax value in this file is recomputed independently by verify.py.
The four things everything here is built on:
  • 1. \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\). Greedy orders on \(h\) alone, uniform cost on \(g\) alone, A* on the sum. Every trace below is the same loop with a different \(f\).
  • 2. The loop: take the best node off OPEN \(\rightarrow\) put it on CLOSED \(\rightarrow\) generate its successors onto OPEN \(\rightarrow\) re-order OPEN \(\rightarrow\) repeat. Stop when the node taken off OPEN is the goal, not when the goal is first generated.
  • 3. If a successor is already known with a larger \(g\), replace it and put it back on OPEN. Skipping this returns the wrong answer on both A* graphs in these papers, because both heuristics are admissible but not consistent.
  • 4. Alpha-beta: \(\alpha\) only rises, \(\beta\) only falls, a child inherits both, and you test the cut rule after every child. MIN cuts when its value \(\leq \alpha\); MAX cuts when its value \(\geq \beta\).

column3:

column4:
The trace
  • MAX root over three MIN nodes, each with three leaves: \(\{3,5,10\}\), \(\{2,8,19\}\), \(\{2,7,3\}\).
Node\((\alpha, \beta)\)What happens
\(m_1\)\((-\infty, \infty)\)3 \(\rightarrow\) 5 \(\rightarrow\) 10, value \(= 3\). Nothing can be pruned here, because \(\alpha\) is still \(-\infty\)
root\(\alpha \leftarrow 3\)
\(m_2\)\((3, \infty)\)leaf 2 gives 2; \(2 \leq 3\) \(\rightarrow\) PRUNE 8 and 19

  • Minimax value 3, MAX plays the leftmost branch.
  • 4 of the 9 leaves pruned (8, 19, 7, 3); five examined: 3, 5, 10, 2, 2.
Why this tree prunes so much better
  • §3.N.4 pruned 2 leaves in 12, about 17 %. This one prunes 4 in 9, about 44 %. The algorithm is identical; the move ordering is not.
  • Here the best branch happens to be examined first. That sets \(\alpha = 3\) immediately, and every later MIN node that finds any child below 3 can stop at once. Both of them do, on their very first leaf.
  • The general rule: alpha-beta is only as good as the order in which moves are examined.
    • Best case (best move first everywhere): \(O(b^{m/2})\), so the same time searches twice as deep.
    • Worst case (best move last everywhere): \(O(b^m)\), i.e. no saving at all \(-\) alpha-beta never prunes more than minimax examines, and can prune nothing.
  • This is why real game programs spend effort on move ordering heuristics before they spend it on searching deeper.
Two things to say when asked to “discuss” it
  • It returns exactly the minimax value. Pruning removes work, never accuracy. Say this first.
  • A pruned branch is one whose value cannot change the root, because a player higher up already has a better guaranteed alternative.

column1: Chapter 4 — Knowledge Representation, Inference and Reasoning: how is it examined?
column4:
4 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in all 41 papers  \(\cdot\) 4 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 638 marks, 18.8 % of every mark ever set, against a 7.8 % share of the teaching hours  \(\cdot\)  33 resolution proofs and 15 Bayes numericals worked in Ch4 – Knowledge Representation, Inference and Reasoning – Solved Problems.
Read this first:
  • This is the highest-paying chapter in the subject, by a factor of 2.4. Four teaching hours, nearly a fifth of every mark. Whatever time the timetable suggests for it, spend more.
  • One question dominates everything: prove a goal from given premises by resolution refutation TOP 33. It is in 33 of the 41 papers, always for 6 to 10 marks. The premises change; the procedure never does. Learn the procedure once and the question is answered for the rest of your life.
  • Its two feeder topics are asked in their own right: conversion to CNF TOP 9 and the rules of inference. You cannot resolve without CNF, so this is one topic wearing two hats.
  • The other two reliable topics: forward Vs backward chaining TOP 11, always a comparison with an example, and belief / causal networks HOT 7.
  • Fifteen papers set a Bayes numerical, usually bolted onto a 2–3 mark theory opener. The arithmetic is one formula; all 15 are worked in the companion.
  • Pairs the examiner reliably asks together: a resolution proof preceded by the CNF steps, skolemization or the rules of inference, and a Bayes numerical preceded by prior/posterior. The short part is always the definition; the long part is always the work.
  • The 5-mark saver: if a resolution proof stalls in the exam, write the FOPL, write the clause form, write the negated goal, and show the resolution steps you do have. The marks are spread across those stages, not parked on the empty clause.

column1: What is knowledge, representation and reasoning? What kinds of knowledge are there?
column4:
The three words
  • Knowledge \(=\) facts, concepts, rules and relationships about a domain that an agent can use. It sits above data and information:
    • data \(\rightarrow\) raw symbols; information \(\rightarrow\) data with context; knowledge \(\rightarrow\) information plus how to use it; intelligence \(\rightarrow\) knowledge applied to a new situation.
  • Representation \(=\) writing that knowledge in a formal notation a machine can store and manipulate. Not any notation: one that supports inference.
  • Reasoning \(=\) deriving new sentences from the stored ones, so the agent knows things nobody explicitly told it.
  • The four questions KR exists to answer: how do we represent facts about the world, how do we reason about them, which representation suits the real world, and how do we put it in a form a machine can compute with.
The five kinds of knowledge
KindWhat it isExample
DeclarativeKnowing that. Facts, concepts, objects, stated without saying how to use them“Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal”
ProceduralKnowing how. Rules, strategies, procedures, agendasthe steps to sort a list
HeuristicRules of thumb from experience: good, not guaranteedin chess, keep the opponent's king exposed
StructuralRelationships between concepts and objects“a cow is-a mammal”
MetaKnowledge about knowledge: what the agent knows, and how reliable it is“my map of Pokhara is out of date”
  • Name all five with one example each. Papers award a mark per kind, and meta-knowledge and structural are the two students forget.
What a good representation must give you
  • Representational adequacy \(-\) can it express everything in the domain?
  • Inferential adequacy \(-\) can new knowledge be derived from it?
  • Inferential efficiency \(-\) can the derivation be steered, so the search does not explode?
  • Acquisitional efficiency \(-\) can new knowledge be added easily?
Why logic is the representation of choice
  • It is concise, unambiguous, context-insensitive and expressive, and it comes with a proof theory, i.e. inference is defined for you. That last property is what the rest of this chapter is built on.
  • Logic is fixed by three things, and papers ask for them by name: syntax (which strings are sentences), semantics (what a sentence means about the world) and proof theory (which new sentences may be derived from old ones).

column1: What is a knowledge-based agent? How does it work?
column4:
Definition and structure
  • An agent whose behaviour comes from a knowledge base (KB) of sentences about the world, plus an inference engine that derives new sentences from it. It acts on what it can prove, not on hard-wired reflexes.
  • Two levels, and papers like the distinction:
    • Knowledge level \(-\) what the agent knows and what goal it has, independent of any notation.
    • Implementation level \(-\) the sentences, the data structures and the algorithm that actually run.
  • Three operations, in this order, once per time step:
    • TELL the KB what was perceived;
    • ASK the KB which action to take;
    • TELL the KB that the action was taken.
Why it matters, with the standard example
  • The Wumpus world: an agent in a cave perceives breeze, stench, glitter. No single percept names a pit, but breeze in (1,2) and (2,1) with none in (1,1) proves where the pit is. That inference, not the percept, is the whole point.
  • ✓It can be told new facts without reprogramming: add a sentence and the behaviour changes.
  • ✓It handles partially observable worlds, because it reasons about what it has not seen.
  • ×It is only as good as its KB, and inference costs time: a large KB with an undirected engine is exactly the search-explosion problem of Ch 3.
  • Every expert system (Ch 7) is a knowledge-based agent with a domain KB and a chaining inference engine. Say that sentence and the examiner sees you have connected the chapters.

column1: Define a WFF with its properties. Prove that \((A \wedge (A \rightarrow B)) \rightarrow B\) is a tautology
column4:
Proposition and well-formed formula
  • A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false, never both. “5 is a prime number” is one; “close the door” is not.
  • An atomic sentence is a single propositional symbol (\(P\), \(Q\)). A compound sentence joins atomic ones with the connectives \( eg, \wedge, \vee, ightarrow, \leftrightarrow\).
  • A WFF is a string built only by these recursive rules:
    • any propositional symbol is a WFF;
    • if \(\alpha\) is a WFF then \( eg\alpha\) and \((\alpha)\) are WFFs;
    • if \(\alpha, eta\) are WFFs then so are \((\alpha \wedge eta)\), \((\alpha \vee eta)\), \((\alpha ightarrow eta)\), \((\alpha \leftrightarrow eta)\);
    • nothing else is a WFF. That closing clause is worth a mark and is the one students leave out.
  • Precedence, when brackets are missing: \( eg\), then \(\wedge\), then \(\vee\), then \( ightarrow\), then \(\leftrightarrow\).
The four properties to name
  • Valid (a tautology): true under every interpretation. Eg \(P \vee eg P\).
  • Satisfiable: true under at least one. Eg \(P \wedge Q\).
  • Unsatisfiable (a contradiction): true under none. Eg \(P \wedge eg P\).
  • Equivalent: \(\alpha \equiv eta\) when they have the same truth value in every row. Equivalently, \(\alpha \leftrightarrow eta\) is valid.
  • The link resolution depends on: \(\alpha\) is valid iff \( eg\alpha\) is unsatisfiable. That single line is why proving a goal is done by refuting its negation in §4.5.
Equivalences you must be able to quote
  • \(\alpha ightarrow eta \;\equiv\; eg\alpha \vee eta\)  (the workhorse)
  • \(\alpha \leftrightarrow eta \;\equiv\; (\alpha ightarrow eta) \wedge ( eta ightarrow \alpha)\)
  • De Morgan: \( eg(\alpha \wedge eta) \equiv eg\alpha \vee eg eta\); \( eg(\alpha \vee eta) \equiv eg\alpha \wedge eg eta\)
  • Distribution: \(\alpha \vee ( eta \wedge \gamma) \equiv (\alpha \vee eta) \wedge (\alpha \vee \gamma)\)
  • Contrapositive \( eg eta ightarrow eg\alpha\) is equivalent to \(\alpha ightarrow eta\); the converse \( eta ightarrow \alpha\) and the inverse \( eg\alpha ightarrow eg eta\) are not.

column1: List the rules of inference. When can we use them?
column4:
The eight propositional rules
RuleFrom \( herefore\) concludeTautological form
Modus ponens\(P ightarrow Q\), \(P\) \( herefore\) \(Q\)\([(P ightarrow Q) \wedge P] ightarrow Q\)
Modus tollens\(P ightarrow Q\), \( eg Q\) \( herefore\) \( eg P\)\([(P ightarrow Q) \wedge eg Q] ightarrow eg P\)
Hypothetical syllogism\(P ightarrow Q\), \(Q ightarrow R\) \( herefore\) \(P ightarrow R\)chains two implications
Disjunctive syllogism\(P \vee Q\), \( eg P\) \( herefore\) \(Q\)eliminates a disjunct
Addition\(P\) \( herefore\) \(P \vee Q\)weakens
Simplification\(P \wedge Q\) \( herefore\) \(P\)splits
Conjunction\(P\), \(Q\) \( herefore\) \(P \wedge Q\)joins
Resolution\(P \vee Q\), \( eg P \vee R\) \( herefore\) \(Q \vee R\)the only one §4.5 needs
The four quantifier rules
  • Universal instantiation: from \( orall x\,P(x)\) infer \(P(c)\) for any constant \(c\).
  • Existential instantiation: from \(\exists x\,P(x)\) infer \(P(c)\) for a brand-new constant \(c\). Reusing an existing name is the classic mistake; this is skolemization in one line.
  • Universal generalisation: from \(P(c)\) for an arbitrary \(c\) infer \( orall x\,P(x)\).
  • Existential generalisation: from \(P(c)\) infer \(\exists x\,P(x)\).
When can we use them (the second half of the question)
  • Only when the premises match the pattern exactly, after unification. A rule is a syntactic licence: it never looks at meaning.
  • They are sound: applied to true premises they can only produce true conclusions, so a derivation is a proof.
  • They are used when the KB is in the right form: modus ponens needs implications, resolution needs CNF (§4.4), and forward/backward chaining (§4.6) need definite clauses.

column1: Why do we need FOPL? Explain its syntax and quantifiers
column4:
Why propositional logic is not enough
  • In PL a whole statement is one indivisible symbol. “All humans are intelligent” and “Some humans are intelligent” become two unrelated letters \(P\) and \(Q\), with no way to see that one implies the other.
  • It cannot express objects, their properties or relations between them, and it has no quantifiers, so a fact about a million individuals needs a million sentences.
  • FOPL fixes exactly that: it breaks a sentence into subject and predicate, and quantifies over objects.
  • The three-line answer: PL has limited expressive power; FOPL adds objects, predicates and quantifiers; so one FOPL sentence replaces an unbounded set of PL ones.
Syntax: the seven elements
  • Constants \(-\) John, Nepal, 2. Named objects.
  • Variables \(-\) \(x, y, z\).
  • Predicates \(-\) Brother, Loves, \(>\). Relations, true or false of their arguments.
  • Functions \(-\) FatherOf, sqrt. Return an object, not a truth value. Predicate Vs function is a favourite one-mark trap.
  • Connectives \( eg, \wedge, \vee, ightarrow, \leftrightarrow\), equality \(=\), and quantifiers \( orall, \exists\).
The two quantifiers, and the connective each takes
  • \( orall\) (universal, “for all”) goes with \( ightarrow\):
    \( orall x\; man(x) ightarrow drinks(x, coffee)\)
  • \(\exists\) (existential, “there exists”) goes with \(\wedge\):
    \(\exists x\; student(x) \wedge fails(x, maths)\)
  • Swap the connectives and the sentence is nonsense. \( orall x\, (man(x) \wedge drinks(x,coffee))\) says everything in the universe is a coffee-drinking man; \(\exists x\, (student(x) ightarrow fails(x))\) is satisfied by any non-student. This single pairing earns or loses the translation marks.
  • Duality, needed in every CNF conversion: \( eg orall x\, P \equiv \exists x\, eg P\) and \( eg \exists x\, P \equiv orall x\, eg P\).
Translation patterns worth memorising
  • “All A are B” \( ightarrow\) \( orall x\, A(x) ightarrow B(x)\)
  • “Some A are B” \( ightarrow\) \(\exists x\, A(x) \wedge B(x)\)
  • “No A is B” \( ightarrow\) \( orall x\, A(x) ightarrow eg B(x)\), or \( eg \exists x\, (A(x) \wedge B(x))\)
  • “A has at least one B” \( ightarrow\) \(\exists x\, B(x) \wedge has(A, x)\)
  • “Everyone who … all animals” \( ightarrow\) a \( orall\) inside the antecedent of another \( ightarrow\); that nesting is what makes the standard CNF example in §4.4 hard.

column1: Skolemization
column4:
• Definition: removing an existential quantifier by replacing its variable with a new symbol, so the sentence can be written as a clause.
  • Two cases, and the second is the one papers test:
    • \(\exists\) not inside any \(\forall\) \(\rightarrow\) replace with a new Skolem constant. \(\exists x\, rich(x) \Rightarrow rich(A)\).
    • \(\exists\) inside \(\forall\) \(\rightarrow\) replace with a Skolem function of the enclosing universal variables. \(\forall x\, \exists y\, loves(x,y) \Rightarrow loves(x, F(x))\).
  • Why a function and not a constant: the person loved depends on who is loving. A constant would assert that everyone loves the same individual, which is a different and stronger claim, and the proof built on it is wrong.
  • The new symbol must be one not already used anywhere in the KB.

column1: Horn clause and definite clause
column4:
• A clause is a disjunction of literals: \( eg P \vee Q \vee eg R\).
  • Definite clause: a clause with exactly one positive literal. \( eg P \vee eg Q \vee K\).
  • Horn clause: a clause with at most one positive literal. So every definite clause is a Horn clause, and the extra case is the goal clause with no positive literal at all.
  • Why the restriction exists, which is what the 3 marks are for: a definite clause is exactly an implication with a single conclusion, \((P \wedge Q) ightarrow K\), so
    • inference collapses to modus ponens, and
    • forward and backward chaining (§4.6) become possible, in time linear in the size of the KB rather than exponential.
  • Prolog is exactly this: a program is a set of definite clauses.

column1: Unification and the most general unifier
column4:
What it does
  • Unification finds a substitution \(\theta\) that makes two atomic sentences identical: \(\text{UNIFY}(\alpha, \beta) = \theta\) where \(\alpha\theta = \beta\theta\).
  • The substitution with the fewest commitments is the most general unifier (MGU), and it is the one to use: a more specific one can lose proofs.
  • Written \([term/variable]\), Eg \(\theta = [John/x]\).
  • It fails, and the resolution step is then illegal, when
    • the predicate symbols or the arities differ;
    • two different constants must match, Eg \(King(John)\) Vs \(King(Ram)\);
    • a variable would have to be bound to a term containing itself (the occurs check).
Worked, in the form the papers expect
  • \(King(x)\) and \(King(John)\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta = [John/x]\).
  • \(P(x, y)\) and \(P(a, f(z))\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta = [a/x,\; f(z)/y]\).
  • \(P(x, f(y))\) and \(P(a, f(g(x)))\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta = [a/x,\; g(a)/y]\): substitute \(a\) for \(x\) first, then apply that binding inside the second term too. Writing \(g(x)/y\) and stopping is the common half-answer.
  • \(Q(a, g(x,a), f(y))\) and \(Q(a, g(f(b),a), x)\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta = [f(b)/x,\; b/y]\).
  • Standardise apart first: if both clauses use \(x\), rename one of them. Two clauses that share a variable name will unify wrongly and the proof will be rejected.

column1: Why is CNF required? Explain all the steps involved in converting to CNF, with an example
column4:
Why CNF is required (the 2 marks, and the only part students skip)
  • CNF \(=\) a conjunction of clauses, each clause a disjunction of literals: \((A \vee eg B) \wedge (C \vee D \vee eg E)\)
  • Resolution is a single inference rule and it only operates on clauses. Everything else \(-\) implications, biconditionals, nested negations, quantifiers \(-\) has to go before the machinery can start.
  • Because the whole formula is one big AND, each clause can be asserted separately and stored as its own line in the KB.
  • Every sentence of propositional or first-order logic has a CNF equivalent, so nothing is lost by insisting on it. That completeness is what makes resolution a general proof procedure.
  • Contrast DNF, a disjunction of conjunctions. Papers sometimes ask for both: CNF is joined by AND, DNF by OR.
The eight steps, in this order
  1. Eliminate \(\leftrightarrow\): \(\alpha \leftrightarrow eta \Rightarrow (\alpha ightarrow eta) \wedge ( eta ightarrow \alpha)\).
  2. Eliminate \( ightarrow\): \(\alpha ightarrow eta \Rightarrow eg\alpha \vee eta\).
  3. Move \( eg\) inwards, until it sits on atoms only: De Morgan, \( eg eg\alpha \equiv \alpha\), and the quantifier duals \( eg orall x\,P \equiv \exists x\, eg P\), \( eg\exists x\,P \equiv orall x\, eg P\).
  4. Standardise variables apart: rename so that no two quantifiers bind the same variable name.
  5. Skolemize: drop each \(\exists\), replacing its variable by a new constant, or by a function of the enclosing universal variables (§4.3).
  6. Drop the universal quantifiers: every remaining variable is understood to be universally quantified.
  7. Distribute \(\vee\) over \(\wedge\): \(\alpha \vee ( eta \wedge \gamma) \Rightarrow (\alpha \vee eta) \wedge (\alpha \vee \gamma)\).
  8. Split the conjunction into separate clauses, and rename variables again so no two clauses share one.
Steps 4, 7 and 8 are the ones the local textbook leaves out, and a proof that skips 4 or 8 unifies two unrelated variables and derives nonsense. Write all eight; the marks are per step.
The worked example the papers use (79 Ch, 75 Bh, 73 Bh)
  • “Everyone who loves all animals is loved by someone.”
  • FOPL: \( orall x\,[ orall y\; Animal(y) ightarrow Loves(x,y)] ightarrow [\exists z\; Loves(z,x)]\)
  • 2. Eliminate \( ightarrow\), twice: \( orall x\, eg[ orall y\; eg Animal(y) \vee Loves(x,y)] \vee [\exists z\; Loves(z,x)]\)
  • 3. Move \( eg\) in, using the dual and De Morgan: \( orall x\, [\exists y\; Animal(y) \wedge eg Loves(x,y)] \vee [\exists z\; Loves(z,x)]\)
  • 5. Skolemize. Both \(\exists\) are inside \( orall x\), so both become functions of \(x\): \(y \Rightarrow F(x)\), \(z \Rightarrow G(x)\): \( orall x\, [Animal(F(x)) \wedge eg Loves(x, F(x))] \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
  • 6. Drop \( orall\), 7. distribute, 8. split:
    • \(Animal(F(x)) \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
    • \( eg Loves(x, F(x)) \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
  • Read the Skolem functions back: \(F(x)\) is “the animal \(x\) does not love, if there is one” and \(G(x)\) is “someone who loves \(x\)”. Saying that in one line shows the step was understood, not copied.
Where marks are actually lost
  • Skolemizing to a constant inside a \( orall\). \( orall x \exists y\) becomes \(F(x)\), never \(A\). This is the single commonest error, and it silently changes the meaning.
  • Distributing where you must not. \( eg(A \wedge eg B) \vee C\) is \( eg A \vee B \vee C\) \(-\) one clause. It is not \(( eg A \vee C) \wedge (B \vee C)\). The local textbook makes exactly this error in its “likes all food” problem, then quietly uses the correct single clause in the proof underneath. The companion works that family properly.
  • Forgetting to standardise apart. Two clauses both using \(x\) will unify on a variable they do not share in meaning.
  • Dropping \( orall\) before skolemizing. The order in the list is not decoration: once the \( orall\) is gone there is nothing to make the Skolem function depend on.
  • Simplification is allowed and is worth doing: a clause containing both \(P\) and \( eg P\) is a tautology and can be dropped, and duplicate literals in one clause collapse.

column1: Prove the given goal from the given premises using resolution refutation
column4:
The procedure. This is the chapter.
  • 1. Convert every premise into FOPL.
  • 2. Convert every FOPL sentence into CNF (§4.4), and number the clauses.
  • 3. Negate the goal, convert that to CNF too, and add it to the clause set.
  • 4. Repeatedly resolve two clauses containing complementary literals, unifying them with the MGU, and add the resolvent.
  • 5. Stop when the empty clause \(\square\) is derived. The clause set is then unsatisfiable, so the negated goal is false, so the goal is true.
Why refute instead of prove directly
  • Resolution is refutation complete, not complete: it is guaranteed to find a contradiction in an unsatisfiable set, but it is not guaranteed to derive an arbitrary true sentence.
  • So the proof is turned round using \(KB \models \alpha\) iff \(KB \wedge \neg\alpha\) is unsatisfiable, the equivalence from §4.2.
How to write one that scores
  • Number every clause and, beside each resolvent, write which two clauses it came from and which substitution was used. Examiners award those annotations.
  • Resolve towards the goal. Start from the negated goal clause and work down: it prunes the search and it reads as a proof rather than a search log.
  • One complementary pair per step. Cancelling two pairs in one line is unsound and is a standard trap.
  • Standardise variables apart before each step (§4.4, step 8).
  • Finish with the sentence “the empty clause is derived, so the assumption contradicts the premises, hence the goal is proved”. It is worth a mark and takes one line.
The shape the answer must take: clauses down the left, each resolvent to its right, the empty clause \(\square\) at the foot. Premises are the Colonel West set, asked in 7 papers.
Contradiction Vs extraction (the textbook's two methods)
  • Answer by contradiction: negate the goal, derive \(\square\). Use this whenever the paper says prove that …, which is 21 of the 23 sets.
  • Answer by extraction: do not negate; chain the clauses forward until the goal literal itself is produced. Use it when the paper asks who or what rather than prove, Eg 72 Ma's “did Marcus hate Caesar?”
  • Same clauses, same resolution rule; only the starting point differs.
33 papers, but only 26 different premise sets, and four families cover 22 of them
  • Likes-all-food / peanuts \(-\) 7 papers, five wordings of one puzzle (John/Bill/Sue, Ram/Krishna/Radha, Ram/Anil, Sita/mushroom, Bhogendra/chicken). Learn this one first.
  • Charlie is a horse / a mammal \(-\) 6 papers, three wordings. Tests inverse relations, and two of its six premises are never used.
  • Selling weapons to a hostile nation \(-\) 7 papers under six names, one asking for forward chaining instead. Tests existential instantiation.
  • Light sleeper, hounds and mice \(-\) 2 papers. The hardest of the four: the goal is itself an implication, so negating it gives three clauses.
  • Then 10 one-off sets, from Marcus and Caesar to Curiosity and the cat.
The two things that go wrong in an exam
  • Negating a goal that is an implication. “If John is a light sleeper then John has no mice” negates to “John IS a light sleeper AND John HAS a mouse”, which after skolemization is three clauses: \(LS(John)\), \(Have(John, b)\), \(Mouse(b)\). Students negate it to one clause and the proof cannot close.
  • “Has some” is existential. “Nono has some missiles” is \(\exists x\, Missile(x) \wedge Owns(Nono, x)\), which skolemizes to a new constant \(M_1\): two clauses, \(Missile(M_1)\) and \(Owns(Nono, M_1)\). Writing \(Missile(x)\) with a free variable claims everything is a missile.
  • Both are worked step by step in the companion, which prints each paper's premises exactly as the paper words them.

column1: Differentiate between forward and backward chaining with a suitable example
column4:
Forward chaining: data-driven
  • Start from the known facts. Fire every rule whose premises are all satisfied, add its conclusion to the fact base, repeat until the goal appears or nothing new can be derived.
  • Bottom-up, and it uses modus ponens on definite clauses.
  • ✓Derives everything that follows, so it suits monitoring, alarms and planning, where new data arrives and consequences must be found.
  • ×Does a lot of irrelevant work: it proves facts nobody asked for.
Backward chaining: goal-driven
  • Start from the goal. Find a rule that concludes it, make that rule's premises the new sub-goals, and recurse until every sub-goal is a known fact.
  • Top-down, depth first, and again modus ponens.
  • ✓Touches only what the goal needs, so it suits diagnosis, query answering and theorem proving. Prolog works this way.
  • ×Can loop on recursive rules, and it answers only the question asked.
Forward chaining on the Colonel West premises: facts on the bottom row, one new row per iteration, until \(Criminal(Robert)\) appears.
Backward chaining, same premises: the goal at the top, its four conjuncts below it, each expanded until it meets a fact. The binding that made each unification succeed sits under its node.
Forward chainingBackward chaining
Starts fromKnown facts / dataThe goal to be proved
DirectionBottom-up, data-drivenTop-down, goal-driven
Question answered“What can I conclude?”“Can I prove this?”
SearchBreadth-first in effect: all consequences of the current factsDepth-first: one sub-goal chain at a time
Work doneDerives many facts, most irrelevant to any one goalDerives only what the goal needs
SuitsMonitoring, alarms, planning, real-time control, designDiagnosis, query answering, theorem proving, Prolog
Number of goalsHandles many goals at onceHandles one goal at a time
EfficiencySlow when the goal is specificSlow when the fact base is small and rules are deep
  • The one-line discriminator to write: forward chaining asks what follows from what I know, backward chaining asks what would I need to know for this to be true. Same rules, same modus ponens, opposite ends.

column1: What is rule-based reasoning?
column4:
Definition and parts
  • Knowledge stored as IF condition THEN action rules, and reasoning done by an inference engine that decides which rule to fire.
  • Three components:
    • Rule base \(-\) the IF-THEN rules (long-term knowledge);
    • Working memory \(-\) the facts known right now;
    • Inference engine \(-\) match, resolve conflicts, fire.
  • The engine's cycle is match \(\rightarrow\) conflict resolution \(\rightarrow\) execute, exactly the production system of Ch 2. Say so: the examiner set that question too.
Why it is used, and the worked shape
  • ✓Rules are modular: add or remove one without touching the rest. ✓They are readable by a domain expert who is not a programmer. ✓The chain of fired rules is the explanation, which is how an expert system justifies itself (Ch 7).
  • ×No learning, and ×large rule bases become slow and can conflict.
  • The example to give, since every paper asks for one:
    • R1: IF fever AND cough THEN flu. R2: IF flu THEN prescribe rest.
    • Facts: fever, cough. Forward: R1 fires, flu added, R2 fires, prescribe rest. Backward from prescribe rest: needs flu, which needs fever and cough, both known. Two directions, one rule base.

column1: How is reasoning done under uncertainty? What are the approaches for measuring it?
column4:
Why logic is not enough
  • FOPL is monotonic and categorical: a fact is true or false, and adding knowledge never retracts a conclusion. The real world is neither.
  • Three sources of uncertainty, and papers want them named:
    • incomplete knowledge (not all facts are available);
    • imprecise / unreliable data (a sensor, a symptom);
    • rules that are only usually true (a stiff neck suggests meningitis).
  • Writing stiff neck \(\rightarrow\) meningitis in logic is simply false, and listing every exception is impossible. So attach a number to the belief instead.
The approaches for measuring uncertainty
  • Probability theory \(-\) degree of belief in \([0,1]\), updated by Bayes' rule. The mainstream answer, and the only one the numericals use.
  • Certainty factors \(-\) an ad-hoc \([-1, +1]\) score attached to each rule, as used in MYCIN. Simple, but not probabilistically sound.
  • Dempster-Shafer theory \(-\) assigns belief to sets of hypotheses, so it can represent ignorance separately from disbelief.
  • Fuzzy logic \(-\) handles vagueness (“tall”, “warm”), which is a different thing from uncertainty. Covered in Ch 6.
  • Non-monotonic / default reasoning \(-\) assume the normal case, retract the conclusion when contradicted.
  • The distinction worth one mark: probability is about not knowing which case holds; fuzzy logic is about the case not having a sharp boundary.

column1: What is prior and posterior probability? Explain Bayes' theorem and its role in reasoning
column4:
The vocabulary
  • Prior \(P(A)\) \(-\) belief in \(A\) before any evidence. Eg 1 person in 50,000 has meningitis.
  • Posterior \(P(A|B)\) \(-\) belief in \(A\) after evidence \(B\) is observed. Eg the chance of meningitis given a stiff neck.
  • Likelihood \(P(B|A)\) \(-\) how probable the evidence is if the hypothesis holds. This is the number a doctor actually knows, and it is the reason the theorem is needed.
  • Marginal \(P(B)\) \(-\) the probability of the evidence however it arose.
The theorem
\[ P(A|B) \;=\; rac{P(B|A)\,P(A)}{P(B)} \]
  • When \(P(B)\) is not given, expand it by the law of total probability, which is what most papers require:
\[ P(A|B) = rac{P(B|A)P(A)}{P(B|A)P(A) + P(B| eg A)P( eg A)} \]
How it aids inference (the marks in the theory half)
  • It reverses the direction of a conditional. Causal knowledge runs cause \( ightarrow\) effect (\(P( extit{symptom}\,|\, extit{disease})\), stable and measurable); diagnosis needs effect \( ightarrow\) cause. Bayes converts one into the other.
  • It gives a principled update rule: posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \( imes\) prior. Evidence does not replace belief, it revises it.
  • It makes the base rate explicit. A 99 %-accurate test for a 1-in-10,000 disease still leaves you far more likely to be healthy than ill, because the prior is tiny. This is asked directly (72 Ash) and it is the single most useful sentence in the section.
  • It composes: a chain of evidence can be applied one piece at a time, which is exactly what a belief network does below.
Getting the arithmetic right
  • Name the events before substituting. Half the lost marks are a \(P(A|B)\) written where \(P(B|A)\) was meant.
  • If the question gives percentages of a population that split into groups (factories, men and women), the denominator is always the total-probability sum over those groups.
  • \(P( eg A) = 1 - P(A)\) is almost always needed and almost never given.

column1: What is a causal / belief network? How is reasoning done in it?
column4:
Definition and the two parts
  • A directed acyclic graph in which
    • each node is a random variable, and
    • each edge \(X \rightarrow Y\) says \(X\) has a direct causal influence on \(Y\);
    plus a conditional probability table (CPT) at every node giving \(P(\textit{node} \mid \textit{its parents})\).
  • A root node has no parents, so its CPT is just its prior.
  • The whole network in one equation, and this is what the numericals use:
\[ P(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{n} P\big(x_i \mid parents(x_i)\big) \]
  • Why it is worth having: a full joint distribution over \(n\) binary variables needs \(2^n - 1\) numbers. The alarm network below has 5 variables and needs only 10, because each node depends on its parents alone. That compactness is the answer to when do we use a Bayesian network.
  • Conditional independence is the property being exploited: a node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents.
Reasoning in the network (the 5 or 6 marks)
  • Causal / top-down \(-\) from cause to effect. Burglary happened; how likely is John to call? Uses the CPTs directly.
  • Diagnostic / bottom-up \(-\) from effect to cause. John called; how likely is a burglary? This is where Bayes' theorem enters, and it is the answer to “how is Bayes' theorem used in a belief network” (77 Ch).
  • Intercausal \(-\) between two causes of one observed effect. The alarm rang and an earthquake is reported, so burglary becomes less likely: explaining away. Worth naming; almost nobody does.
  • Mixed \(-\) evidence above and below the query node at once.
  • The method for a numerical: write the product form, substitute one CPT entry per variable, and read \(P(\neg X) = 1 - P(X)\) off the same table.
A causal net: Cloudy influences Sprinkler and Rain, both influence WetGrass. The shape 78 Ba prints.
The standard alarm network, with a CPT at every node. Burglary and Earthquake both cause Alarm; the alarm makes John and Mary call. Five variables, and the graph plus these five tables hold the whole joint distribution in 10 numbers instead of \(2^5 - 1 = 31\). The worked line beside it is the product form applied straight down the network, which is exactly what 78 Ba and 82 Bh ask for.
  • The connection the papers ask for in one sentence: a belief network stores causal conditional probabilities, and Bayes' theorem is what lets you run them backwards to a diagnosis. Without the network you would need the full joint distribution; without Bayes you could only reason in the direction the arrows point.

column1: Chapter 4 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
The biggest companion in the subject. 33 papers set a resolution refutation, 15 set a Bayes calculation, 4 set a CNF conversion and 1 sets a truth-table proof. Every one is worked below under the question exactly as its paper prints it. Renamings of a puzzle already worked get the paper's own statement plus what changes, so nothing is left to guess and no proof is copied out twice.
The five procedures everything here is built on
  • P1 Truth table \(-\) \(2^n\) rows for \(n\) symbols; a tautology is a column of all T.
  • P2 CNF \(-\) eliminate \(\leftrightarrow\), eliminate \( ightarrow\), move \( eg\) in, standardise apart, skolemize, drop \( orall\), distribute \(\vee\) over \(\wedge\), split.
  • P3 Resolution refutation \(-\) FOPL, CNF, negate the goal, resolve on complementary literals with the MGU, derive \(\square\).
  • P4 Chaining \(-\) forward from the facts, or backward from the goal, on definite clauses.
  • P5 Bayes \(-\) \(P(A|B) = \dfrac{P(B|A)P(A)}{P(B|A)P(A) + P(B| eg A)P( eg A)}\), and for a network \(P(x_1 \ldots x_n) = \prod P(x_i \mid parents(x_i))\).
Notation used throughout: constants start with a capital, variables are \(x, y, z\), and a clause is written as a disjunction of literals. Beside every resolvent, (i, j) names the two clauses it came from and \([t/x]\) the substitution used. That annotation is where a third of the marks sit.

column1: P1. Truth tables: WFF, validity and tautology — Define a WFF with its properties. Prove that \((A \wedge (A \rightarrow B)) \rightarrow B\) is a tautology
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2071 Bhadra · CT 78506 · [4+4]
Define a WFF with its properties. Prove that the proposition (A \(\wedge\) (A \(\rightarrow\) B) \(\rightarrow\) B) is a tautology.
column4:
Solution: build the table
  • Two symbols, so \(2^2 = 4\) rows. Work left to right, one column per sub-formula.
AB\(A \rightarrow B\)\(A \wedge (A \rightarrow B)\)\(\ldots \rightarrow B\)
TTTTT
TFFFT
FTTFT
FFTFT
  • The last column is T in every row, so the proposition is valid: a tautology. ✓
  • Rows 2–4 are true vacuously: the antecedent \(A \wedge (A \rightarrow B)\) is false, and \(F \rightarrow\) anything is T. Say that or the last mark is at risk.
The definition half of the answer
  • A well-formed formula is a string built only by the recursive rules in §4.2: a symbol; \(\neg\alpha\); \((\alpha)\); and \((\alpha \wedge \beta)\), \((\alpha \vee \beta)\), \((\alpha \rightarrow \beta)\), \((\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta)\) for WFFs \(\alpha, \beta\) \(-\) and nothing else.
  • Properties to list: it is finite; it is uniquely parsed (brackets or precedence fix the reading); it has a truth value under every interpretation; and it is exactly the set of strings the inference rules may be applied to.
  • \(A \wedge \rightarrow B\) and \((A \vee B\) are not WFFs: no rule builds them. Giving one non-example is worth a mark.
  • This formula is modus ponens written as a single proposition, which is the point of the question: an inference rule is sound exactly when its implication form is a tautology. Cross-refer to the rules table and the two marks for “properties” are safe.

column1: P2. Conversion to CNF — P \(\vee\) (\(\neg\)P \(\wedge\) Q \(\wedge\) R), and “Everyone who loves all animals is loved by someone”
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2073 Bhadra · CT 78506 · [2+2+2+3]
Why is conjunctive normal form required? Explain all the steps to convert to CNF, and transform the given sentences into CNF: P \(\vee\) (\(\neg\)P \(\wedge\) Q \(\wedge\) R); and “Everyone who loves all animals is loved by someone.”
column4:
Part 1: \(P \vee ( eg P \wedge Q \wedge R)\)
  • No \(\leftrightarrow\), no \( ightarrow\), no negation to move: go straight to step 7, distribute \(\vee\) over \(\wedge\).
  • \(P \vee ( eg P \wedge Q \wedge R)\) \[ = (P \vee eg P) \wedge (P \vee Q) \wedge (P \vee R) \]
  • \(P \vee eg P\) is a tautology, true in every model, so the clause adds nothing and is dropped: \[ oxed{(P \vee Q) \wedge (P \vee R)} \]
  • Two clauses: \(\{P, Q\}\) and \(\{P, R\}\).
  • Dropping the tautologous clause is worth doing and worth saying. Leaving it in is not wrong, but the simplification is the part that shows the definition was understood.
Part 2: the quantified sentence
  • FOPL: \( orall x\,[ orall y\; Animal(y) ightarrow Loves(x,y)] ightarrow [\exists z\; Loves(z,x)]\)
  • Eliminate \( ightarrow\) (both of them): \( orall x\, eg[ orall y\; eg Animal(y) \vee Loves(x,y)] \vee \exists z\; Loves(z,x)\)
  • Move \( eg\) inwards, dual then De Morgan: \( orall x\, [\exists y\; Animal(y) \wedge eg Loves(x,y)] \vee \exists z\; Loves(z,x)\)
  • Skolemize. Both \(\exists\) sit inside \( orall x\), so both become functions of \(x\): \(y \Rightarrow F(x)\), \(z \Rightarrow G(x)\).
  • Drop \( orall\), distribute, split:
    • \(Animal(F(x)) \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
    • \( eg Loves(x, F(x)) \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
  • \(F\) and \(G\) must be functions, not constants. A constant would claim one single animal, and one single admirer, for the whole universe.

column1: P2. Conversion to CNF — P \(\rightarrow\) ((Q \(\wedge\) \(\neg\)R) \(\rightarrow\) S)
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2074 Magh · CT 78506 · [6]
Why is conjunctive normal form required? Explain all the steps to convert to CNF, and transform the given sentence into CNF: P \(\rightarrow\) ((Q \(\wedge\) \(\neg\)R) \(\rightarrow\) S)
column4:
Solution
  • Inner implication first: \((Q \wedge eg R) ightarrow S \;=\; eg(Q \wedge eg R) \vee S\)
  • Outer implication: \(P ightarrow [ eg(Q \wedge eg R) \vee S] \;=\; eg P \vee eg(Q \wedge eg R) \vee S\)
  • De Morgan, then double negation: \( eg(Q \wedge eg R) = eg Q \vee R\)
  • \[ oxed{ eg P \vee eg Q \vee R \vee S} \]
The point of this one
  • Nothing to distribute, so the answer is a single clause with four literals. A conjunction of one clause is still CNF.
  • Students who expect several clauses often invent a split that is not there. \(\vee\) distributes over \(\wedge\), never the reverse, and there is no \(\wedge\) left at the top level here.
  • Written as a set: \(\{ eg P, eg Q, R, S\}\). It is a definite clause \(-\) two positive literals, so no; it is a plain clause. (Definite needs exactly one positive literal, and this has two, \(R\) and \(S\).) A one-line check like that is what 78 Ch's Horn-clause part is testing.

column1: P2. Conversion to CNF — P \(\rightarrow\) ((Q \(\wedge\) \(\neg\)R) \(\leftrightarrow\) S)
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Ashwin · CT 78506 · [8]
Why is conjunctive normal form required? Explain all the steps to convert to CNF, and transform the given sentence into CNF: P \(\rightarrow\) ((Q \(\wedge\) \(\neg\)R) \(\leftrightarrow\) S)
column4:
Solution: the biconditional first
  • Write \(M = Q \wedge eg R\) to keep the algebra readable.
  • Step 1, eliminate \(\leftrightarrow\): \(M \leftrightarrow S \;=\; (M ightarrow S) \wedge (S ightarrow M)\)
  • Step 2, eliminate \( ightarrow\) inside: \(= ( eg M \vee S) \wedge ( eg S \vee M)\)
  • Substitute \(M\) back and apply De Morgan to \( eg M\): \[ ( eg Q \vee R \vee S) \wedge ( eg S \vee (Q \wedge eg R)) \]
  • Step 7, distribute in the right half: \( eg S \vee (Q \wedge eg R) = ( eg S \vee Q) \wedge ( eg S \vee eg R)\)
  • So the inner formula is \(( eg Q \vee R \vee S) \wedge ( eg S \vee Q) \wedge ( eg S \vee eg R)\).
  • Now the outer implication: \(P ightarrow X = eg P \vee X\), and \( eg P\) distributes into every clause of \(X\): \[ oxed{ egin{aligned} &( eg P \vee eg Q \vee R \vee S) \;\wedge \ &( eg P \vee eg S \vee Q) \;\wedge \ &( eg P \vee eg S \vee eg R) \end{aligned}} \]
  • Three clauses.
Where this one goes wrong
  • Expanding \(\leftrightarrow\) the other way. \(A \leftrightarrow B\) is also \((A \wedge B) \vee ( eg A \wedge eg B)\). That is correct logic but it is a disjunction of conjunctions, so it takes twice the work to push back into CNF. Always use the two-implications form.
  • Forgetting to distribute \( eg P\) into all three clauses. \( eg P \vee (C_1 \wedge C_2 \wedge C_3)\) is not \( eg P \vee C_1 \wedge C_2 \wedge C_3\); the \( eg P\) joins each clause.
  • Sanity check that costs 10 seconds: set \(P\) false. Every clause contains \( eg P\), so all three are satisfied \(-\) which is right, because \(P ightarrow \ldots\) is vacuously true. Set \(P\) true, \(S\) true, \(Q\) false: clause 2 becomes \(F \vee F \vee F\), false, and indeed \(S\) true with \(Q\) false breaks the biconditional. The CNF behaves like the original.

column1: P2. Conversion to CNF — \(\neg\)(P \(\wedge\) Q) \(\vee\) (P \(\vee\) S) \(\rightarrow\) R
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Jestha · CT 653 · [2+2+4]
Why is conjunctive normal form required? Explain all the steps to convert to CNF, and transform the given sentences into CNF: (i) \(\neg\)(P \(\wedge\) Q) \(\vee\) (P \(\vee\) S) \(\rightarrow\) R   (ii) P \(\rightarrow\) ((Q \(\wedge\) \(\neg\)R) \(\leftrightarrow\) S)
column4:
Solution
  • \( ightarrow\) binds loosest, so the sentence reads \( ig[ eg(P \wedge Q) \vee (P \vee S) ig] ightarrow R\). Reading the brackets wrongly here changes the answer; state the reading before starting.
  • Eliminate \( ightarrow\): \( eg ig[ eg(P \wedge Q) \vee P \vee S ig] \vee R\)
  • Move \( eg\) in (De Morgan on the bracket): \( ig[(P \wedge Q) \wedge eg P \wedge eg S ig] \vee R\)
  • Distribute \(\vee R\) over the four conjuncts: \[ oxed{(P \vee R) \wedge (Q \vee R) \wedge ( eg P \vee R) \wedge ( eg S \vee R)} \]
  • Four clauses.
Reading the answer back
  • Clauses 1 and 3 are \((P \vee R)\) and \(( eg P \vee R)\). Resolving them gives \(R\) on its own, so the whole sentence is equivalent to \(R\).
  • That is correct: the antecedent \( eg(P \wedge Q) \vee P \vee S\) is a tautology (if \(P\) is false the first disjunct is true, if \(P\) is true the second is), and \( ext{True} ightarrow R\) is just \(R\).
  • Saying this earns the last mark and proves the conversion was not mechanical. It is also the cleanest possible demonstration of why resolution wants CNF: two clauses in, one simpler clause out.

column1: P3. Translating English into FOPL — Convert the following into FOL
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Bhadra · CT 78506 · [2]
Convert the following into FOL.
  1. Arya hates Joffery and Cersei.
  2. No Lannister loves Bran.
  3. Sansa has at least one sister.
  4. Every Stark hates at least one Lannister.
column4:
Solution
  • a) Two separate facts, joined by \(\wedge\). No quantifier: both are named individuals. \[ hates(Arya, Joffery) \wedge hates(Arya, Cersei) \]
  • b) “No A loves B” \(=\) there is no A that loves B, or equivalently every A fails to love B: \[ eg \exists x\, ig[Lannister(x) \wedge loves(x, Bran) ig] \] \[ \equiv\; orall x\, ig[Lannister(x) ightarrow eg loves(x, Bran) ig] \]
  • c) “at least one” \(=\) \(\exists\), and \(\exists\) takes \(\wedge\): \[ \exists x\, ig[sister(x) \wedge sisterOf(x, Sansa) ig] \]
  • d) \( orall\) outside, \(\exists\) inside, because each Stark may hate a different Lannister: \[ orall x\, \Big[Stark(x) ightarrow \exists y\, ig(Lannister(y) \wedge hates(x,y) ig)\Big] \]
The four rules this question tests
  • \( orall\) takes \( ightarrow\); \(\exists\) takes \(\wedge\). Every wrong answer to (c) or (d) breaks this.
  • Quantifier order carries meaning. \( orall x \exists y\) (each Stark hates some Lannister) is not \(\exists y orall x\) (one Lannister is hated by all Starks). The English “at least one” after “every” fixes the order as \( orall\exists\).
  • “No” negates the whole existential, not the predicate. Writing \( orall x\, Lannister(x) \wedge eg loves(x,Bran)\) says everything in the universe is a Lannister.
  • Both forms of (b) are correct and equivalent by the dual \( eg\exists \equiv orall eg\). Giving both, with that one-line justification, is a complete answer to a 2-mark part.
  • Predicate names are your choice, but stay consistent: \(sisterOf(x,y)\) must mean the same thing every time it appears.

column1: P4. Unification: finding the MGU
column4:
Worked
  • 1. \(King(x)\), \(King(John)\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta = [John/x]\).
  • 2. \(P(x, y)\), \(P(a, f(z))\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta = [a/x,\; f(z)/y]\). \(z\) stays free: binding it would be less general.
  • 3. \(P(x, f(y))\), \(P(a, f(g(x)))\) \(\rightarrow\) start with \([a/x]\), then \(y\) must match \(g(x)\), and \(x\) is already \(a\): \[ \theta = [a/x,\; g(a)/y] \]
  • 4. \(Q(a, g(x,a), f(y))\), \(Q(a, g(f(b),a), x)\) \(\rightarrow\) \(x\) must be \(f(b)\) from the second argument, and then \(f(y)\) must match \(x = f(b)\), giving \(y = b\): \[ \theta = [f(b)/x,\; b/y] \]
The three ways it fails
  • Different predicate or arity. \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) never unify; neither do \(P(x)\) and \(P(x,y)\).
  • Two different constants. \(King(John)\) and \(King(Ram)\) fail: a constant cannot be substituted.
  • Occurs check. \(x\) cannot bind to \(f(x)\); the substitution would never terminate.
  • Apply each binding to everything already found, as in example 3. Reporting \([a/x, g(x)/y]\) instead of \([a/x, g(a)/y]\) is the standard half-mark loss.
  • Standardise apart before unifying two clauses. If both clauses call their variable \(x\), rename one to \(x'\) first, or the unifier will tie together two variables that have nothing to do with each other.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  Family A: likes all kinds of food
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Ashwin · Q10 · [7] also 2074 Bhadra [8], 2073 Bhadra CT 78506 [8]
Assume the following facts: John likes all kinds of food; apples are food; chicken is food; anything anyone eats and isn't killed by is food; Bill eats peanuts and is still alive; Sue eats everything Bill eats. Prove that John likes peanuts using resolution refutation.
column4:
Step 1 Facts into FOPL
  • 1. \( orall x\; food(x) ightarrow likes(John, x)\)
  • 2. \(food(Apple)\)
  • 3. \(food(Chicken)\)
  • 4. \( orall y orall x\; ig[eats(y,x) \wedge eg killed(y) ig] ightarrow food(x)\)
  • 5. \(eats(Bill, Peanuts) \wedge eg killed(Bill)\)
  • 6. \( orall x\; eats(Bill, x) ightarrow eats(Sue, x)\)
“is still alive” is written \( eg killed\), not a new predicate \(alive\). One predicate fewer, one resolution step fewer.
Step 2 Into CNF
  • 1. \( eg food(x) \vee likes(John, x)\)
  • 2. \(food(Apple)\)
  • 3. \(food(Chicken)\)
  • 4. \( eg eats(y,x) \vee killed(y) \vee food(x)\)
  • 5a. \(eats(Bill, Peanuts)\)
  • 5b. \( eg killed(Bill)\)
  • 6. \( eg eats(Bill, x) \vee eats(Sue, x)\)
Step 3 Negate the goal
  • 7. \( eg likes(John, Peanuts)\)
Step 4 Resolution
  • 8. \( eg food(Peanuts)\) (7, 1) \([Peanuts/x]\)
  • 9. \( eg eats(y, Peanuts) \vee killed(y)\) (8, 4) \([Peanuts/x]\)
  • 10. \(killed(Bill)\) (9, 5a) \([Bill/y]\)
  • 11. \(\square\) (10, 5b)
Final answer
  • The empty clause is derived, so \(KB \wedge eg goal\) is unsatisfiable. “John likes peanuts” is proved. ✓
  • Clauses 2, 3 and 6 are never used: apples, chicken and Sue are distractors. Saying so is a mark in a 8-mark answer, not a risk.
The step the textbook gets wrong
  • Fact 4 has the shape \( eg[A \wedge eg B] \vee C\), which is \( eg A \vee B \vee C\): one clause.
  • Insights splits it into two, \( eg eats(y,x) \vee food(x)\) and \( eg killed(y) \vee food(x)\). That is not a valid equivalence \(-\) it asserts that merely not being killed makes something food \(-\) and the book's own resolution graph then quietly uses the correct single clause.
  • Write the one clause. If the marker expects the book's two, the proof still closes, and yours is the sound one.

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2071 Bhadra · CT 78506 · [8]
Assume the following facts: a) Ram likes all kinds of food; b) Apples are food; c) Chicken is food; d) Anything anyone eats and is not killed by is food; e) Krishna eats peanuts and is still alive; f) Radha eats everything Krishna eats. Prove the statement “Ram likes peanut” using resolution.

Assume the following facts: i) Ram likes all kinds of food; ii) apples and vegetables are food; iii) anything anyone eats and not killed is food; iv) Anil eats peanuts and is still alive; v) Ram eats everything that Anil eats. Prove that “Ram likes peanuts” using resolution refutation.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Baishakh · CT 710 · [8]
Assume the following facts: a) Sita likes all kinds of food; b) Momo and Burger are food; c) anything anyone eats and isn't killed by is food; d) Bill eats mushroom and is still alive; e) Sue eats everything Bill eats. Prove that “Sita likes mushroom” using resolution refutation method.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Magh · CT 78506 · [6+4]
Bhogendra likes all kinds of food. Oranges are food. Chicken is food. Anything anyone eats and isn't killed by is food. If a person likes a food it means that person has eaten it. Jogendra eats peanuts and is still alive. Shailendri eats everything Bhogendra eats. Express them in FOPL, put them into clause form, and use resolution to prove that Shailendri likes chicken.
column4:
What changes, and what does not
PaperLikes all foodEats itGoal
72 Ash, 74 Bh, 73 BhJohnBill (Sue copies)peanuts
71 BhRamKrishna (Radha copies)peanuts
80 BhRamAnil (Ram copies)peanuts
80 BaSitaBill (Sue copies)mushroom
  • The proof is identical in all four: negate, resolve with clause 1 to get \(\neg food(g)\), resolve with clause 4 to get \(\neg eats(y,g) \vee killed(y)\), then the two halves of the eating fact. Substitute the names and the four steps are unchanged.
  • 80 Bh is the one worth a second look: there the copier is Ram himself, the same person who likes all food. It changes nothing \(-\) the copying clause is still unused \(-\) but it looks like it should, and that is the trap.
  • 80 Ba swaps apples and chicken for momo and burger. Also unused.
2072 Magh (CT 78506) is a different problem
  • It adds a fifth premise, “if a person likes a food it means that person has eaten it”, and asks for Shailendri \(-\) the copier \(-\) to like chicken.
  • Take the premises literally:
    • \(food(Chicken)\) and \(\forall x\, food(x) \rightarrow likes(Bhogendra, x)\) give \(likes(Bhogendra, Chicken)\);
    • \(\forall x \forall y\, likes(x,y) \rightarrow eats(x,y)\) gives \(eats(Bhogendra, Chicken)\);
    • \(\forall x\, eats(Bhogendra,x) \rightarrow eats(Shailendri,x)\) gives \(eats(Shailendri, Chicken)\).
  • And there it stops. Nothing in the premise set makes Shailendri like anything: only Bhogendra has a likes-rule, and the new premise runs likes \(\rightarrow\) eats, not back.
  • How to answer it: prove \(eats(Shailendri, Chicken)\) in full, then add one line \(-\) “to reach likes the fifth premise must be read as a biconditional, \(likes(x,y) \leftrightarrow eats(x,y)\); with that reading one more resolution step gives \(likes(Shailendri, Chicken)\).”
  • Do not silently reverse the implication and hope. Stating the gap is worth more than a proof that assumes it away.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  Family B: Charlie is a horse
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2073 Bhadra · Q10 · [8] also 2078 Poush [8], 2074 Bhadra CT 78506 [8], 2079 Jestha [6]
Assume the following facts: i) horses, cows, pigs are mammals; ii) an offspring of a horse is a horse; iii) Bluebeard is a horse; iv) Bluebeard is Charlie's parent; v) offspring and parent are inverse relations; vi) every mammal has a parent. Prove Charlie is a horse using resolution refutation.
column4:
Step 1 Facts into FOPL
  • 1. \( orall x\; horse(x) ightarrow mammal(x)\), and the same for \(cow\), \(pig\)
  • 2. \( orall x orall y\; ig[offspring(x,y) \wedge horse(y) ig] ightarrow horse(x)\)
  • 3. \(horse(Bluebeard)\)
  • 4. \(parent(Bluebeard, Charlie)\)
  • 5. \( orall x orall y\; offspring(x,y) \leftrightarrow parent(y,x)\)
  • 6. \( orall x\; mammal(x) ightarrow \exists y\; parent(y, x)\)
Step 2 Into CNF
  • 1a. \( eg horse(x) \vee mammal(x)\) (1b, 1c likewise for cow, pig)
  • 2. \( eg offspring(x,y) \vee eg horse(y) \vee horse(x)\)
  • 3. \(horse(Bluebeard)\)
  • 4. \(parent(Bluebeard, Charlie)\)
  • 5a. \( eg offspring(x,y) \vee parent(y,x)\)
  • 5b. \( eg parent(y,x) \vee offspring(x,y)\)
  • 6. \( eg mammal(x) \vee parent ig(f(x),\, x ig)\)
The \(\exists y\) in premise 6 sits inside \( orall x\), so it skolemizes to a function \(f(x)\): each mammal has its own parent. Insights writes a free variable \(y\) here, which claims every object is a parent of every mammal. It changes nothing in this proof, because clause 6 is never used, but it is wrong and in another problem it would prove anything.
Step 3 Negate the goal
  • 7. \( eg horse(Charlie)\)
Step 4 Resolution
  • 8. \( eg offspring(Charlie, y) \vee eg horse(y)\) (7, 2) \([Charlie/x]\)
  • 9. \( eg offspring(Charlie, Bluebeard)\) (8, 3) \([Bluebeard/y]\)
  • 10. \( eg parent(Bluebeard, Charlie)\) (9, 5b) \([Charlie/x, Bluebeard/y]\)
  • 11. \(\square\) (10, 4)
Final answer
  • “Charlie is a horse” is proved. ✓ Four resolution steps.
  • Premises 1 and 6 are never used. The mammal chain is a complete red herring for this goal: being a horse follows from the offspring rule alone. Say it in one line \(-\) examiners set the extra premises to see whether the proof is understood or remembered.
  • The whole problem is premise 5. Written as a biconditional it yields the two clauses 5a and 5b, and only 5b is used: it turns the given \(parent(Bluebeard, Charlie)\) into the \(offspring(Charlie, Bluebeard)\) that rule 2 needs. A one-directional reading of “inverse relations” cannot close the proof.
  • Watch the argument order: \(offspring(x,y)\) means \(x\) is the offspring of \(y\), so its inverse is \(parent(y,x)\), not \(parent(x,y)\). Getting this backwards is the commonest failure on this set.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2077 Chaitra · Q10 · [8] also 2082 Kartik [8]
It is a crime for an American to sell weapons to hostile nations. Nono has some missiles. All the missiles owned by Nono were sold to it by Colonel West. Missiles are weapons. An enemy of America counts as hostile. Colonel West is an American. The country Nono is an enemy of America. Prove that Colonel West is a criminal by using FOPL based Resolution Refutation.
column4:
Step 1 Facts into FOPL
  • 1. \( orall p orall q orall r\; ig[American(p) \wedge Weapon(q) \wedge Sells(p,q,r) \wedge Hostile(r) ig] ightarrow Criminal(p)\)
  • 2. \(\exists x\; Missile(x) \wedge Owns(Nono, x)\)
  • 3. \( orall x\; ig[Missile(x) \wedge Owns(Nono,x) ig] ightarrow Sells(West, x, Nono)\)
  • 4. \( orall x\; Missile(x) ightarrow Weapon(x)\)
  • 5. \( orall x\; Enemy(x, America) ightarrow Hostile(x)\)
  • 6. \(American(West)\)
  • 7. \(Enemy(Nono, America)\)
Step 2 Into CNF
  • 1. \( eg American(p) \vee eg Weapon(q) \vee eg Sells(p,q,r) \vee eg Hostile(r) \vee Criminal(p)\)
  • 2a. \(Missile(M_1)\) skolem constant
  • 2b. \(Owns(Nono, M_1)\)
  • 3. \( eg Missile(x) \vee eg Owns(Nono,x) \vee Sells(West,x,Nono)\)
  • 4. \( eg Missile(x) \vee Weapon(x)\)
  • 5. \( eg Enemy(x, America) \vee Hostile(x)\)
  • 6. \(American(West)\)   7. \(Enemy(Nono, America)\)
“Nono has some missiles” is existential. It is not \( orall x\, Missile(x)\), which would make everything a missile, and it is not a named missile either \(-\) the paper never names one. Skolemize to a brand-new constant \(M_1\) and it splits into two ground facts.
Step 3 Negate the goal
  • 8. \( eg Criminal(West)\)
Step 4 Resolution
  • 9. \( eg American(West) \vee eg Weapon(q) \vee eg Sells(West,q,r) \vee eg Hostile(r)\) (8, 1) \([West/p]\)
  • 10. \( eg Weapon(q) \vee eg Sells(West,q,r) \vee eg Hostile(r)\) (9, 6)
  • 11. \( eg Missile(q) \vee eg Sells(West,q,r) \vee eg Hostile(r)\) (10, 4) \([q/x]\)
  • 12. \( eg Missile(q) \vee eg Owns(Nono,q) \vee eg Hostile(Nono)\) (11, 3) \([q/x,\, Nono/r]\)
  • 13. \( eg Owns(Nono, M_1) \vee eg Hostile(Nono)\) (12, 2a) \([M_1/q]\)
  • 14. \( eg Hostile(Nono)\) (13, 2b)
  • 15. \( eg Enemy(Nono, America)\) (14, 5) \([Nono/x]\)
  • 16. \(\square\) (15, 7)
Final answer
  • “Colonel West is a criminal” is proved. ✓ Eight resolution steps, and every premise is used \(-\) unusual, and worth noticing, because it means no step can be skipped.
  • Work down the negated goal. Clause 1 has five literals; resolving it against clause 8 first turns the proof into a checklist of four conditions, each discharged by one premise. Starting anywhere else wanders.
  • In step 12 the literal \( eg Missile(q)\) appears twice after the substitution and collapses to one. Duplicate literals in a clause always do.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  Family C: selling weapons to a hostile nation — 2069 Bhadra and 2075 Baishakh: two premises are missing
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2069 Bhadra · Q10 · [10]
Every American who sells weapons to hostile nations is a criminal. The country Abc is enemy of America. All of the missiles in Abc were sold by John. John is an American. Prove John is a criminal.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2075 Baishakh · [8]
Every American who sells weapons to hostile nations is a criminal. The country XYZ is enemy of America. All of its missiles in XYZ were sold by Donald, who is an American. Prove that Donald is a criminal using FOPL based resolution refutation.
column4:
What is missing, and what to write
  • Clause 1 needs four things about \(p\): American, a weapon, a sale, and a hostile buyer. These two papers supply American, the sale and the enemy \(-\) but nothing links
    • missile to weapon, and
    • enemy of America to hostile.
  • Add both, and say you are adding them:
    • \(\forall x\; Missile(x) \rightarrow Weapon(x)\)
    • \(\forall x\; Enemy(x, America) \rightarrow Hostile(x)\)
  • Then the proof is exactly the 8 steps above with \([John/West,\, Abc/Nono]\) or \([Donald/West,\, XYZ/Nono]\).
  • This is not pedantry. A resolution proof is a formal derivation: if the bridging axiom is not in the clause set, the empty clause cannot be derived, and a proof that pretends otherwise is the thing being marked.
Also read “all of the missiles in Abc” carefully
  • It says every missile in Abc was sold by John, i.e. \(\forall x\, \big[Missile(x) \wedge In(x, Abc)\big] \rightarrow Sells(John, x, Abc)\).
  • It does not say Abc has any. Strictly, with no missile in existence the antecedent is never satisfied and nothing follows \(-\) so the existential “Abc has some missiles” has to be assumed too, exactly as 77 Ch states it outright.
  • Three assumptions, one line each, then the standard proof. An 10-mark answer has room for them and the examiner is looking for whether the gap was noticed.
  • 75 Ba's “All of its missiles in XYZ were sold by Donald” is the same sentence with a typo; treat it identically.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Bhadra · CT 710 · [9]
Every American who sells weapons to hostile nations is a criminal. Every enemy of America is a hostile. Nono has some missiles. All missiles of Nono were sold by Gorge. Gorge is an American. Nono is a Country. Nono is the enemy of America. Missiles are weapons. Prove that “Is Gorge a criminal?” using Resolution by Refutation.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Bhadra · CT 710 · [6]
It is a crime for a Nepali to sell weapons to an enemy of Nepal. Mr. A is an enemy of Nepal. Mr. A has some missiles. Missiles are weapons. Mr. R is a Nepali. If Mr. A has missiles then those missiles were sold to Mr. A by Mr. R. Prove “Mr. A is a criminal”.
column4:
2081 Bhadra: complete, with one spare premise
  • All eight premises of the canonical set are present, plus “Nono is a Country”, \(Country(Nono)\), which appears in no rule and is never used.
  • Substitute \([Gorge/West]\) and the eight steps run unchanged. Answer: Gorge is a criminal. ✓
  • The question is phrased as “Is Gorge a criminal?” but asks for resolution by refutation, so still negate: assume \( eg Criminal(Gorge)\) and derive \(\square\). Do not switch to extraction just because the sentence ends in a question mark.
2082 Bhadra: the goal is the wrong person
  • Read the roles: Mr. R is the Nepali who sells; Mr. A is the enemy who buys. The crime rule makes the seller the criminal.
  • So the premises prove \(Criminal(Mr.R)\), and the printed goal “Mr. A is a criminal” does not follow.
  • How to answer: prove \(Criminal(Mr.R)\) in full by the standard eight steps, then one line \(-\) “the premises make the seller the criminal, so what follows is \(Criminal(Mr.R)\); \(Criminal(Mr.A)\) is not derivable from this set.”
  • The sixth premise is a conditional, if Mr. A has missiles then they were sold to him by Mr. R, which is the same clause 3 as ever: \( eg Missile(x) \vee eg Owns(A,x) \vee Sells(R,x,A)\).
  • Enemy of Nepal is used directly as the hostile predicate here, so no bridging axiom is needed.

column1: P6. The same premises by forward and backward chaining — Prove Col. West is criminal using forward chaining
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Ashwin · [2+6]
The law says that it is a crime for an American to sell weapons to hostile nations. The country Nono, an enemy of America, has some missiles, and all of its missiles were sold to it by Colonel West, who is American. Prove that Col. West is criminal using forward chaining.
column4:
Forward chaining, iteration by iteration
  • Start with the ground facts (the clauses with no premises):
    • \(American(West)\), \(Missile(M_1)\), \(Owns(Nono, M_1)\), \(Enemy(Nono, America)\)
  • Iteration 1 \(-\) fire every rule whose premises are all present:
    • rule 4 with \([M_1/x]\) \(\rightarrow\) \(Weapon(M_1)\)
    • rule 3 with \([M_1/x]\), needing \(Missile(M_1)\) and \(Owns(Nono,M_1)\), both present \(\rightarrow\) \(Sells(West, M_1, Nono)\)
    • rule 5 with \([Nono/x]\) \(\rightarrow\) \(Hostile(Nono)\)
    • rule 1 does not fire yet: its four premises are not all known.
  • Iteration 2 \(-\) rule 1 now matches with \([West/p,\, M_1/q,\, Nono/r]\), because \(American(West)\), \(Weapon(M_1)\), \(Sells(West,M_1,Nono)\) and \(Hostile(Nono)\) are all in the fact base:
    • \(\rightarrow\) \(Criminal(West)\)
  • Goal reached, stop. ✓
Draw it as three rows: the four given facts along the bottom, the three iteration-1 facts above them, \(Criminal(West)\) at the top, with an arrow from each premise into the fact it helped derive. That picture is the answer; see §4.6.
The same thing backwards, for the 2 marks of comparison
  • Goal \(Criminal(West)\). Only rule 1 concludes \(Criminal\), so unify \([West/p]\) and take its four premises as sub-goals:
    • \(American(West)\) ✓a fact, done;
    • \(Weapon(q)\) \(\rightarrow\) sub-goal \(Missile(q)\) ✓ matches the fact \(Missile(M_1)\), binding \([M_1/q]\);
    • \(Sells(West, M_1, r)\) \(\rightarrow\) sub-goals \(Missile(M_1)\) ✓ and \(Owns(Nono, M_1)\) ✓, binding \([Nono/r]\);
    • \(Hostile(Nono)\) \(\rightarrow\) sub-goal \(Enemy(Nono, America)\) ✓.
  • Every leaf is a fact, so the goal is proved. Four sub-goals, depth first, left to right.
What the examiner is comparing
  • Forward derived three facts nobody asked for on the way (\(Weapon\), \(Sells\), \(Hostile\) are all needed here, but on a bigger KB most would not be).
  • Backward touched only the four conjuncts of one rule, and the binding \([M_1/q]\) found in the second sub-goal was carried into the third, which is why \(Sells(West,M_1,r)\) could be matched at all.
  • Same rules, same modus ponens, opposite ends. One sentence, and the comparison marks are secured.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  Family D: the light sleeper
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Baishakh · [2+8]
List down the rule for Inference. Consider the following axioms: All hounds howl at night. Anyone who has any cats will not have any mice. Light sleepers do not have anything which howls at night. John has either a cat or a hound. Prove: “If John is a light sleeper, then John does not have any mice” by resolution refutation.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Bhadra · CT 78506 · [7]
Consider the following axioms: All direwolves howl at night. Anyone who has any cat will not have any mice. Light sleepers do not have anything that howls at night. Jon has either a cat or a direwolf. Prove that if Jon is a light sleeper, then Jon does not have any mice, using the resolution method.
column4:
Step 1 Facts into FOPL
  • 1. \( orall x\; Hound(x) ightarrow Howl(x)\)
  • 2. \( orall x orall y\; ig[Have(x,y) \wedge Cat(y) ig] ightarrow orall z\, ig[Have(x,z) ightarrow eg Mouse(z) ig]\)
  • 3. \( orall x\; LS(x) ightarrow orall y\, ig[Have(x,y) ightarrow eg Howl(y) ig]\)
  • 4. \(\exists x\; Have(John, x) \wedge ig[Cat(x) \vee Hound(x) ig]\)
  • Goal \(LS(John) ightarrow orall z\, ig[Have(John,z) ightarrow eg Mouse(z) ig]\)
Step 2 Into CNF
  • 1. \( eg Hound(x) \vee Howl(x)\)
  • 2. \( eg Have(x,y) \vee eg Cat(y) \vee eg Have(x,z) \vee eg Mouse(z)\)
  • 3. \( eg LS(x) \vee eg Have(x,y) \vee eg Howl(y)\)
  • 4a. \(Have(John, a)\) skolem constant \(a\)
  • 4b. \(Cat(a) \vee Hound(a)\)
Step 3 Negate the goal, and get three clauses
  • \( eg ig[LS(John) ightarrow orall z (Have(John,z) ightarrow eg Mouse(z)) ig]\)
  • \(= LS(John) \wedge \exists z\, ig[Have(John,z) \wedge Mouse(z) ig]\)
  • 5a. \(LS(John)\)   5b. \(Have(John, b)\)    5c. \(Mouse(b)\) skolem \(b\)
\( eg(P ightarrow Q) = P \wedge eg Q\). This is the whole difficulty of the problem: students negate an implication to another implication, get one clause instead of three, and then cannot close the proof.
Step 4 Resolution
  • 6. \( eg LS(x) \vee eg Have(x,y) \vee eg Hound(y)\) (3, 1) \([y/x]\)
  • 7. \( eg Have(John,y) \vee eg Hound(y)\) (6, 5a) \([John/x]\)
  • 8. \( eg Hound(a)\) (7, 4a) \([a/y]\)
  • 9. \(Cat(a)\) (8, 4b)
  • 10. \( eg Have(x,a) \vee eg Have(x,z) \vee eg Mouse(z)\) (9, 2) \([a/y]\)
  • 11. \( eg Have(John,z) \vee eg Mouse(z)\) (10, 4a) \([John/x]\)
  • 12. \( eg Mouse(b)\) (11, 5b) \([b/z]\)
  • 13. \(\square\) (12, 5c)
Final answer
  • “If John is a light sleeper then John has no mice” is proved. ✓ Eight steps.
  • The shape of the argument, worth stating in words underneath: John is a light sleeper, so he has nothing that howls, so what he has is not a hound; it was a cat or a hound, so it is a cat; anyone with a cat has no mice; so he has no mice.
  • Two skolem constants, and they are different. \(a\) is the animal John owns (from premise 4); \(b\) is the mouse the negated goal claims he has. Reusing one letter for both is a wrong proof that happens to close.
  • Premise 2 needs four literals. Both the cat and the mouse are things John has, so \(Have\) appears twice with different second arguments. Writing it with one \(Have\) loses the proof.

Identical: substitute \([Jon/John,\; Direwolf/Hound]\) and the same eight steps close the proof. Nothing else changes.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 1. Did Marcus hate Caesar?
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Magh · [7]
Using resolution, solve the following statements: All pompeian are Romans. All Romans were either loyal to Caesor or hated him. Everyone is loyal to someone. People only try to assassinate rulers they not loyal to. Marcus tried to assassinate Caesor. Marcus was pompeian. Find, did Marcus Caesor?
column4:
FOPL and CNF
  • 1. \( eg Pompeian(x) \vee Roman(x)\)
  • 2. \( eg Roman(x) \vee loyal(x, Caesar) \vee hate(x, Caesar)\)
  • 3. \(loyal ig(x,\, f(x) ig)\) \(\exists\) inside \( orall\): skolem function
  • 4. \( eg tryAssassinate(x,y) \vee eg ruler(y) \vee eg loyal(x,y)\)
  • 5. \(tryAssassinate(Marcus, Caesar)\)
  • 6. \(Pompeian(Marcus)\)   7. \(ruler(Caesar)\)
\(ruler(Caesar)\) is not printed but rule 4 is about rulers, so state it as an assumption. “Everyone is loyal to someone” is \( orall x \exists y\, loyal(x,y)\), and it skolemizes to \(f(x)\), not to a constant \(-\) each person is loyal to their own someone.
Proof negated goal 8. \( eg hate(Marcus, Caesar)\)
  • 9. \(Roman(Marcus)\) (6, 1)
  • 10. \(loyal(Marcus,Caesar) \vee hate(Marcus,Caesar)\) (9, 2)
  • 11. \(loyal(Marcus, Caesar)\) (10, 8)
  • 12. \( eg ruler(Caesar) \vee eg loyal(Marcus, Caesar)\) (5, 4) \([Marcus/x, Caesar/y]\)
  • 13. \( eg loyal(Marcus, Caesar)\) (12, 7)
  • 14. \(\square\) (13, 11)
  • Marcus hated Caesar. ✓
  • Clause 3 is never used, and it is the only clause with a Skolem function in it. It is there to see whether you skolemize it correctly, not because the proof needs it.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 2. Scrooge is not a child
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Chaitra · [8]
Every child loves Santa. Everyone who loves Santa loves any reindeer. Rudolph is a reindeer, and Rudolph has a red nose. Anything which has a red nose is weird or is a clown. No reindeer is a clown. Scrooge does not love anything which is weird. Using Resolution Refutation, derive the conclusion: Scrooge is not a child.
column4:
CNF
  • 1. \( eg child(x) \vee loves(x, Santa)\)
  • 2. \( eg loves(x, Santa) \vee eg reindeer(y) \vee loves(x,y)\)
  • 3. \(reindeer(Rudolph)\)   4. \(redNose(Rudolph)\)
  • 5. \( eg redNose(x) \vee weird(x) \vee clown(x)\)
  • 6. \( eg reindeer(x) \vee eg clown(x)\)
  • 7. \( eg weird(x) \vee eg loves(Scrooge, x)\)
The goal is already a negation, so negating it removes the \( eg\): clause 8 is \(child(Scrooge)\), not \( eg child(Scrooge)\). Getting this backwards is the standard error on this set.
Proof negated goal 8. \(child(Scrooge)\)
  • 9. \(loves(Scrooge, Santa)\) (8, 1) \([Scrooge/x]\)
  • 10. \( eg reindeer(y) \vee loves(Scrooge, y)\) (9, 2)
  • 11. \(loves(Scrooge, Rudolph)\) (10, 3) \([Rudolph/y]\)
  • 12. \( eg weird(Rudolph)\) (11, 7) \([Rudolph/x]\)
  • 13. \( eg redNose(Rudolph) \vee clown(Rudolph)\) (12, 5)
  • 14. \(clown(Rudolph)\) (13, 4)
  • 15. \( eg reindeer(Rudolph)\) (14, 6)
  • 16. \(\square\) (15, 3)
  • “Scrooge is not a child” is proved. ✓ Eight steps, every premise used.
  • The argument in words: if Scrooge were a child he would love Santa, hence love Rudolph; but Scrooge loves nothing weird, so Rudolph is not weird, so (red nose) he is a clown, and no reindeer is a clown \(-\) contradiction.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 3. Did Curiosity kill the cat?
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Chaitra · [3+5]
Convert the following sentences into FOPL and answer “Did Curiosity kill the cat” by resolution refutation:
  1. Everyone who loves all animals is loved by someone.
  2. Anyone who kills an animal is loved by no one.
  3. Jack loves all animals.
  4. Either Jack or Curiosity killed the cat.
column4:
CNF (the cat is named Tuna; “cats are animals” is assumed)
  • A1. \(Animal(F(x)) \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
  • A2. \( eg Loves(x, F(x)) \vee Loves(G(x), x)\)
  • B. \( eg Animal(y) \vee eg Kills(x,y) \vee eg Loves(z,x)\)
  • C. \( eg Animal(x) \vee Loves(Jack, x)\)
  • D. \(Kills(Jack, Tuna) \vee Kills(Curiosity, Tuna)\)
  • E. \(Cat(Tuna)\)   F. \( eg Cat(x) \vee Animal(x)\)
A1 and A2 are premise (a) put through all eight CNF steps in P2 above. \(F(x)\) is “an animal \(x\) does not love” and \(G(x)\) is “someone who loves \(x\)”. Both must be functions of \(x\).
Proof negated goal G. \( eg Kills(Curiosity, Tuna)\)
  • 1. \(Kills(Jack, Tuna)\) (G, D)
  • 2. \(Animal(Tuna)\) (E, F)
  • 3. \( eg Animal(Tuna) \vee eg Loves(z, Jack)\) (1, B) \([Jack/x, Tuna/y]\)
  • 4. \( eg Loves(z, Jack)\) (3, 2)
  • 5. \( eg Animal(F(Jack)) \vee Loves(G(Jack), Jack)\) (C, A2) \([Jack/x,\, F(Jack)/x]\)
  • 6. \(Loves(G(Jack), Jack)\) (5, A1) \([Jack/x]\), duplicate collapses
  • 7. \(\square\) (6, 4) \([G(Jack)/z]\)
  • Curiosity killed the cat. ✓
  • Steps 5 and 6 are the whole difficulty. They prove somebody loves Jack, using (c) to satisfy the antecedent of (a): Jack loves all animals, so in particular he loves \(F(Jack)\), so the second clause of (a) fires. Only then does step 4, nobody loves Jack, become a contradiction.
  • Two facts have to be assumed because the paper omits them: the cat has a name, and cats are animals. State both.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 4. Sneha is happy
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Baishakh · CT 710 · [2+6]
Define skolemization with example. Consider the following axioms: a) anyone passing his engineering exams and winning the lottery is happy; b) anyone who studies or is lucky can pass all his exams; c) Sneha did not study but she is lucky; d) anyone who is lucky wins the lottery. Using resolution refutation, prove that Sneha is happy.
column4:
CNF
  • 1. \( eg pass(x) \vee eg win(x) \vee happy(x)\)
  • 2. \( ig[study(x) \vee lucky(x) ig] ightarrow pass(x)\) \(= ig[ eg study(x) \wedge eg lucky(x) ig] \vee pass(x)\), so
    • 2a. \( eg study(x) \vee pass(x)\)
    • 2b. \( eg lucky(x) \vee pass(x)\)
  • 3a. \( eg study(Sneha)\)   3b. \(lucky(Sneha)\)
  • 4. \( eg lucky(x) \vee win(x)\)
Why this splits and the food premise does not: here the negation lands on a disjunction, \( eg(A \vee B) = eg A \wedge eg B\), so distributing is forced. In the food family it lands on a conjunction, \( eg(A \wedge eg B) = eg A \vee B\), and there is nothing to split. One De Morgan apart, opposite answers.
Proof negated goal 5. \( eg happy(Sneha)\)
  • 6. \( eg pass(Sneha) \vee eg win(Sneha)\) (5, 1) \([Sneha/x]\)
  • 7. \( eg lucky(Sneha) \vee eg win(Sneha)\) (6, 2b)
  • 8. \( eg win(Sneha)\) (7, 3b)
  • 9. \( eg lucky(Sneha)\) (8, 4) \([Sneha/x]\)
  • 10. \(\square\) (9, 3b)

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 5. Steve likes BK301
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Ashwin · [7]
Assume the following facts: a) Steve only likes easy courses; b) Science courses are hard; c) All the courses in the basket weaving department are easy; d) BK301 is a basket weaving course. Prove that Steve likes BK301 using Resolution Refutation.
column4:
Read premise (a) carefully first
  • Literally, “Steve only likes easy courses” is \( orall x\; likes(Steve,x) ightarrow easy(x)\): liking implies easy.
  • From that you can prove a course Steve likes is easy. You cannot prove he likes anything, because nothing in the set ever concludes \(likes\).
  • The question is only answerable under the converse reading, “Steve likes every easy course”: \[ orall x\; easy(x) ightarrow likes(Steve, x) \]
  • Write that line, then prove it. Stating the reading you adopted is a mark; silently reversing an implication is not.
CNF and proof
  • 1. \( eg easy(x) \vee likes(Steve, x)\) (a), converse reading
  • 2. \( eg science(x) \vee eg easy(x)\) (b)
  • 3. \( eg basketWeaving(x) \vee easy(x)\) (c)
  • 4. \(basketWeaving(BK301)\) (d)
  • 5. \( eg likes(Steve, BK301)\) negated goal
  • 6. \( eg easy(BK301)\) (5, 1) \([BK301/x]\)
  • 7. \( eg basketWeaving(BK301)\) (6, 3)
  • 8. \(\square\) (7, 4)
  • “Steve likes BK301” is proved under that reading. ✓ Three steps.
  • Premise (b) is unused, and it is the only one mentioning science. Hard is written \( eg easy\); inventing a separate \(hard\) predicate needs a fifth premise saying the two are opposites.
