column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 6. You will enjoy
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2077 Chaitra · CT 78506 · [8]
If it is a sunny and warm day you will enjoy. If it is a warm and pleasant day you will do strawberry picking. If it is raining, no strawberry picking. If it is raining you will get wet. It is a warm day. It is raining. It is sunny. Prove that “You will enjoy” using resolution by refutation.
column4:
CNF
  • 1. \( eg sunny \vee eg warm \vee enjoy\)
  • 2. \( eg warm \vee eg pleasant \vee picking\)
  • 3. \( eg raining \vee eg picking\)
  • 4. \( eg raining \vee wet\)
  • 5. \(warm\)   6. \(raining\)   7. \(sunny\)
Each implication becomes one clause by \(\alpha ightarrow eta = eg\alpha \vee eta\) plus De Morgan on the conjunctive antecedent. No quantifiers means no unification: every resolution step here is on a ground literal.
Proof negated goal 8. \( eg enjoy\)
  • 9. \( eg sunny \vee eg warm\) (8, 1)
  • 10. \( eg warm\) (9, 7)
  • 11. \(\square\) (10, 5)
  • “You will enjoy” is proved in three steps. ✓
  • Clauses 2, 3, 4 and 6 are never touched. The strawberry picking and the rain are a complete decoy: they are consistent with the rest and irrelevant to the goal.
  • The lesson worth writing under the proof: resolve from the negated goal. Starting from the facts, this set will happily generate \(wet\), \( eg picking\) and several other true-but-useless literals before it stumbles on the answer.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 7. Ram is naughty
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Bhadra · [8]
All oversmart persons are stupid. Children of oversmart persons are naughty. Ram is children of Hari. Hari is oversmart. Show that Ram is naughty using FOPL based resolution.
column4:
CNF
  • 1. \( eg oversmart(x) \vee stupid(x)\)
  • 2. \( eg child(x,y) \vee eg oversmart(y) \vee naughty(x)\)
  • 3. \(child(Ram, Hari)\)   4. \(oversmart(Hari)\)
Proof negated goal 5. \( eg naughty(Ram)\)
  • 6. \( eg child(Ram, y) \vee eg oversmart(y)\) (5, 2) \([Ram/x]\)
  • 7. \( eg oversmart(Hari)\) (6, 3) \([Hari/y]\)
  • 8. \(\square\) (7, 4)
Notes
  • “Ram is naughty” is proved in three steps. ✓
  • Premise 1 is unused. Stupid appears nowhere else, so the whole first sentence is a decoy \(-\) the same trick as the mammal rule in Family B.
  • \(child(x,y)\) must mean “\(x\) is a child of \(y\)” and be used that way in both clause 2 and clause 3. The English “Ram is children of Hari” fixes the order; write the reading down before you write the clause, because reversing it silently breaks the unification in step 6.
  • Predicate names are free, but \(naughty\) must be a property of the child, not a relation: \(naughty(x)\), one argument.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 8. The book supports the cup
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2071 Bhadra · [8]
If X is on the top of Y, Y supports X. If X is above Y and they are touching each other, X is on the top of Y. A cup is above a book. A cup is touching a book. Show that supports(book, cup) is true.
column4:
CNF
  • 1. \( eg onTop(x,y) \vee supports(y,x)\)
  • 2. \( eg above(x,y) \vee eg touching(x,y) \vee onTop(x,y)\)
  • 3. \(above(Cup, Book)\)   4. \(touching(Cup, Book)\)
Proof negated goal 5. \( eg supports(Book, Cup)\)
  • 6. \( eg onTop(Cup, Book)\) (5, 1) \([Cup/x, Book/y]\)
  • 7. \( eg above(Cup,Book) \vee eg touching(Cup,Book)\) (6, 2)
  • 8. \( eg touching(Cup, Book)\) (7, 3)
  • 9. \(\square\) (8, 4)
Notes
  • \(supports(Book, Cup)\) is proved in four steps. ✓
  • Clause 1 reverses its arguments and that is the point. \(onTop(x,y)\) has the supporter second; \(supports(y,x)\) has it first. The goal \(supports(Book,Cup)\) therefore unifies with \([Cup/x, Book/y]\), giving \(onTop(Cup,Book)\) \(-\) cup on book, which is what the facts describe.
  • Every premise is used, and there is no quantifier subtlety: the two rules are plain universals, so drop the \( orall\) and go.
  • “they are touching each other” is symmetric in English but \(touching(x,y)\) is not symmetric in the clause set. It does not matter here because the facts are given in the same order the rule wants; if they were not, a symmetry axiom \( eg touching(x,y) \vee touching(y,x)\) would be needed.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 9. If John does not study, Mary does not love John
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2073 Magh · [10]
Consider the following axioms: i) anyone whom Mary loves is a football star; ii) any student who does not pass does not play; iii) John is a student; iv) any student who does not study does not pass; v) anyone who does not play is not a football star. Prove that “If John does not study, then Mary does not love John” using resolution by refutation.
column4:
CNF
  • 1. \( eg loves(Mary,x) \vee star(x)\)
  • 2. \( eg student(x) \vee pass(x) \vee eg play(x)\)
  • 3. \(student(John)\)
  • 4. \( eg student(x) \vee study(x) \vee eg pass(x)\)
  • 5. \(play(x) \vee eg star(x)\)
Negate the goal: two clauses
  • \( eg ig[ eg study(John) ightarrow eg loves(Mary, John) ig] = eg study(John) \wedge loves(Mary, John)\)
  • 6a. \( eg study(John)\)   6b. \(loves(Mary, John)\)
Premises (ii), (iv) and (v) are all of the form not-\(P\) implies not-\(Q\). Convert each one mechanically: \([\,S \wedge eg P\,] ightarrow eg Q\) becomes \( eg S \vee P \vee eg Q\). Trying to simplify them into positive form first is where this question is usually lost.
Proof
  • 7. \(star(John)\) (6b, 1) \([John/x]\)
  • 8. \(play(John)\) (7, 5) \([John/x]\)
  • 9. \( eg student(John) \vee pass(John)\) (8, 2) \([John/x]\)
  • 10. \(pass(John)\) (9, 3)
  • 11. \( eg student(John) \vee study(John)\) (10, 4) \([John/x]\)
  • 12. \(study(John)\) (11, 3)
  • 13. \(\square\) (12, 6a)
  • The implication is proved. ✓ Seven steps, every premise used, and clause 3 used twice.
  • The chain in words: suppose Mary loves John and he does not study. Loved by Mary \( ightarrow\) football star \( ightarrow\) plays \( ightarrow\) (being a student) passes \( ightarrow\) studies. Contradiction with does not study.
  • A clause may be reused as often as needed. Students often cross a clause off after one use; nothing in resolution says that.

column1: P5. Resolution refutation  The ten one-off premise sets — 10. Can anyone be found with an exciting life?
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Ashwin · [3+5]
List the rules of inference. Convert the following into FOPL and prove using Resolution Refutation System: “All people who are not poor and are smart are happy. Those people who can read are not stupid. John can read and is wealthy. Happy people have exciting lives. Can anyone be found with an exciting life?”
column4:
CNF with wealthy \(= eg poor\) and smart \(= eg stupid\)
  • 1. \(poor(x) \vee eg smart(x) \vee happy(x)\)
  • 2. \( eg read(x) \vee eg stupid(x)\)
  • 3a. \(read(John)\)   3b. \( eg poor(John)\)
  • 4. \( eg happy(x) \vee exciting(x)\)
  • 5. \( eg smart(x) \vee eg stupid(x)\) is not needed; instead state the bridging fact \( eg stupid(x) ightarrow smart(x)\), i.e. 5. \(stupid(x) \vee smart(x)\)
Two vocabulary bridges must be stated: wealthy is \( eg poor\), and not stupid is smart. Without them the clause set has five predicates that never meet and no proof exists. Say so in one line before starting \(-\) the examiner's own wording forces it.
Proof negated goal 6. \( eg exciting(x)\), for all \(x\)
  • 7. \( eg happy(x)\) (6, 4)
  • 8. \(poor(x) \vee eg smart(x)\) (7, 1)
  • 9. \( eg smart(John)\) (8, 3b) \([John/x]\)
  • 10. \(stupid(John)\) (9, 5) \([John/x]\)
  • 11. \( eg read(John)\) (10, 2) \([John/x]\)
  • 12. \(\square\) (11, 3a)
  • Yes: John has an exciting life. ✓
  • How the name is recovered, which is what “can anyone be found” asks: the goal \(\exists x\, exciting(x)\) negates to \( orall x\, eg exciting(x)\), one clause with a free variable. The substitutions used along the way bound that variable to John, and that binding is the answer.
  • The formal device is an answer literal: carry \(exciting(x) \vee Ans(x)\) instead of the bare negation, and read the answer off the clause that survives. Worth naming even if you do not use it.

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B1–B2. Meningitis and the stiff neck
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2071 Magh · [3+5]
What is neural network? Describe its types. A doctor knows that the disease meningitis causes the patient to have a stiff neck 50% of the time. The doctor also knows that the probability that a patient has meningitis is 1/50,000, and the probability that any patient has a stiff neck is 1/20. Find the probability that a patient with a stiff neck has meningitis?
column4:
B1 2071 Magh
  • Given \(P(s|m) = 0.5\), \(P(m) = 1/50000 = 2 \times 10^{-5}\), \(P(s) = 1/20 = 0.05\).
  • Wanted \(P(m|s)\).
  • \[ P(m|s) = \frac{P(s|m)\,P(m)}{P(s)} = \frac{0.5 \times 2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.05} = \frac{10^{-5}}{0.05} \]
  • \[ \boxed{P(m|s) = 0.0002 = 0.02\,\%} \]
  • \(P(s)\) is given here, so no total-probability step is needed. That is the only easy version of this question in the archive.
B2 2081 Baishakh (CT 710)
  • Given \(P(s|m) = 0.8\), \(P(m) = 1/50000\), \(P(s) = 0.01\).
  • \[ P(m|s) = \frac{0.8 \times 2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.01} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-5}}{0.01} \]
  • \[ \boxed{P(m|s) = 0.0016 = 0.16\,\%} \]
  • The first 2 marks are prior Vs posterior defined: \(P(m)\) is the prior, \(P(m|s)\) the posterior, and the stiff neck raised the belief from 0.002 % to 0.16 % \(-\) eighty times higher, and still under one in six hundred.
  • That last sentence is the exam answer to “what does this tell you”: a strong likelihood cannot outweigh a tiny prior.

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B3. Measles or flu?
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2073 Magh · [8]
A doctor is called to see a sick child. The doctor has prior information that 90% of sick children in that neighborhood have the flu, while the other 10% are sick with measles. Let F stand for an event of a child being sick with Flu and M stand for an event of a child being sick with measles. Assume for simplicity that there no other maladies in that neighborhood. A well-known (and common) symptom of measles is a rash and has probability of 0.95. However, very occasionally, children with flu also develop rash and has probability of 0.08. Upon examining the child, the doctor finds a rash. What is the probability that the child has measles?
column4:
Solution
  • Given \(P(F) = 0.9\), \(P(M) = 0.1\), \(P(R|M) = 0.95\), \(P(R|F) = 0.08\).
  • Total probability of a rash: \[ P(R) = P(R|M)P(M) + P(R|F)P(F) \] \[ = 0.95 \times 0.1 + 0.08 \times 0.9 = 0.095 + 0.072 = 0.167 \]
  • \[ P(M|R) = \frac{P(R|M)P(M)}{P(R)} = \frac{0.095}{0.167} \]
  • \[ \boxed{P(M|R) = 0.5689 \approx 56.9\,\%} \]
Reading the answer
  • Measles goes from a 10 % prior to a 57 % posterior: the rash is strong evidence, but flu is nine times commoner, so it stays a coin flip.
  • Check the complement: \(P(F|R) = 0.072/0.167 = 0.4311\), and \(0.5689 + 0.4311 = 1\). ✓ Two extra lines, and they catch an arithmetic slip in the denominator every time.
  • The trap: reading 0.95 as \(P(M|R)\) and answering “95 %”. The paper gives the likelihood \(P(R|M)\); the whole point of the question is that the two are not the same number.

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B4. The cigar smoker
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Bhadra · CT 710 · [2+6] also 2073 Bhadra CT 78506 [8]
What do you understand by Bayesian Network? In a County, 51% of the adults are males and the other 49% are females. One adult is randomly selected for a survey involving credit card usage. i) Find the prior probability that the selected person is a male. ii) It is later learned that the selected survey subject was smoking a cigar. Also, 9.5% of males smoke cigars, whereas 1.7% of females smoke cigars (based on data from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration). Use this additional information to find the probability that the selected subject is a male.
column4:
Solution
  • (i) Prior \(P(M) = 0.51\). That is the whole answer to part (i); no calculation is intended.
  • (ii) Given \(P(F) = 0.49\), \(P(C|M) = 0.095\), \(P(C|F) = 0.017\).
  • \[ P(C) = 0.095 \times 0.51 + 0.017 \times 0.49 \] \[ = 0.04845 + 0.00833 = 0.05678 \]
  • \[ P(M|C) = \frac{0.04845}{0.05678} \]
  • \[ \boxed{P(M|C) = 0.8533 \approx 85.3\,\%} \]
Notes
  • The prior 51 % rises to 85 % because men are five and a half times as likely to smoke a cigar. Here the likelihood ratio does dominate, which is the opposite lesson to B1 and B2 \(-\) and the difference is entirely that this prior is near a half rather than near zero.
  • Keep five decimal places in the denominator. Rounding \(0.05678\) to \(0.057\) moves the answer to 85.0 %, and the marks for the final figure are awarded on the exact value.
  • 73 Bh prints the same scenario for a single 8-mark part. Same two answers.

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B5. The 99 % accurate test for a rare disease
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Ashwin · CT 78506 · [8]
After your yearly checkup, the doctor has bad news and good news. The bad news is that you tested positive for a serious disease, and that the test is 99% accurate (i.e. the probability of testing positive given that you have the disease is 0.99, as is the probability of testing negative given that you don't have the disease). The good news is that this is a rare disease, striking only one in 10,000 people. Why is it good news that the disease is rare? What are the chances that you actually have the disease?
column4:
Solution
  • Given \(P(D) = 10^{-4}\), \(P(+|D) = 0.99\), \(P(-|\neg D) = 0.99\), so \(P(+|\neg D) = 0.01\).
  • \[ P(+) = 0.99 \times 10^{-4} + 0.01 \times 0.9999 \] \[ = 0.000099 + 0.009999 = 0.010098 \]
  • \[ P(D|+) = \frac{0.000099}{0.010098} \]
  • \[ \boxed{P(D|+) = 0.0098 \approx 0.98\,\%} \]
  • Fewer than 1 in 100 people with a positive result actually have the disease.
“Why is it good news that the disease is rare”
  • Because the false positives outnumber the true ones, and by a lot. In 1,000,000 people: 100 have the disease and 99 of them test positive; 999,900 do not, and 9,999 of them still test positive. 9,999 against 99 is roughly 100 to 1.
  • So a rare disease means a positive result is far more likely to be an error than a diagnosis. Rarity protects you.
  • Write the population count. It is worth more marks than the algebra and it is much harder to get wrong.
  • The general lesson: the posterior depends on the prior as much as on the test. A 99 % test is not a 99 % answer.

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B6. The genetic defect
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Ashwin · [2+6]
What are the approaches for measuring uncertainty? 1% of people have a certain genetic defect. 90% of tests for the gene detect the defect (true positives). 10% of the tests are false positives. a) What might be the probability of getting the genetic defect result? b) If a person gets a positive test result, what are the odds they actually don't have the genetic defect?
column4:
Solution
  • Given \(P(D) = 0.01\), \(P(+|D) = 0.90\), \(P(+|\neg D) = 0.10\).
  • (a) The probability of a positive result: \[ P(+) = 0.90 \times 0.01 + 0.10 \times 0.99 \] \[ = 0.009 + 0.099 = \boxed{0.108 = 10.8\,\%} \]
  • (b) \[ P(\neg D \,|\, +) = \frac{0.099}{0.108} \] \[ = \boxed{0.9167 \approx 91.7\,\%} \]
  • And so \(P(D|+) = 0.009/0.108 = 0.0833 = 8.3\,\%\). \(91.7 + 8.3 = 100\). ✓
Notes
  • As true odds, which is what part (b) literally asks for: \(0.099 : 0.009\), i.e. 11 to 1 against actually having the defect. Give both the probability and the odds and neither reading can cost a mark.
  • Part (a) is ambiguous as printed \(-\) “the probability of getting the genetic defect result” could mean \(P(D)\), which is stated in the question and would make the part worthless. It means \(P(+)\). Say which reading you took.
  • Same shape as B5 with a much weaker test (10 % false positives instead of 1 %) and a much commoner condition (1 % instead of 0.01 %). The posterior lands at 8 % rather than 1 %.

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B7. Which factory made the defective bulb?
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Ashwin · [3+5]
How is reasoning done under uncertainty? Three factories produce light bulbs to supply the market. Factory A produces 20%, 50% of the bulbs are produced in factory B and 30% in factory C. 2% of the bulbs produced in factory A, 5% of the bulbs produced in factory B and 3% of the bulbs produced in factory C are defective. A bulb is selected at random in the market and found to be defective. What is the probability that this bulb was produced by factory B?
column4:
Solution
  • Given \(P(A) = 0.2\), \(P(B) = 0.5\), \(P(C) = 0.3\); \(P(D|A) = 0.02\), \(P(D|B) = 0.05\), \(P(D|C) = 0.03\).
  • Total probability of a defective bulb, one term per factory: \[ P(D) = 0.2(0.02) + 0.5(0.05) + 0.3(0.03) \] \[ = 0.004 + 0.025 + 0.009 = 0.038 \]
  • \[ P(B|D) = \frac{P(D|B)P(B)}{P(D)} = \frac{0.025}{0.038} \]
  • \[ \boxed{P(B|D) = 0.6579 \approx 65.8\,\%} \]
Notes
  • The partition must be exhaustive: \(0.2 + 0.5 + 0.3 = 1\). ✓ Check it before you start; a partition that does not sum to 1 means a misread question.
  • Factory B's share rises from 50 % to 66 % because it is both the biggest producer and the worst. The other two posteriors are \(P(A|D) = 0.004/0.038 = 10.5\,\%\) and \(P(C|D) = 0.009/0.038 = 23.7\,\%\), and the three sum to 100 %. ✓
  • This is the template for every “which source did it come from” question, and there are three of them in the archive (bulbs, factories, and the tall-student one below).

column1: P7. Bayes' theorem: the twelve numericals — B8–B9. The tall student, and the mammogram
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2078 Chaitra · [3+5]
Explain how statistical reasoning aids in inference and reasoning in light of Bayes' theorem. At a certain University, 5% of men are over 6 feet tall and 2% of women are 6 feet tall. 60% of students are female. If a student is selected at random from among all those over six feet tall, what is the probability that the selected student is a woman?
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Baishakh · CT 710 · [2+6]
What are casual networks? Given the following statistics, what is the probability that a woman has cancer if she has a positive mammogram result? i) One percent of women over 50 have breast cancer. ii) Ninety percent of women who have breast cancer test positive on mammograms. iii) Eight percent of women will have false positives.
column4:
B8 the tall student
  • Given \(P(W) = 0.6\), \(P(M) = 0.4\), \(P(T|W) = 0.02\), \(P(T|M) = 0.05\).
  • \[ P(T) = 0.02(0.6) + 0.05(0.4) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032 \]
  • \[ P(W|T) = rac{0.012}{0.032} = oxed{0.375 = 37.5\,\%} \]
  • Women are the majority of students and the minority of tall ones: 60 % prior, 37.5 % posterior. The evidence reverses the balance, which is the sentence the 3-mark theory part wants.
B9 the mammogram
  • Given \(P(C) = 0.01\), \(P(+|C) = 0.90\), \(P(+| eg C) = 0.08\).
  • \[ P(+) = 0.90(0.01) + 0.08(0.99) \] \[ = 0.009 + 0.0792 = 0.0882 \]
  • \[ P(C|+) = rac{0.009}{0.0882} = oxed{0.1020 \approx 10.2\,\%} \]
  • Nine positives in ten are false alarms, even though the test catches 90 % of real cancers. Same base-rate lesson as B5, in the setting it was originally made famous in.
  • “Eight percent of women will have false positives” means \(P(+| eg C) = 0.08\), not \(P( eg C \wedge +) = 0.08\). The looser reading gives \(0.009/0.089 = 10.1\,\%\), close enough to hide the error \(-\) state your reading.

column1: P8. Bayesian networks: reading a joint probability off the graph — B10. The wet grass network
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2078 Baishakh · [2+6]
What do you understand by Bayesian Network? For the given Bayesian network below, find the probability of grass being wet when the weather is cloudy, there is some sprinkler but no rain, i.e. C = True, S = True, R = False and W = True.
column4:
Solution
  • The product form, one factor per node, each conditioned on its parents: \[ P(C, S, eg R, W) = P(C)\,P(S|C)\,P( eg R|C)\,P(W|S, eg R) \]
  • Read each factor off its own table:
    • \(P(C) = 0.6\) root node, prior
    • \(P(S|C{=}T) = 0.10\) sprinkler table, row T
    • \(P(R|C{=}T) = 0.80\), so \(P( eg R|C{=}T) = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20\)
    • \(P(W|S{=}T, R{=}F) = 0.90\) wet-grass table, row T F
  • \[ = 0.6 imes 0.10 imes 0.20 imes 0.90 \]
  • \[ oxed{P = 0.0108 = 1.08\,\%} \]
The three ways this goes wrong
  • Forgetting to complement \(R\). The query says no rain, and the table gives \(P(R|C)\). Take \(1 - 0.80\). Using 0.80 gives 0.0432, four times too big, and it is the commonest wrong answer.
  • Picking the wrong CPT row. The wet-grass table is indexed by (S, R), and the query is \(S = T\), \(R = F\): row T F, value 0.90. Row F T is also 0.90, so a misread here happens to give the right number in this one query and the wrong one in every other.
  • Conditioning on the wrong parent. Sprinkler and Rain both depend on Cloudy only; WetGrass depends on both of them and not on Cloudy. That is the conditional independence the network encodes, and it is what makes four numbers enough.
  • The 2-mark part: a Bayesian network is a DAG of random variables with a CPT at each node, and the joint distribution is the product above. Six variables of this kind would need 31 free numbers as a full joint table; this one needs 9.

column1: P8. Bayesian networks: reading a joint probability off the graph — B11. Smoker \(\rightarrow\) cancer \(\rightarrow\) test
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Bhadra · CT 710 · [7]
A Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) is used in a medical diagnosis system. The network includes the binary variables C (Patient has Cancer), T (Test result is Positive) and S (Patient is a Smoker), with structure S \(\rightarrow\) C \(\rightarrow\) T and conditional probabilities P(S=Yes)=0.3, P(C=Yes \(|\) S=Yes)=0.2, P(C=Yes \(|\) S=No)=0.05, P(T=Yes \(|\) C=Yes)=0.9, P(T=Yes \(|\) C=No)=0.1. Explain how the Bayesian Belief Network enables reasoning under uncertainty in this medical context.
column4:
The three kinds of reasoning, each with its number
  • Causal, top-down \(-\) a smoker walks in; how likely is a positive test? \[ P(T|S) = 0.9(0.2) + 0.1(0.8) = \mathbf{0.26} \] against \(P(T| eg S) = 0.9(0.05) + 0.1(0.95) = 0.14\).
  • Prior belief, before anyone is seen: \[ P(C) = 0.2(0.3) + 0.05(0.7) = 0.06 + 0.035 = \mathbf{0.095} \] \[ P(T) = 0.9(0.095) + 0.1(0.905) = 0.0855 + 0.0905 = \mathbf{0.176} \]
  • Diagnostic, bottom-up \(-\) the test came back positive; how likely is cancer? This is Bayes on the second edge: \[ P(C|T) = rac{0.9 imes 0.095}{0.176} = rac{0.0855}{0.176} = \mathbf{0.4858} \]
  • Through the chain \(-\) the test is positive; how likely is the patient a smoker? \[ P(S|T) = rac{P(T|S)P(S)}{P(T)} = rac{0.26 imes 0.3}{0.176} = rac{0.078}{0.176} = \mathbf{0.4432} \]
Consistency check: \(P(T)\) computed through \(C\) gives 0.176, and computed through \(S\) gives \(0.26(0.3) + 0.14(0.7) = 0.078 + 0.098 = 0.176\). ✓ Two routes, one answer \(-\) that is the network being coherent, and it is worth showing.
What to say in words, which is what the question asks
  • The network separates what is known from what is asked. The doctor can only measure causal probabilities \(-\) how often smokers get cancer, how often cancer shows on a test \(-\) and the network stores exactly those. Bayes then runs them backwards on demand.
  • It handles partial evidence: with no observation the belief in cancer is 9.5 %; knowing the patient smokes raises it to 20 %; a positive test raises it to 48.6 %. Each piece of evidence revises, none replaces.
  • Conditional independence keeps it small. \(T\) depends on \(C\) alone: once the cancer status is known, smoking tells you nothing more about the test. So three variables need 5 numbers instead of \(2^3 - 1 = 7\), and the saving grows exponentially with the network.
  • It never claims certainty. A positive test leaves the patient more likely not to have cancer than to have it \(-\) 51.4 % against 48.6 % \(-\) which is precisely the kind of conclusion a logic-based KB cannot express at all.
B12. The three papers that ask for an example of your own 75+33+5
73 Bh 7, 80 Ba 5+3, 80 Ch 3+5  \(\cdot\) no data printed, so bring your own \(-\) and the smallest one that shows everything is the two-node version of B9
The example to memorise
  • Network: \(Cancer ightarrow Test\), two nodes, one edge.
  • CPTs: \(P(C) = 0.01\); \(P(+|C) = 0.9\), \(P(+| eg C) = 0.08\).
  • Causal use (down the arrow): a patient with cancer tests positive 90 % of the time. Straight from the table, no calculation.
  • Diagnostic use (against the arrow): a positive test means cancer with probability \[ rac{0.9 imes 0.01}{0.9(0.01) + 0.08(0.99)} = rac{0.009}{0.0882} = 10.2\,\% \]
  • Three numbers, four lines, and it demonstrates the entire connection the three papers ask about.
The connection, stated
  • The network supplies the numbers Bayes needs. \(P(C)\) is the prior sitting at the root; \(P(+|C)\) and \(P(+| eg C)\) are the CPT of the child; the denominator is the law of total probability over that same CPT.
  • Bayes supplies the direction the network lacks. The arrows point from cause to effect, which is the direction knowledge is available in. Diagnosis needs the other direction, and Bayes is the only thing that turns it round.
  • So the answer to “is there any connection” is: a belief network is a factored store of exactly the conditional probabilities Bayes' theorem consumes, and inference in the network is repeated application of Bayes plus the product rule.
  • 80 Ba's “how can inference be done” is answered by the four modes in §4.7: causal, diagnostic, intercausal and mixed. Name all four; work one.

column1: What is knowledge representation? What do you understand by structured knowledge representation?
column4:
Knowledge representation
  • Encoding what an agent knows about the world in a form a computer can manipulate, chosen so that inference is easy.
  • Two things exist and must not be confused:
    • Facts \(-\) truths in the world. The knowledge level.
    • Representations of those facts in some formalism. The symbol level.
  • KR is the mapping between the two, and it must run both ways: Tommy is a dog \(\rightarrow\) dog(Tommy); add \(\forall x: dog(x) \rightarrow hastail(x)\), deduce hastail(Tommy); map back to Tommy has a tail.
  • The backward map is where representations fail. A formalism that cannot say its answer back in the user's terms is useless in an expert system.
  • Three levels a fact sits at: knowledge (what is true), logical (the sentence encoding it), implementation (the data structure holding the sentence).
  • The kinds of knowledge to name if asked: objects, events, performance (how to do a task), meta-knowledge, facts.
Structured knowledge representation
  • In logic, everything known about one object is scattered across many separate clauses. Nothing in the formalism ties them together.
  • Structured KR concentrates all of an object's knowledge in one place: one node of a graph, or one record of slots. The structure itself carries meaning.
  • So the definition to write: a representation in which knowledge is stored in named, linked units rather than in flat sentences, each unit holding an object and everything known about it.
  • The four structured schemes on this syllabus: semantic nets, frames, conceptual dependency, scripts.
  • Rich and Knight call them slot-and-filler structures, weak where the slots carry no fixed meaning (nets, frames) and strong where they do (CD, scripts).
  • What it buys you: inheritance, default values, and the ability to answer “what do you know about \(X\)” by looking in one place.

column1: What are the different approaches / models / schemes of knowledge representation? How do you choose among them?
column4:
The four schemes (answer 73 Bh with these)
  • 1. Logical \(-\) knowledge as formal sentences, manipulated by rules of inference.
    • Eg propositional logic, first-order predicate logic (Ch 4).
    • ✓Precise, sound, complete. ×Rigid, and a single object's facts end up scattered.
  • 2. Procedural \(-\) knowledge as procedures that do something.
    • Eg IF–THEN production rules, an expert system's rule base.
    • ✓Directly executable, control built in. ×Knowledge and the code using it are inseparable, so nothing can be modified independently.
  • 3. Network \(-\) knowledge as a labelled graph.
    • Eg semantic nets, conceptual dependency, conceptual graphs.
    • ✓Visual, inheritance is free. ×No quantifiers, no negation.
  • 4. Structured \(-\) a network whose nodes are themselves complex data structures.
    • Eg frames, scripts.
    • ✓Defaults, procedures and constraints per slot. ×No inference engine of its own.
  • One sentence that ties them together: 3 and 4 are the structured half of this chapter; 1 and 2 are Ch 4 and the expert system of Ch 7.
The five methods (the wording BJ Sir and PS Sir use)
  • Procedural \(-\) facts plus the step-by-step operations on them, hard-coded.
  • Declarative \(-\) states, facts, rules and relations declared separately from the algorithm that reasons over them.
    • This separation is the whole advantage: the knowledge can be changed without rewriting the reasoner, and one optimised reasoner serves many knowledge bases.
  • Relational \(-\) facts as rows of a table, exactly as a database holds them. Simple, but carries no inference at all.
  • Hierarchical \(-\) inheritable knowledge as a tree of classes, each level inheriting the level above.
  • Complex network graph \(-\) the general labelled graph: semantic nets.
How to choose 80 Ch 2
  • Score the candidates on the four adequacies of §5.3, against the domain you actually have.
  • Then three practical questions:
    • Is the knowledge mostly taxonomic? Use a net or frames, and get inheritance for nothing.
    • Does it need proof, quantifiers or negation? Use logic \(-\) a net cannot express “no bird is a mammal”.
    • Does it need defaults and exceptions? Use frames; logic has no clean way to say “birds fly, except penguins”.
  • The examiner's expected closing line: no single scheme wins. Real systems are hybrid \(-\) frames for the objects, rules for the reasoning.

column1: How is a knowledge representation evaluated? What are the issues in knowledge representation?
column4:
Evaluating a KR: the four adequacies
  • 1. Representational adequacy \(-\) can it represent all the kinds of knowledge the domain needs?
  • 2. Inferential adequacy \(-\) can its structures be manipulated to derive new structures, ie new knowledge from old?
  • 3. Inferential efficiency \(-\) can it carry extra guidance that focuses the inference engine in productive directions, rather than letting it search blindly?
  • 4. Acquisitional efficiency \(-\) can new knowledge be added easily, ideally automatically rather than by a human?
  • Two practical criteria worth adding for the last mark: it must be easy to use, and easy to modify and extend.
  • The honest closing line: no known representation scores well on all four at once. That is exactly why hybrid systems exist, and it is what 80 Ch's “is it possible to evaluate a KR” is fishing for \(-\) yes, on these four axes, but only relative to a domain.
The five issues in knowledge representation
  • 1. Important attributes \(-\) are there attributes so basic that they occur in almost every domain, and so deserve special handling?
    • Yes: isa and instance. Both carry property inheritance, and every scheme in this chapter is built on them. This is the expected answer, not a shrug.
  • 2. Relationships among attributes \(-\) four to name:
    • inverses (owns / owned-by), existence in an isa hierarchy (height generalises batting-height), techniques for reasoning about values (types, ranges, rules), single-valued attributes (a person has one date of birth).
  • 3. Level of representation, ie granularity \(-\) how fine should the primitives be?
    • Coarse: few facts, but similar sentences look different. Fine: identical meanings collapse together, but the store explodes. CD (§5.7) is the extreme fine-grained answer.
  • 4. Representing sets of objects \(-\) by listing members, or by stating the defining property? Only the second can say “there are lots of sheep”, which is a property of the set and of no member.
  • 5. Finding the right structure \(-\) given a huge store, how do you select the relevant structure and revise it when it turns out wrong? Indexing, matching and frame selection all live here.
  • Two more the decks add: interpretation is informal in a net, and complex relationships are hard to draw with binary links.

column1: What is a semantic net? Explain with an example. When do we use one?
column4:
What it is
  • A directed labelled graph that stores knowledge as nodes and arcs.
    • Nodes \(=\) objects, concepts, situations or events.
    • Arcs \(=\) the relationship between two nodes, and the arc is labelled with that relationship.
  • A declarative graphic representation: it states what is true and supports automated reasoning over it, but contains no procedure.
  • Proposed as an alternative to predicate logic. Same facts, but all of one object's facts meet at one node instead of being scattered over clauses.
  • Oldest KR in the subject: the Tree of Porphyry, 3rd century AD. Worth a line in an 8-mark answer.
The two links every paper wants named
  • isa / a-kind-of \(-\) class to class. A cat is a mammal. Set inclusion: \(Cats \subset Mammals\).
  • instance / member \(-\) individual to class. Tom is a cat. Set membership: \(Tom \in Cats\).
  • Getting these two the wrong way round is the commonest lost mark in the drawing questions. Sakti Gauchan is an instance of Person; Person is isa Mammal.
  • Everything else is an ordinary relation arc: has-part, owns, likes, team, uniform-color.
isa runs class to class, instance-of runs individual to class, and owns is an ordinary relation. Source: BA Sir CH-05.
The canonical net, and its FOPL
Rich and Knight's figure. Every “convert these sentences” question in the papers is this net with the names changed: a class chain at the top, an individual hung off it by instance, and its own properties fanning out. Source: PS Sir ch5.
Why a net can do things logic cannot
  • Inheritance is free. A property put on Person is automatically available to Pee-Wee-Reese by following instance then isa upward. No inference rule is needed; the arcs are the rule.
  • Intersection search. Spread activation outward from two nodes and see where the two wavefronts meet. That is how a net answers “what connects the Brooklyn Dodgers and blue?” \(-\) a question logic can only answer by proving a conjecture you already had to guess.
  • This is the advantage to quote, because it exploits the entity-based organisation that slot-and-filler structures have and logic does not.

column1: Advantages and limitations of a semantic net; how do you represent a three-place relation?
column4:
Advantages
  • Natural and transparent: close to how people link ideas, so it is readable by a non-programmer.
  • Easy to visualise, and easy to check by eye.
  • Inheritance of properties comes for free down isa chains.
  • Space-efficient: each object appears once, however many facts mention it.
  • Related facts sit next to each other, so relevant knowledge is found by following links instead of by searching the whole store.
Limitations
  • Cannot express quantification, negation or disjunction. There is no way to draw “every mammal has some parent”, “no bird is a mammal” or “Tom is black or white”. This is the limitation to write first.
  • No standard meaning for link names. has-part means whatever the person who drew it meant, so two nets are not comparable.
  • No inference mechanism of its own: it stores, it does not deduce.
  • Slow at query time \(-\) answering may need a traversal of the whole graph.
  • Does not scale: a net that really modelled human memory cannot be built by hand.
  • Interpretation is informal, so the net depends entirely on its creator.
Three-place relations: use an event node
  • Arcs are binary, so “John gave the book to Mary” cannot be one arc: it has three arguments.
  • The fix: create a new node for the event itself, then hang one binary arc on it per argument.
EV7 is the giving-event node. agent \(\rightarrow\) John, object \(\rightarrow\) the book, beneficiary \(\rightarrow\) Mary, and instance says EV7 is a Give. Source: PS Sir ch5.
  • Same trick for a baseball game with two teams and a score: isa(G23, Game), home_team(G23, Dodgers), visiting_team(G23, Cubs), score(G23, 5-3).
  • Say why it works: it converts an \(n\)-place predicate into \(n\) binary ones by reifying the relation as an object.

column1: What do the arcs of a semantic net actually mean?
column4:
• Subset arc \(=\) set inclusion, \(A \subset B\). Eg \(Cats \subset Mammals\).
  • Member arc \(=\) set membership, \(A \in B\). Eg \(Felix \in Cats\).
  • A named arc between two individuals \(=\) the ground fact \(R(A,B)\). Eg Friend(Felix, Opus).
  • A named arc drawn out of a class box means \(\forall x\, (x \in A \Rightarrow R(x,B))\): every member has that value. Eg Legs out of Birds \(\rightarrow 2\).
  • Same arc with an existential reading: \(\forall x\, (x \in A \Rightarrow \exists y\, (y \in B \wedge R(x,y)))\). Eg Parent out of Bird \(\rightarrow\) Birds: every bird has some bird parent.
  • Why it matters: the last two are the only quantification a net can express, and only because the reader agrees to read the picture that way. Nothing in the drawing says which of the two is meant. That ambiguity is the “lack of formality” limitation.
  • Source: BJ Sir AI_Chapter5_new.

column1: What is a frame? Explain with a suitable example. What is its significance in AI?
column4:
Definition
  • A frame is a collection of attributes and their values that describes one entity, together with that entity's relationship to other frames.
    • Slot \(=\) the attribute name. Filler \(=\) its value.
    • So a frame is a record structure with meaning attached.
  • A single frame is almost useless. The power is in a frame system: many frames, connected because the value of one frame's slot is another frame.
  • The line that earns the mark: a semantic net is a two-dimensional representation, nodes and arcs; frames add a third dimension by letting a node have internal structure.
  • A frame is designed to represent a stereotypical object or situation: what is normally true, with defaults for what has not been observed.
  • Frames are static. A script (§5.7) is the same idea made sequential.
The four parts of a frame
  • 1. Frame identification name \(-\) what entity this frame is about.
  • 2. Relationship to other frames \(-\) isa, instance, part-of, superclass.
  • 3. Slot and filler \(-\) the attribute–value pairs themselves.
  • 4. Default information \(-\) values taken as true until contradicted. Logic has no clean way to do this; frames do, and it is the strongest single argument for them.
Types of frame
  • Class frame \(-\) the generic frame others inherit from. Eg Vehicle.
  • Subclass frame \(-\) inherits a class frame and adds slots. Eg Car.
  • Instance frame \(-\) one individual. Eg Ram's Car.
  • An instance or subclass frame inherits every slot above it and may add its own. Generic frames sit at the top of the hierarchy.
Class, subclass and instance in one picture
Vehicle (class) \(\rightarrow\) Truck and Car (subclass, is-a) \(\rightarrow\) Ram's Car (instance), with part_of links out to Basket and Ram. Note the instance frame fills in the slots it inherited empty. Source: Insights book p136.
Part of a frame description of a hotel room. Source: BA Sir CH-05.
A frame system: four frames pointing at each other
  • hotel room carries three ordinary slots (specialization of, location, contains), and the third one's filler is three pointers, not three strings. That is what makes this a frame system.
  • Each frame it points at repeats the pattern. hotel chair has specialization of: chair, so it inherits everything a chair has and overrides only height, legs and use.
  • hotel bed adds a part slot filled by the mattress frame, which is part-of, not is-a. Confusing those two is the commonest error in a frame answer: is-a inherits, part-of does not.
  • The line to write under your own drawing: the diagram is a graph whose nodes happen to be records. That is structured knowledge representation in one picture, and it is why 80 Bh can ask for a net and a frame in the same breath.

column1: What can a slot hold, and what are demons?
column4:
One STUDENT frame with every facet filled in. Source: PS Sir ch5.
A generic property frame carrying two demons: if-added: ADD_PROPERTY on types, if-needed: FIND_OWNER on owner, which also shows a default of government. Source: PS Sir ch5.
Facets: what a slot carries besides its value
  • Value \(-\) the current filler.
  • Default \(-\) the filler used when nothing has been observed.
  • Cardinality \(-\) minimum and maximum number of fillers allowed.
  • Type \(-\) a restriction on what a filler may be, usually another frame.
  • Procedures \(-\) attached code, see demons below.
  • Salience \(-\) how important this slot is to the frame.
  • Constraints \(-\) axioms the value must satisfy, eg \(0 \le CGPA \le 4.0\).
Demons (attached procedures, Insights §5.4.3)
  • A demon is a procedure stored in a slot and fired automatically when the slot is touched. The frame does not just hold data, it reacts.
  • IF-NEEDED \(-\) fires when a value is required and none is stored. Compute it now.
  • IF-ADDED \(-\) fires when a value is put into the slot. Propagate the consequences.
  • IF-REMOVED \(-\) fires when a value is deleted.
  • IF-CHANGED \(-\) fires when a stored value is replaced.
  • Why this matters for the exam: demons are what make a frame system active, and they are the honest answer to “frames have no inference mechanism” \(-\) they have no general one, but each slot can carry its own.
  • Frames Vs objects: slots are data members, demons are methods, isa is inheritance and part-of is containment. A frame system is object-oriented programming, invented for AI a decade earlier. One sentence, and it is often worth a mark.

column1: Advantages and limitations of frames
column4:
Advantages
  • Groups related knowledge together, so programming and retrieval are easier: everything about an object is in one record.
  • Defaults, and therefore the ability to reason with incomplete information and to detect missing values.
  • Easy to extend: adding a slot, a property or a relation costs one line.
  • Inheritance down the class hierarchy, exactly as in a semantic net.
  • Procedural attachment: a slot can compute or validate itself.
  • Flexible and widely used \(-\) vision and natural language processing both run on frames.
  • Good at causal knowledge, because the information is organised by cause and effect.
Limitations
  • No inference mechanism of its own. Frames store and inherit; they do not deduce. Any reasoning has to be bolted on.
  • Modification is dangerous: change one frame and every frame that inherits from it is affected.
  • Redundancy \(-\) the same fact easily ends up in several frames.
  • No standard structure: the frame for a room and the frame for a person look nothing alike, so nothing generic can be written over them.
  • Defaults can be wrong, and nothing in the formalism flags it when they are.
  • The examiner's expected trade-off line: frames win on organisation and defaults, logic wins on proof, nets win on visibility.

column1: Explain semantic nets and frames with examples. Compare them, and list their advantages and limitations
column4:
Semantic netFrame
Shapelabelled directed graphcollection of records, slots and fillers
Dimensiontwo: node and arcthree: node, and structure inside the node
Unit of knowledgeone arc \(=\) one factone frame \(=\) one whole object
Node holdsa name onlyslots, values, defaults, types, constraints, procedures
Relationsdrawn as arcswritten as slot values that are other frames
Inheritance✓down isa / instance arcs✓down class \(\rightarrow\) subclass \(\rightarrow\) instance
Defaults×cannot express✓first-class, with if-needed to compute one
Procedures×none✓demons on any slot
Best atseeing the relationships at a glanceholding everything about one object in one place
Weakest atcomplex or structured facts about a single nodeshowing the shape of the knowledge as a whole
Reasoningintersection search, link followinginheritance and slot lookup only
Both fail atquantification, negation, disjunction, and having no inference engine of their own
How frames are useful in semantic nets 72 Ash 7
  • The question sounds like two topics. It is one: a frame is what you get when you let a semantic-net node have contents.
  • A net node called Tom can only be named. Make it a frame and it can carry colour: ginger, age: default 2, owner: John, plus a demon that computes age from a birth date.
  • So frames fix the net's weakest point: they let one node hold structured, defaulted, constrained knowledge instead of forcing every detail out onto its own arc.
  • And the net fixes the frame system's weakest point: it shows the shape of the whole knowledge base, which a pile of records does not.
  • Answer in one sentence: frames give a semantic net depth at each node, and the net gives a frame system its map.
Why both matter in AI 78 Ba 2
  • They give inheritance and defaults, which is how an agent reasons with incomplete knowledge.
  • They are human-readable, so a domain expert can check the knowledge base without knowing logic \(-\) the bottleneck in every expert system (Ch 7).
  • They organise knowledge by object rather than by sentence, so retrieval is local instead of a search of the whole store.
Converting a semantic net into a frame 81 Ba 5
  • Step 1. Every node becomes a frame, named after the node.
  • Step 2. Every outgoing arc of that node becomes a slot in its frame. The arc label is the slot name, the arc's target is the filler.
  • Step 3. isa and instance arcs become the frame's class link, not ordinary slots: isa \(\rightarrow\) a subclass frame, instance \(\rightarrow\) an instance frame.
  • Step 4. Any slot whose filler is a node that has its own frame is left as a pointer to that frame, which is what makes the result a frame system.
  • Step 5. Push each property to the highest class that has it, and let everything below inherit. A property drawn on three individuals in the net belongs on their class in the frame system.
  • Check: no information may be lost. Count the arcs in the net; count the filled slots in the frames. They must match.
  • 81 Ba is worked end to end in the companion, on this net.
The same knowledge three ways
  • Frame, net and FOPL are interchangeable for taxonomic knowledge, and 75 Ba 6 asks for exactly that: examples of both, with FOPL statements.
  • Read the figure left to right: a frame-based knowledge base, then the first-order sentences that say the same thing.
  • Subset(Birds, Animals) is the isa arc. Member(Opus, Penguins) is the instance arc. Rel(Legs, Birds, 2) is a slot with a value.
  • Write the FOPL line beside every arc you draw in that question. It is 2 free marks and most answers skip it.
(a) a frame-based knowledge base and (b) its translation into first-order logic, the same nine facts twice. Source: PS Sir ch5.

column1: What is conceptual dependency? Explain the common primitives used in it
column4:
What it is
  • Schank, 1973–75, built for natural language understanding.
  • A representation of the meaning of a sentence, built from a small fixed set of primitive acts instead of from the sentence's own words.
  • Three goals, and the papers want all three:
    • to help draw inferences from a sentence;
    • to be independent of the words used in the input;
    • so that any two sentences identical in meaning have exactly one representation.
  • Hence I gave the man a book, the man got a book from me and the book was given to the man by me all draw the same diagram. That is the point of the whole theory.
  • A strong slot-and-filler structure: unlike a frame, the slots have fixed, agreed meanings.
The four conceptual categories
  • ACT \(-\) an action, always one of the primitives below.
  • PP \(-\) picture producer, an object or actor.
  • AA \(-\) action aider, a modifier of an ACT (how, when, where).
  • PA \(-\) picture aider, a modifier of a PP (colour, size, quality).
  • Dependency rule: PP and ACT are governors, PA and AA are dependents. A dependent cannot stand alone; a conceptualization needs at least two governors.
  • Eg Sally stroked her fat cat: PP \(=\) Sally, cat; ACT \(=\) stroke; PA \(=\) fat.
The eleven primitive acts
PrimitiveTransfer or action, and a verb that maps to it
ATRANStransfer of an abstract relationship, ie possession. give, lend, borrow
PTRANStransfer of the physical location of an object. go, come, went
PROPELapplication of a physical force to an object. push, pull
MOVEmovement of a body part by its owner. kick, punch
GRASPan actor grasping an object. clutch, catch
INGESTan animal taking something in. eat, drink
EXPELan animal forcing something out. cry, sweat, throw
MTRANStransfer of mental information. tell, ask, read
MBUILDbuilding new information out of old. decide, infer, conclude
SPEAKproducing a sound. say, talk, play music
ATTENDfocusing a sense organ on a stimulus. listen, watch
  • Learn the first three and MTRANS. Every example in every paper and every scene of the restaurant script is built from those four.

column1: Draw the conceptual dependency of a sentence
column4:
The seven dependency forms, then each one used on a sentence. Row 6 is John pushed the cart (\(ACT \xleftarrow{o} PP\), PROPEL); row 7 is John took the book from Mary (ATRANS with a recipient pair). Source: BA Sir CH-05.
The notation
  • \(\Leftrightarrow\) two-way link between an actor and the action. Every conceptualization has exactly one.
  • \(\rightarrow\) direction of dependency: the dependent points at its governor.
  • o \(=\) objective case, what the act is done to.
  • R \(=\) recipient case, drawn as a fork: the arrow up is the receiver, the arrow down is the giver.
  • I \(=\) instrumental case, what it was done with.
  • D \(=\) directive case, from where to where.
  • p \(=\) past tense, f future, t transition, ? interrogative, / negative. Tense sits on the \(\Leftrightarrow\).
  • Worked example \(-\) I gave a book to Ram:
    • \(I \Leftrightarrow ATRANS\), with p on the link;
    • \(\xleftarrow{o}\) book;
    • \(\xleftarrow{R}\) forking up to Ram and down to I.
Problems with CD
  • The original sentence cannot be reconstructed from the diagram; meaning survives, wording does not.
  • Choosing the primitive is hard: one verb may map to several ACTs depending on context.
  • The structures get huge. “John bet Mike that Nepal will win the World Cup” needs an enormous diagram for one sentence.
  • Rules must be hand-written per primitive, so the theory does not scale to a general-purpose KR.

column1: How is knowledge represented using scripts? Explain with an example
column4:
What a script is
  • Schank and Abelson, 1977, written in the CD notation.
  • A structured description of a stereotyped sequence of events in a known context: going to a restaurant, going to the theatre, visiting a doctor.
  • It extends a frame by making the slot values ordered in time and by representing expectations about what happens next.
  • Justified by three facts about the world: events occur in known patterns, events cause one another, and entry conditions decide whether a pattern applies at all.
The six components (write all six)
  • Entry conditions \(-\) must be true before the script can be invoked. Eg S is hungry, S has money.
  • Results \(-\) true once it has run. Eg S is not hungry, O has more money.
  • Props \(-\) the objects involved. Eg tables, menu, food, check, money.
  • Roles \(-\) the participants and what each does. Eg S \(=\) customer, W \(=\) waiter, C \(=\) cook, M \(=\) cashier, O \(=\) owner.
  • Track \(-\) a variation on the general pattern. Eg coffee shop Vs fancy restaurant: same script, different track.
  • Scenes \(-\) the ordered sequence of events, each written in CD primitives.
The RESTAURANT script, header and scene 1
  • Script: RESTAURANT. Track: coffee shop.
  • Props: tables, menu, F \(=\) food, check, money.
  • Roles: S \(=\) customer, W \(=\) waiter, C \(=\) cook, M \(=\) cashier, O \(=\) owner.
  • Entry conditions: S is hungry, S has money.
  • Results: S has less money, O has more money, S is not hungry, S is pleased (optional).
  • Scene 1, entering: S PTRANS S into restaurant \(\cdot\) S ATTEND eyes to tables \(\cdot\) S MBUILD where to sit \(\cdot\) S PTRANS S to table \(\cdot\) S MOVE S to sitting position.
Scene 2, ordering, with both tracks: menu already on the table, or the waiter brings it. Source: BA Sir CH-05.
Invocation, and why it is the hard part
  • A script is opened when its topic is significant in the input; if merely mentioned, only a pointer is kept.
  • “John enjoyed the play in the theatre” \(\rightarrow\) invoke, and every implicit question is answered: did he go, did he buy a ticket, did he have money.
  • The failure case to quote: “John went to the theatre to pick up his daughter”. Same words, low significance, and invoking the script produces confident wrong answers.
  • There is no reliable rule for judging significance, only heuristics. That is the honest limitation to close on.
Advantages and disadvantages
  • ✓Predicts implicit events: it fills in what the text never said, which is exactly what language understanding needs.
  • ✓Builds one coherent interpretation out of scattered observations.
  • ×Far more specific and less general than a frame. One script covers one situation.
  • ×Not suitable for knowledge that is not event-sequenced.
  • ×Wrong invocation gives confidently wrong answers.
  • The cure for the inflexibility: MOPs, memory organization packets \(-\) smaller reusable modules recombined to fit the situation.
Scene 3 eating and scene 4 exiting, including the no pay path. Source: BA Sir CH-05.

Source notes. Insights §5.4.2 (book p135) converts the Tom-the-cat semantic net into frames, but its figure prints like John and type Ginger where the net says is-owned-by and is-coloured, and gives the John frame an Age 22 / Color white pair carried over from the car example on the facing page. The net-to-frame recipe in §5.6 above follows the book's method and Rich and Knight's figures, and the companion works the conversion on a net that is drawn correctly.  \(\cdot\)  The syllabus files this chapter as five sub-topics but the papers only ever set four: representations and mappings is never asked on its own, always as the two-mark opener to what is knowledge representation.

column1: Chapter 5 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
Every problem opens with the question exactly as the paper prints it, the paper's own spelling and slips included.  \(\cdot\) 11 sentence sets over 12 papers, plus the net-to-frame conversion and the net/frame/FOPL question.  \(\cdot\) Where a lecture deck or the textbook already draws the answer, the published figure is printed and the caption says exactly what differs from the paper's wording. Where none does, the answer is given as an arc list \(-\) every node, every link, every direction \(-\) from which the drawing is mechanical.
The four-step recipe. It works on all eleven sets:
  • Step 1. Underline every noun phrase. Each distinct one is a node. Do not invent nodes and do not merge two that the paper keeps apart.
  • Step 2. Sort the nodes into classes and individuals. A proper name, or anything the sentences call a something, is an individual. Anything that other things can be is a class.
  • Step 3. Draw the class spine first, bottom to top, joined by isa arcs, then hang each individual off its class with an instance arc.
    • Class to class is isa. Individual to class is instance. Getting these two the wrong way round is the single commonest lost mark in this question.
  • Step 4. Add one labelled arc per remaining sentence, always out of the thing the sentence is about. The verb becomes the arc label.
  • Then check three things, which is what separates a 6 from a 4:
    • Count. One arc per sentence, plus the spine. If a sentence produced no arc you have lost a mark.
    • Push properties up. If two individuals of the same class both carry a property, draw it once on the class and let them inherit. Say in one line that you did, and why.
    • Flag what the net cannot say. Quantifiers, negation and disjunction do not draw. A sentence like “every mammal gives birth to a baby” gets an arc out of the class node and a note saying the arc is read as \(\forall x \in Mammal\). Examiners give marks for that note.
  • Layout that always works: most general class at the top, isa arcs pointing up, individuals on a row near the bottom, and their own properties fanning sideways. Every published figure in this chapter is drawn that way.

column1: 5.N.10 Converting a semantic net into a frame — Compare semantic net and frame. How do you convert a semantic net into a frame? Explain with example
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 81 Ba · Q6 · 3+5
Compare semantic net and frame. How you convert semantic net into frame? Explain with example.
column4:
The five steps, applied
  • 1. Every node becomes a frame. The net of §5.N.2 has seven nodes, so the frame system has seven frames: Person, Adult-Male, ML-Baseball-Player, Fielder, Pee-Wee-Reese, ML-Baseball-Team, Brooklyn-Dodgers.
  • 2. Every outgoing arc becomes a slot. Arc label \(\rightarrow\) slot name, arc target \(\rightarrow\) filler. Adult-Male height \(\rightarrow\) 5-10 becomes a height slot in the Adult-Male frame with filler 5-10.
  • 3. isa and instance become the class link, not ordinary slots. Fielder gets isa: ML-Baseball-Player and is a subclass frame; Pee-Wee-Reese gets instance: Fielder and is an instance frame.
  • 4. A filler that has its own frame stays a pointer. Pee-Wee-Reese team \(\rightarrow\) Brooklyn-Dodgers is a link to that frame, not the string. This is what makes the result a frame system rather than seven separate tables.
  • 5. Push each property to the highest class that has it, and let everything below inherit. height sits on Adult-Male, batting-average on ML-Baseball-Player, and Pee-Wee-Reese overrides both with his own values.
Then check, and say you checked
  • No information may be lost. Count the arcs in the net, count the filled slots in the frames. They must agree.
  • What the frames gained: cardinality (6,000,000,000 persons), defaults (handed: Right), and slots marked with * for values that belong to the class rather than to each member. None of those can be drawn in a net.
The net of §5.N.2 after conversion. Seven frames, each slot either an inherited class link, a value, or a pointer to another frame. The * marks a value stored on the class. Compare with c5_semnet_peewee above: same knowledge, different formalism. Source: PS Sir ch5, after Rich and Knight Fig 9.5.
The reverse direction, if asked
  • Frame \(\rightarrow\) net is step 1 to 4 run backwards: one node per frame, one arc per filled slot, and isa / instance arcs from the class links.
  • The conversion is lossy in this direction. Defaults, cardinalities, type restrictions and demons have no arc to become, so they are simply dropped. Say so \(-\) it is the cleanest one-line proof that a frame carries more than a net.

column1: What is machine learning? Explain the learning framework with a block diagram.
column4:
Definition
  • Machine learning is the branch of AI in which a program improves its performance on a task from experience, without being explicitly programmed for that task.
  • Tom Mitchell's form, worth quoting: a program learns from experience \(E\) w.r.t. task \(T\) and measure \(P\) if its performance at \(T\), measured by \(P\), improves with \(E\).
  • In AI terms: the agent observes data, builds a model of it, and uses that model as both a hypothesis about the world and a program that solves problems.
  • Three things learning always does, and the three-word answer to “what is learning”:
    • Change \(-\) the learner itself is altered.
    • Generalization \(-\) performance improves on similar tasks, not only on the ones seen.
    • Improvement \(-\) and the design must stop changes that make performance worse.
  • Why an intelligent agent needs it (asked as “learning is an essential characteristic of intelligent agents, comment”, Ch 1): a designer cannot enumerate every situation; the environment changes after deployment; and some tasks have no known algorithm, only examples.
The learning framework: four components
Environment feeds the learning element; the learning element writes the knowledge base; the performance element uses it and reports back.
  • 1. Environment \(-\) supplies the information. Judge it on:
    • Level: high level \(=\) abstract, covers a broad class of problems; low level \(=\) detailed, covers one problem.
    • Quality: noise free, reliable, ordered.
  • 2. Learning element \(-\) turns that information into knowledge. Rote learning, learning by example, by analogy, explanation-based (§6.2).
  • 3. Knowledge base \(-\) stores what was learnt. Must be expressive, modifiable and extendible (holds meta-knowledge, so its own structure can change).
  • 4. Performance element \(-\) uses the knowledge to act, measures how well it did, and feeds the error back to the learning element. That feedback arrow is the whole point of the diagram: draw it.

column1: What are the different ways / methods of learning? Describe each.
column4:
The five ways, easiest to hardest
  • 1. Rote learning \(-\) memorise and recall.
    • Solved problem \(\rightarrow\) store \(\rightarrow\) look up next time.
    • No inference at all: nothing new is derived.
    • Only worth it if retrieval is cheaper than recomputing.
    • Eg Samuel's checkers player, which stored board positions it had seen.
  • 2. Learning by example (inductive) \(-\) specific cases \(\rightarrow\) general rule. Eg decision trees, ID3 (§6.5).
  • 3. Learning by analogy \(-\) transfer a solution from a known similar problem (§6.4).
  • 4. Explanation-based learning (EBL) \(-\) use existing domain knowledge to explain one example, then generalise the explanation into a rule.
    • Learns from a single example, because the prior knowledge does the work the extra examples would have done.
    • Eg see one cup once, know what makes it a cup, recognise every cup after.
  • 5. Learning by deduction \(-\) general rules \(\rightarrow\) specific facts, or new general rules from old ones. \(A=B\), \(B=C\), so \(A=C\).
Induction Vs deduction
asked as a short note by 73 Bh 3.
Read the left ladder downwards and the right one upwards: that direction is the whole distinction.
InductiveDeductive
Directionobservation \(\rightarrow\) hypothesishypothesis \(\rightarrow\) observation
Goes fromspecificgeneral
Producesa general rule from raw dataa specific fact from known rules
Truthnot guaranteed, only probableguaranteed if the premises hold
Reasoningprobabilisticlogical (Ch 4)
Example1000 white swans \(\rightarrow\) “swans are white”all men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal
  • The one-line answer: induction generalises and can be wrong; deduction specialises and cannot.
  • Both appear in §6.2's list of ways of learning, and the papers ask them as a 3 short note, so three rows of that table plus this line is a full answer.
  • Where each one lives in this subject: deduction is Chapter 4 (resolution, forward and backward chaining, all truth-preserving); induction is this chapter (ID3, §6.5) and every learning algorithm in it.
  • Abduction is worth one extra line if you have room: reasoning from an observation to its most likely cause. Medical diagnosis. Also not truth-preserving.

column1: Differentiate supervised and unsupervised learning. Clustering falls under which category? Justify, stating algorithms.
column4:
SupervisedUnsupervised
Training datalabelled: every input carries its correct outputunlabelled: inputs only
Aimlearn the input \(\rightarrow\) output mapping, then predict for new inputsfind hidden structure, groups and patterns in the data
Feedbackdirect: error \(=\) predicted \(-\) actual, at every samplenone; the model is judged only by the structure it finds
Tasksclassification, regressionclustering, association
Algorithmslinear + logistic regression, SVM, naive Bayes, KNN, decision tree, back-propagation ANNK-means, hierarchical (agglomerative), DBSCAN, Apriori, SOM
Human efforthigh: someone has to label everythinglow
Accuracyhigher, and measurablelower, and hard to measure
Examplespam filter trained on mails already marked spam / not spamsegment customers by purchase behaviour, with no idea of the segments beforehand
Reinforcement learning
  • Feedback-based: the agent acts, the environment returns a reward or a penalty, and the agent adjusts.
  • No labelled data and no supervisor. The agent discovers which actions pay by trying them.
  • Goal \(=\) maximise cumulative reward over the long run, not the next reward.
  • Four elements to name (78 Po):
    • Policy \(-\) state \(\rightarrow\) action mapping.
    • Reward signal \(-\) one number per step, defines the goal.
    • Value function \(-\) total reward expected from a state: good in the long run, where reward is good in the short run.
    • Model of the environment (optional).
  • Example: a robot that gets \(+10\) for reaching the goal square and \(-50\) for falling in a pit. Also game playing, robot navigation, self-driving control.
  • Semi-supervised is the fourth type worth one line: a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled one, used when labelling everything is too costly.
The rider: which category is clustering?  (74 Ma, 72 Ash, 4 of the 6)
  • Clustering is unsupervised, because the data carries no class label \(-\) the algorithm both invents the groups and assigns points to them.
  • Justify by naming algorithms, which is what the question asks for and where the marks are:
    • K-means \(-\) choose \(k\), assign every point to the nearest centroid, recompute the centroids, repeat until nothing moves. Nobody ever tells it a right answer.
    • Hierarchical (agglomerative) \(-\) start with every point its own cluster, repeatedly merge the two nearest, stop at \(k\) clusters or one.
    • DBSCAN \(-\) groups by density, and finds the number of clusters itself.
    • SOM / Kohonen (Ch 7) is a clustering network, and is unsupervised for exactly the same reason.
  • Contrast with classification, which draws the same picture but is supervised: the classes exist before training and every training point already carries one.
Deciding the type of any example the examiner invents
What does the data carry?Then it is
a correct output for every inputsupervised
nothing but inputsunsupervised
a few labelled, most notsemi-supervised
no outputs, but a reward after actingreinforcement
  • Worked on the examples the papers use: spam filter \(=\) supervised (mails already marked); customer segmentation \(=\) unsupervised; game-playing agent \(=\) reinforcement; handwriting recognition trained on labelled digits \(=\) supervised; market-basket association \(=\) unsupervised.
  • One sentence that is always worth writing: supervised learning is told the answer and learns the mapping; unsupervised learning is told nothing and learns the structure; reinforcement learning is told only whether it did well, and learns the policy.

column1: What is learning by analogy? Give an example, with a semantic network.
column4:
• Learning by analogy \(=\) acquiring knowledge about a new entity by transferring it from a known, similar entity.
  • It carries a solution across domains: find the analogous states and operators in the two domains, then reuse the old solution.
  • One example is enough, which is what makes it different from inductive learning (which needs many).
  • The five steps (write these for a 6 or 7 mark answer):
    • 1. Recognition \(-\) notice the new problem resembles a past one.
    • 2. Access and recall \(-\) the resemblance indexes memory; retrieve one or more candidate analogues.
    • 3. Selection and mapping \(-\) pick the relevant parts and map them from the base (known) domain to the target (new) one.
    • 4. Extension \(-\) modify and extend the mapped solution to fit the target.
    • 5. Validation and generalization \(-\) test it; if it holds, form a general rule covering both situations.
  • Analogy Vs induction  (71 Ma 3): analogy maps one case onto one case and reasons by similarity; induction generalises many cases into a rule. Analogy transfers, induction abstracts.
First example: hydraulics and Kirchhoff
  • Flow into a junction equals flow out; current into a node equals current out. Knowing \(Q_a=3\), \(Q_b=9\) gives \(Q_c\) the same way \(I_3=I_1+I_2\) does.
  • The mapping: pressure drop \(\leftrightarrow\) voltage drop, pipe \(\leftrightarrow\) wire, flow rate \(\leftrightarrow\) current, junction \(\leftrightarrow\) node.
  • So a student who knows Kirchhoff's law can solve the hydraulics problem without being taught hydraulics. That sentence is the definition made concrete, and it is what the examiner wants.
  • Second example: the atom and the solar system, the one to draw as a semantic net for 71 Bh: two small nets, one arc list mapped onto the other.
    • Base net: Sun –greater-mass–> Earth, Sun –attracts–> Earth, Earth –revolves-around–> Sun.
    • Target net: Nucleus –greater-mass–> Electron, Nucleus –attracts–> Electron, and the arc the analogy supplies: Electron –revolves-around–> Nucleus.
    • Draw the two nets side by side and a dashed arrow between the matching nodes: Sun \(\leftrightarrow\) Nucleus, Earth \(\leftrightarrow\) Electron. That dashed mapping is the answer.
The mapping table, which is the marked half
RoleBase: solar systemTarget: atom
Heavy central bodySunNucleus
Light orbiting bodyEarthElectron
Relation knownattracts, greater massattracts, greater mass
Relation transferredEarth revolves around SunElectron revolves around Nucleus
  • The last row is the whole point: it is not observed, it is carried across by the analogy, and then validated.
  • Say in one line what analogy risks: the mapping may not hold (electrons do not really orbit like planets), so step 5 validation is not optional. Naming that limitation reliably earns a mark.

column1: Define inductive learning. How is the best attribute selected in a decision tree? Explain ID3 with an example.
column4:
Inductive learning, and the tree
  • Inductive learning \(=\) drawing a general hypothesis from a set of specific input–output examples, chosen so that it classifies the examples well and generalises to new ones.
  • A decision tree is the standard hypothesis form:
    • each internal node tests one attribute,
    • each branch is one value of that attribute,
    • each leaf carries a class label.
  • To classify, walk root to leaf and read off the label.
  • ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3, Quinlan) builds that tree greedily, top down: at every node it puts the attribute that separates the classes best, and never goes back.
The two formulas \(-\) memorise these
\[ H(S) \;=\; -\sum_{i} p_i \log_2 p_i \] entropy of set \(S\): \(p_i\) is the fraction of \(S\) in class \(i\). \(H=0\) when \(S\) is pure, \(H=1\) when a two-class set is split 50/50. \[ Gain(S,A) \;=\; H(S) \;-\; \sum_{v \in A} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}\, H(S_v) \] the second term is the weighted average entropy after splitting on \(A\). Gain is the uncertainty removed.
  • Highest gain \(=\) lowest weighted entropy \(=\) best attribute. The two rules are the same rule.
Why it works, in one figure
Splitting on Type leaves every branch as mixed as the parent: gain 0, useless. Splitting on Patrons produces two pure branches and one mixed one: high gain. That comparison is the answer to “how is the best attribute selected”.
The algorithm, as five steps
  • 1. Compute \(H(S)\) for the current set.
  • 2. For each unused attribute \(A\), split \(S\) by its values and compute the weighted entropy of the split.
  • 3. \(Gain(S,A) = H(S) -\) that weighted entropy.
  • 4. Make the attribute with the largest gain the node, and branch on its values.
  • 5. Recurse on each branch with the remaining attributes. Stop a branch when: it is pure (leaf \(=\) that class); no attributes are left (leaf \(=\) majority class); or it is empty (leaf \(=\) parent's majority).
  • Three arithmetic checks that save marks: \(H\) of a pure branch is 0, not 1; \(H\) of an even two-class split is exactly 1; and every gain must be \(\geq 0\), so a negative one is an error in your weighted sum.
Characteristics to list if asked
  • Greedy, so no guarantee of the optimal tree \(-\) it can settle in a local optimum.
  • Produces small trees, but not always the smallest.
  • Overfits the training data; prefer smaller trees, and prune.
  • Awkward on continuous attributes: too many possible split points.
  • Handles noise and missing values badly. C4.5 fixes all four.

column1: What is a genetic algorithm? Explain all its steps with a block diagram, and its operators.
column2: 34578102+8
column4:
Definition and idea
  • A genetic algorithm is a search and optimization technique that imitates natural selection: it keeps a population of candidate solutions and evolves it, generation by generation, towards better ones.
  • Darwin in one line: select the best, discard the rest.
  • Evolutionary computing (asked by name in 79 Ch) is the family; GA is its best-known member, alongside genetic programming, evolutionary strategies and swarm methods.
  • Formally a variant of stochastic beam search: many states kept at once, successors generated by combining pairs rather than mutating one.
  • Vocabulary \(-\) the examiner marks these:
    • Gene \(-\) one position in the string; controls one characteristic.
    • Chromosome (individual) \(-\) a chain of genes \(=\) one candidate solution, usually a binary string.
    • Population \(-\) the set of chromosomes alive in one generation.
    • Fitness function \(-\) scores a chromosome. Problem dependent; it is the only thing that knows what “good” means.
    • Generation \(-\) one full cycle of the loop.
The flowchart 81 Ba asks for by name. Draw START \(\rightarrow\) generate random population \(\rightarrow\) evaluate fitness \(\rightarrow\) good enough? \(\rightarrow\) (no) select and mate \(\rightarrow\) mutate \(\rightarrow\) back to evaluate; (yes) END.
The five steps, which are also the five operators
  • 1. Initialization \(-\) generate the starting population at random.
    • Encode a solution as a string first (chromosome encoding); binary is usual, but integer and permutation encodings exist.
    • Population size trades diversity against run time. Seed it around a promising region if you have one.
  • 2. Fitness evaluation \(-\) score every chromosome with the fitness function. Infeasible chromosomes get fitness 0.
  • 3. Selection \(-\) choose parents, with probability rising with fitness.
    • Roulette wheel: slice proportional to fitness. Tournament: pick \(k\) at random, take the best. Rank: order them, select on rank. Elitism: copy the best one or two through untouched.
    • Keep a few weak ones on purpose \(-\) they hold the diversity the next crossover needs.
  • 4. Crossover (recombination) \(-\) cut two parents and swap the tails, so each child inherits from both. Probability typically 0.6 to 0.9.
  • 5. Mutation \(-\) flip a random gene with a small probability, typically 0.001 to 0.01.
  • 6. Replacement, then termination \(-\) offspring replace the weakest members; stop on a fixed number of generations, a fitness threshold, or when the population has converged (no improvement for several generations).
The same algorithm as one cycle, which is the “block diagram” most papers want: population \(\rightarrow\) selection \(\rightarrow\) parents \(\rightarrow\) crossover, mutation \(\rightarrow\) offspring \(\rightarrow\) replacement \(\rightarrow\) population.
Crossover, drawn
Single-point: one cut, tails swapped. Two-point: two cuts, the middle segment swapped. Uniform: each gene taken from either parent by a coin toss.
Mutation flips one gene of one child.
Why mutation matters  (81 Ba asks exactly this)
  • Crossover only recombines genes already in the population. If every chromosome carries a 0 in some position, no amount of crossover will ever produce a 1 there.
  • Mutation is the only source of new genetic material. It keeps diversity up and stops the search converging early on a local optimum.
  • So the rate must be small: too high and the search degenerates into a random walk, losing the good solutions selection just found.
Mutation Vs crossover  (73 Bh 3)
CrossoverMutation
Parentstwoone
Doesexchanges segments between two chromosomesflips a gene in one chromosome
Ratehigh, 0.6–0.9low, 0.001–0.01
Roleexploitation: combines what already worksexploration: introduces what is missing
If absentpopulation stagnates as copies of a few parentssearch sticks in a local optimum
Where it is applied  (72 Ma 2)
  • Optimization: travelling salesman, knapsack, job-shop scheduling, timetabling.
  • Engineering design, antenna and circuit layout, PID controller tuning.
  • Neural network weight and architecture search; feature selection in ML.
  • Robotics path planning, vehicle routing, bioinformatics (gene sequencing).
  • Why the study of genes belongs in AI (74 Bh 4): evolution is a proven search procedure that solved design problems no designer could; GA borrows the mechanism, not the biology.
Advantages and limitations
  • ✓Simple concept; works on the encoded parameters, so it needs no derivative and no auxiliary information, only a fitness score.
  • ✓Searches many points at once, so it escapes local optima; inherently parallel; the answer improves with run time and can be stopped anywhere.
  • ×No guarantee of the global optimum; ×many fitness evaluations, so slow when each is costly; ×the encoding, population size and rates all need tuning; ×can converge prematurely if diversity is lost.

column1: When shall we use a genetic algorithm?
column4:
One global and four local optima. A hill-climber stops on whichever bump it started under; a population searches all five at once.
  • The search space has many local optima and gradient methods get trapped.
  • The objective function is not smooth, not differentiable, or is only available as a black box, so no derivative method applies.
  • The number of parameters is very large and exhaustive search is impossible.
  • The objective is noisy or stochastic.
  • A good-enough answer is acceptable: GA gives no optimality guarantee.
  • Do not use it when an exact algorithm exists, when a single evaluation of the fitness function is expensive, or when the answer must be provably optimal.
